components.name: Error page
components.description: The whole screen the user gets when the page could not be produced at all. It says what failed in their own terms, whether anything they did was saved, and gives one way back into an application whose navigation is not on this page.
components.when_to_use: The response is not the page that was asked for: a route that does not exist, a record this account may not open, a view that raised, a service that is down for maintenance, a session that had already expired when the request went out, or a navigation that never reached the server. It owns the viewport, because there is no working page left to put a message inside — this and auth-page are the only two screens in the system that do not render inside app-shell, which is exactly why the way back has to be drawn on the page itself. Reach for empty-state instead the moment the page around the failure still works: a register that came back with no rows, one panel whose fragment 500ed while the topbar, the sidebar and the rest of the record are still on screen, a table the account may not read inside a record it may. The test is what is still usable. If the user can still navigate, still read the record, still press Cancel, the failure is a region and it belongs to empty-state's error or permission variant; if the failure is the response, it is this. Getting it the wrong way round costs both ways — a full error screen thrown up because one dashboard tile timed out destroys eleven tiles that loaded fine, and an inline empty state standing in for a 500 leaves somebody on a page that looks like it worked.
rules: There is no shell on this page, and that is the whole design problem. No sidebar, no topbar, no breadcrumb, no search — app-shell's own when says error and auth screens are the two that do not use it, and the reason is not aesthetic: the shell reads the nav, the counts and the signed-in user out of context that the failing request may not have, and a sidebar of live counts drawn around a 500 claims data nobody could read. What replaces it has to be on the page: the wordmark is a real link to the console root, one primary action goes to the nearest thing that still works, and one secondary route reaches support. That is the entire navigation. No search box, no illustration, no third filled button — anything else, the support address and who is signed in included, is a line of footer text.

The support reference is the point of the 500 and it is the part that gets left out. It is tabular-nums, it is selectable, and it has a copy button beside it, because an error the user cannot quote is an error nobody can act on: "it broke this afternoon" and a screenshot of a graphite page is not a ticket anyone can search. The same string goes into the mailto subject on the secondary action, so the user who will not copy anything still gets it into the message. Generate the code in the handler and write it to the log before the page renders — a code minted in the browser matches nothing on the server, which is worse than no code at all because support will spend twenty minutes grepping for it.

Never put a traceback, an exception message or a query on this screen. IntegrityError: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "grn_number_key" tells the user nothing they can act on and tells everyone else the table names; Django's own 403 handler passes {{ exception }} into the template and it is whatever string the raising view happened to type, which is internal wording written for a log. Say what failed in the user's terms — the receipt did not post — and put the traceback in the log next to the reference code, which is what the reference code is for.

Say whether anything was saved. It is the question the user is actually asking and the one most error pages never answer, so they answer it themselves by re-keying a goods receipt that in fact posted. Write it as a fact — the receipt was not posted and nothing was written to the ledger — or, where the outcome genuinely cannot be known from the handler, say that and say how to check: open GRN-24-0912 in the register and look for a posting line. A cheerful "please try again" over an operation that half completed is how a plant ends up with two receipts against one challan.

The primary action is a GET forward to the nearest page that works, never history.back() and never a reload. Back returns to the request that just failed, and after a failed POST the browser offers to submit the form a second time, which is the same defect the page is apologising for. The nearest thing that works is usually the register the record sits in — back to goods receipts, not back to the home page, which throws away everything the user knew about where they were.

Never replace a page holding unsaved input with an error screen. A submit that fails leaves the form exactly where it is with an alert above it and the values still in the fields; swapping the whole document for an error page discards half an hour of a GRN somebody was keying line by line, and no amount of wording on the replacement makes that back. This screen is for a navigation that failed, not for a submission that failed — that is alert, over the form that is still there.

A 403 names the scope and the person who opens it, and the decision about whether to send a 403 at all is made per model. Access is granted by Nilesh Patil, Head of Procurement, not by "your administrator", or the page is a dead end wearing a sentence. But note what a 403 admits: it confirms the record exists. Where the existence of a record is itself confidential — a disciplinary file, a vendor under negotiation — the handler returns 404 and the user gets the not-found screen, because a 403 on that URL and a 404 on the next one is an enumeration oracle.

A 503 carries a Retry-After header and states a clock time, not "shortly". A window with a real end is the difference between a plant supervisor waiting and a plant supervisor phoning IT. Derive the countdown from a server-rendered <time datetime> rather than from a literal in the markup, or a machine whose clock is twenty minutes out reports a time nobody agrees with. Handle the overrun: past the stated time the screen says the work is running late and offers a check, never a negative number and never a counter frozen at zero. Nothing on this page reloads itself on a timer while somebody is reading it — reacting to the browser's own online event is a different thing, because that is a real signal rather than a guess.

The icon well stays graphite on every one of these screens — bg-zinc-200 with ring-1 ring-inset ring-zinc-300 — and the tone lives in the glyph and in the words, exactly as in alert and empty-state. No red field, no amber field, no -50 tint. A full page of red for a two-minute 502 makes a transient blip look like data loss, and a 404, which is nobody's fault and usually a stale link in an email, would then need a colour of its own to say it is not an emergency.

It is still a real document with a real outline: one <main>, one <h1>, and the h1 is the sentence rather than the number. "Error 500" as a heading is a status line promoted by font size — it belongs above the heading as an 11px label, small and muted, for the support call. Nothing is autofocused, because the browser already starts at the top of a freshly loaded document and an autofocused primary action turns a stray Enter left over from the last page into a navigation nobody asked for. Each snippet root here is a bounded preview — min-h-[560px] with rounded-xl border border-zinc-200 — so it renders in a box on this page; as a real page, drop the wrapper border and the rounded corners and put min-h-screen on the root. Unlike app-shell there is nothing to overflow-hidden: the error page scrolls with the document, which is what keeps a long 403 explanation and the actions under it reachable on a 720px laptop.

Announce it. A document load reads the <title>, so the title states the failure first — "Page not found · Konspec Operations" — and not the route that failed. An error screen swapped into the page by htmx is silent: nothing reloads, no title is read, and the h1 that explains everything is never spoken, so the user is left with their last announcement and a page that stopped responding. Put role="alert" on the message block in that case and move focus to the h1, which carries tabindex="-1" for exactly this, so the heading is read and the tab order restarts at the top of the message rather than wherever the destroyed page left it.

These are Django's handler templates and the three do not have the same powers. 404.html is rendered with the request and receives {{ request_path }}; 403.html receives {{ exception }}; 500.html is rendered by django.views.defaults.server_error as template.render() with no context and no request, so every variable on it resolves to an empty string and the incident id cannot be templated at all — either everything on that page is literal, or you register your own handler500 that renders with context. Tags still work in all three, so {% url %} and {% static %} are safe. Do not {% extends "base.html" %} on any of them: base.html reads the nav, the counts and the user out of context the failing request may not have, and a 500 template that raises while rendering drops the user on Django's own bare error page instead.

anatomy.description: The only navigation on the page: a real link to the console root, because the sidebar that normally carries that link is not rendered. It also says which system the user is looking at, which matters when the screen arrives from a bookmark.
size-12 rounded-full bg-zinc-200 with ring-1 ring-inset ring-zinc-300 round a size-5 glyph. Graphite on every variant; only the glyph takes a tone, and it is aria-hidden.
The code — Error 404, Error 503 — at text-[11px]/4 uppercase above the heading. Supporting detail for the support call, and never the heading itself.
The page's single h1, in the user's words rather than the protocol's, and the same sentence the <title> leads with. Carries tabindex="-1" so a swapped-in screen can move focus to it.
What it means for them, whether anything was saved, and what to do next, in a max-w-md line so it wraps to two or three readable lines instead of one wide one.

The thing support needs: the requested path on a 404, the incident id on a 500, the window on a 503. tabular-nums, selectable, break-all so it wraps at 390px, and with a copy button wherever it is a code somebody has to quote.
One primary anchor to the nearest page that works, and one secondary route — support, sign-in, a retry. They stack full width below sm.
Who is signed in and how to reach IT, as text. On a shared plant terminal the signed-in address is the line that tells somebody the session that failed was not theirs.

behaviour: It is the whole viewport and it renders outside app-shell, so the wordmark, the primary action and the support route are the only ways off the screen.

The primary action is a GET forward to a working page — the register the record sat in — never history.back() and never a reload, both of which return to the request that failed and can re-post a form.
The copy of the explanation states whether anything was written, or states that it cannot be known and gives the record to check.
A 500 shows a reference code and nothing about the internals. The code is selectable, has a copy button that confirms, and is repeated in the support mailto so it reaches the ticket either way.
A 503 counts down to a server-rendered clock time and switches to running-late plus a check action once that time passes. Nothing on the page reloads itself on a timer.

The offline screen retries in place: the action swaps to a busy state, the attempt count and the time of the last attempt update on the same screen, and the browser's online event enables the way back rather than navigating out from under whoever is reading.
A session that expired routes back to sign-in carrying the page the user was on as next, encoded, and never redirects on its own.
Below sm the two actions stack full width, the reference block wraps with break-all rather than scrolling sideways, and the header drops to the wordmark alone.
Loaded as a document the <title> announces it; swapped in by htmx it carries role="alert" and moves focus to the h1, because a swap reads no title and reloads nothing.
accessibility: One <main> and one <h1>, and the h1 is the sentence rather than the status code. The code sits above it as an 11px label, so the heading list reads "This page does not exist" and not "404".
The <title> states the failure first — "Page not found · Konspec Operations" — because on a full page load that string is the announcement and the h1 is only read once somebody navigates to it.
Nothing is autofocused on a document load. Focus starts where the browser puts it, at the top, and an autofocused primary action turns a keystroke left over from the previous page into a navigation.

Where the screen arrives by htmx swap, the message block takes role="alert" and focus moves to the h1 carrying tabindex="-1". A swap reads no title, so without both the page silently stops being the page the user was on.
role="alert" belongs only on the swapped case. On a freshly loaded document it competes with the title being read and duplicates it.
The glyph is decoration and is aria-hidden, including alert-circle on the 500. What makes the screen an error is the wording; colour is not available to everyone reading it and is not a message.

The reference is selectable text in the page, never an image and never a title attribute. The copy button carries a name that changes to confirm and writes its confirmation into an sr-only aria-live="polite" line, because a swapped icon announces nothing.
The countdown on the maintenance screen is plain text and not a live region. A two-hour window announced every thirty seconds buries every other thing on the page.

Every action is a real <a> or <button> with a name that says where it goes — "Back to goods receipts", "Sign in again" — reachable by Tab and wearing focus-visible:outline-3 focus-visible:outline-offset-2. No rings anywhere, because forced-colours mode drops every box-shadow and these users are already having a bad afternoon.

components.name: Dashboard
components.description: The screen a user lands on after signing in: a strip of figures, one plot, and the queues that are actually waiting for them. Every part of it already exists — this entry is the composition and the rules that govern it.
components.when_to_use: The first screen after sign-in, and the only screen in the application whose job is to be left. It exists for orientation and triage — what changed since yesterday, what is on fire, what is waiting on you — and it is finished the moment somebody clicks out of it into the record they came to work on. It is not for analysis. A screen with one question rather than eight is a chart in a card with the figures under it and no strip above it, and the moment somebody wants to sort by vendor, narrow to a plant and work down the result, they want index-page, which is where the strip and every queue on this page link to. Reach for list-detail instead when the queue is the whole day's work and each record is decided and left behind — a QC hold run, an approval run of forty — because that layout keeps the queue on screen and this one hands it away on the first click. The test is whether anybody has ever done a second thing here without navigating: if they have, the screen is a register with figures over it and it belongs in index-page. A dashboard that shows a buyer four charts and no list of what needs approving today has failed at this component's job whatever else it does.
rules: The page renders inside app-shell, in <main>, like every other signed-in screen. The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box. As a real page, drop the wrapper's height and border and keep the mx-auto max-w-[1600px] gutter, which is the one app-shell's own main column already uses.

The order of the regions is the component. Figures, then the queues, then the plot. Put the plots second and on a 1280px laptop the list of what needs approving today lands below the fold, so the buyer scrolls past four charts every morning to reach the nine records that are the reason they opened the page — and after a fortnight they stop opening it and work out of the register instead. Nothing on a dashboard is ranked by how much room it takes; it is ranked by whether somebody has to act on it today.

Four figures is the ceiling on the strip, and it is a ceiling on meaning rather than on width. Everything on a dashboard is somebody's most important number, so a strip of four becomes a strip of seven without anyone deciding to, and at seven nobody reads any of them. The fifth metric is a request to demote one of the first four. This is stat-card's rule and it is restated here because the strip is where the pressure lands.

The greeting is not the h1. A heading outline whose top entry is "Good morning, Akshay" is identical on every dashboard the application will ever have and says nothing about which of eleven screens somebody is on. The greeting is a line above the title, the h1 names the desk, and the line under it carries the scope and the time the figures were read.

The as-of time is written once, on the page head, and never on the tiles. Four copies of 09:12 is four chances for the strip to disagree with itself, and the scope — three plants, one shift, this cost centre — is the same for every figure on the page. A figure nobody can reconcile against the register gets reconciled by hand exactly once, disagrees by a lakh, and is never trusted again.

A queue is a card with a count in its header, at most five rows, and a link to the register that holds the rest. Five is where a list stops being read at a glance and starts being a register drawn without a header; the sixth row is a request for index-page. Every row is a real link into a record, using table/linked-rows' stretched anchor, so the whole row is the target and the URL is copyable, openable in a tab and reachable by middle click.

The queue header link says how many and what they are. "All 9" is nine of what — the visible text carries the count and sr-only text finishes the sentence, because a dashboard with four queues is otherwise four links called All in the tab order.

A page made of regions that each load separately must reserve their heights before any of them answer. Every region has a known shape before it has data — a strip of four tiles, a five-row queue, a plot box of h-64 — so each one waits as a skeleton at its own measurements rather than as a spinner in a collapsed box. Eight regions resolving one at a time into boxes that grow on arrival walks the whole page up and down eight times, and the click somebody aimed at an approval lands on the row below it.

A region's retry targets the region, never the page. Inside a composed screen there is exactly one data-kui and it is the dashboard's, so chart/failed's hx-target="closest [data-kui]" swaps the entire dashboard out on a chart that did not answer — including the three regions that did. Give every independently-loading region an id and target that.

Write real hx-* attributes on the regions. htmx never processes hx-* that Alpine created after load, so a bound :hx-get inside an x-for is silently inert; a region that loads itself does it with hx-get and hx-trigger="load" written into the markup.

A period control rebases the figures and the plot and must not touch the queues. "Waiting on your approval" has no period — it is what is true now — and a control that appears to scope the whole page while three of its regions ignore it is worse than no control at all. Put the period over the regions it governs and say in the card what it governs.

Rebasing moves the figure, the magnitude of the delta and the clause naming what the delta is measured against, together, from one record. Move the figure and leave the clause and the page is not stale, it is false: "1,712 vs. July" is a sentence nobody catches because both halves look like data.

A second role is a second page, not the first page with things hidden. A storekeeper's dashboard has different figures, different queues and different links, and the buyer's committed-value plot is absent rather than empty — a storekeeper has no committed-value trend to read and never will. Rendering one page and hiding half of it leaves every hidden region in the DOM, in the tab order on the day somebody gets the class wrong, and it makes the storekeeper's screen a worse version of somebody else's instead of their own.

The exceptions band sits above the figures and is capped at three. Something earns a place there when it is actionable by this person today, time-bound, and not already counted in the strip; a fourth exception is a queue and belongs in a card with a count and a link. Nothing in the band dismisses, because dismissing it does not fix the record and it is back tomorrow — the way to clear an exception is to work it.

The band is alert's shape and it is neutral. White card, zinc border, colour only in the icon. A full-width red field across the top of a dashboard shouts louder than the twelve genuinely overdue orders it is describing, and the moment one region is red the graphite ones read as switched off.

Zero, nothing yet and could not read are three different tiles and a dashboard draws all three in its first week. Zero GRNs posted is a fact and renders as 0. A metric that does not exist yet renders as an em dash with one line saying when it starts. A read that failed renders as an em dash with a reason and a retry, and never as a zero — somebody sees zero QC holds, stops checking, and the line runs a shift on material that was never released.

A first-week dashboard is not empty-state/all-clear. Nothing has been cleared; nothing has happened. All-clear is the reward for emptying a queue and printing it over a queue that has never held anything is the one empty state that reads as a lie.

At 390px the strip and the plot both become a different thing rather than a narrower one, and neither is invented here: the four tiles become stat-card/dense — one card, four cells, two across — and the twelve-month plot keeps its box and drops labels through chart/responsive's autoSkip rather than rotating or abbreviating them. What this entry decides is which of those the dashboard picks and in what order the regions come, which is queues before plot at every width.

The dashboard takes page-header's title and meta without its white band. A dashboard has no record, no status pill and usually no primary action, so a full-bleed band across the column draws a rule under a title and nothing else. Where one does carry an action — New purchase order on a buyer's screen — it is page-header/default unchanged, band and all.

anatomy.description: The greeting line, the one h1 naming the desk, and the line under it carrying the scope and the as-of time. page-header's title block without its band.
Optional, above the figures, at most three alert cards. Actionable today, time-bound, not already counted in the strip, and never dismissible.
stat-card's grid — grid-cols-1, sm:grid-cols-2, xl:grid-cols-4, gap-3 — holding at most four tiles, each an anchor to the register behind its number.
A card: header with the count and a link to the register, then at most five rows, each a stretched anchor into one record. The working half of the page and the half that decides whether it gets used.
The count as visible text with sr-only words finishing the sentence, so four queues are not four links called All.
One chart, last, in a card of its own. It reads its colours out of the legend the way chart requires; the legend is markup, so it is present in every state the card can be in.
Any of the above as an independently-loaded block: its own id, its own hx-get, its own skeleton at its own measurements, and its own retry targeting that id.
button-group/segmented in the header of the region it governs, never floating over a page whose queues ignore it.
The line under the plot naming the source and the period. A figure with no stated period is a figure nobody can check.

behaviour: Every tile and every queue row navigates. There is no state on this page worth keeping, so nothing is worked in place and nothing is edited here.
Regions resolve independently and in any order. Each holds its own height from first paint, so the page does not move as they land and a click aimed at a row lands on that row.
A region that failed keeps the page. Its retry swaps that region by id and a second failure lands back in the same box rather than replacing a working dashboard with an error screen.
Changing the period rebases the figures, their deltas and the comparison clauses, and mutates the existing chart with update(). The queues do not move, because a queue has no period.
The new figure for a period is read for that period and never divided out of the one already on screen. 148 orders in thirty days does not become 34.5 in a week.
The exceptions band appears only when there is something in it. An empty band is a heading over nothing and teaches people to stop looking at that part of the screen.

A queue that empties draws empty-state/all-clear with the evidence in it — how many were cleared and by when — and only when no filter is in force. A queue that has never held anything draws nothing-yet instead.
Below sm the strip restacks and the queues become one column in DOM order, queues before plot. Nothing scrolls sideways at 390px.

The plot thins its axis as its box narrows and thickens it again when the box widens, which also covers the sidebar expanding and the card moving from a three-column grid to one — neither of which is a window resize.
accessibility: One <main> and one <h1>, and the h1 names the screen rather than greeting the user. Every region below it is an h2 and anything inside a region is an h3.

Each region is a <section> with an accessible name, which makes it a landmark. On a dashboard that is the point: the landmark list is how somebody skips past four figures and a plot to the queue they came for, and it is the only navigation this page has.
The figure strip's heading is sr-only where the page head has already named the scope. A named region with no visible heading still needs a real heading element for the outline to hang off.

Each tile is a dt and dd pair inside a dl, so the label and the figure are one unit in the accessibility tree. The delta arrow is aria-hidden and the sign is real text, so the tile still reads with the icon and the colour both gone.

A queue row is one stretched anchor whose accessible name is the row — the document number, the vendor and the figure — and nothing else in the row is focusable, so Tab walks a queue one record at a time.
The queue header link carries its count as text and finishes its sentence with sr-only words naming the queue, because a dashboard of four queues is otherwise four adjacent links called All.
A loading region carries aria-busy and one sr-only role="status" naming what is coming. Its grey blocks are aria-hidden: eight rectangles announced one at a time is noise standing in for a wait.

The period control is a radiogroup and its aria-checked is the announcement. There is no live region over the strip. stat-card/period is right to make one tile a role="status" with aria-atomic, and it is wrong for a page of them — four figures, four comparison clauses and a chart summary read out on every press is a control nobody uses twice.

A failed region says so as ordinary text in the region. No role="alert" in static markup: it fires on first paint whether or not anything just went wrong, and the swap that put the region there is what announces.

A no-data figure spells out "No data" as sr-only text beside the aria-hidden em dash, and a failed one says "Not read". An em dash resolves to nothing, and a silent tile is indistinguishable from a missing one.

The plot canvas is role="img" with a sentence naming the shape, and it repeats its numbers as an sr-only table. A canvas has no text in it, so without one of the two a screen reader gets nothing at all.
Focus is an outline and never a ring, on the tiles, the queue rows and the retries alike. A ring compiles to a box-shadow and forced-colours mode drops every box-shadow.

components.name: Index page
components.description: The register screen as a whole page: the breadcrumb and the one h1, the saved views, the filter band, the toolbar that becomes a selection toolbar, the table, the pager, and the states the page as a whole can be in.
components.when_to_use: The front door of a module, as a whole page — the purchase order register, the GRN register, the indent queue, the vendor list, a ledger. The line that decides most screens is the one against data-table, and it is the line between a region and a page. data-table is the panel: one array of records with a search box, sortable headers, column visibility, selection, totals and a pager, all inside a single bordered card, and it is what you drop into a tab, a dialog, a dashboard column or the body of this layout. This entry is everything around that panel — the trail and the one h1, the count line that answers what the page is showing, the saved views a buyer opens every morning, the filter band in the header and what it becomes below sm, where the primary action lives and why it does not move, the status tabs over the top, the selection toolbar that takes the band over, and the two different nothings a register can be in. Reach for data-table when the register is one region of a screen that has other regions; reach for this when the register is the screen — and then the panel inside it is data-table's markup with its toolbar dropped, because this page has already taken the search and the filters up into the header band and two search boxes on one screen is how a PO number gets typed into the wrong one. Against list-detail: that is a queue worked one record at a time, keyboard-driven, the queue never leaving the screen, and the test is whether the next record matters. On a register it does not — a register is scanned, sorted, filtered and acted on in bulk, and it wants the whole width for the columns being compared rather than a third of it for a queue nobody is walking. Against table: that is rows and a sortable header and nothing else, no page around them, and it is what both this and data-table are built out of. A screen that creates or edits one of these records is form-page.
rules: This is a composition and not a new register. The panel in every variant is data-table's markup — the same sortable header button, the same chevron, the same status pill, the same select-all bound with x-effect, the same range-and-total footer — and the page's own contribution is what sits around it: which regions exist, in what order, what the band does when a selection appears, and which states the whole screen can be in.

When the page carries the filter band, the panel drops its toolbar. data-table puts search and filters inside the panel because the panel is the whole component; a page puts them in the header band because they also drive the count under the h1, the saved view, the tab counts and the export. Keep both and the screen has two search boxes over one list, and the one somebody types into is the one they happen to be nearest.

One h1 and it is the page's, and it survives every state — the selection toolbar, the empty register, the first paint. The band gives up the trail, the count line, the filter row and the action cluster when a selection takes it over, and it keeps the h1, because a heading outline that loses its top-level heading when five rows are ticked is a document that changes its title while you are reading it.

The primary action lives in the header band and does not move between states. It is the page's action, not an answer to what the list currently shows, so it is in the same corner on a full register, a filtered one and an empty one. The empty block underneath never repeats it as a second filled button — it offers the bordered alternative and a link, and the fill stays where it always is.

The empty block under a filter offers no create at all. That is data-table's rule and it survives at page level with one clarification worth writing down, because the two look like a contradiction: the header band's primary stays, because it is the page's action and it is there on every state of the screen, while the block in the middle of an empty result offers only ways back out of the query. A create button drawn as the answer to "nothing matched" is how the same order gets raised twice.

A register nobody has used and a register whose query matched nothing are different screens and must not look the same. The first has no toolbar, no header row and no pager — every one of them is chrome describing an absence — and it says something factual about why it is empty, a commissioning date or an opening balance. The second keeps the filter band and the chips, because the query is the thing that has to be undone, and it names what is in force.

Below sm the whole filter band is a drawer, and the count of what is in force goes on its trigger. Five selects stacked on a phone is a screen of chrome above the first row, and a phone that hides the filters without saying how many are on is a register that looks wrong and cannot be diagnosed. The chips stay on screen at every width — they are the answer to what is applied, and they are the one thing that must not go into the drawer with the controls.

Both copies of a filter — the row at sm and up, the drawer below it — bind to the same state and are both in the DOM, with the inactive one display:none so it is out of the tab order as well as off the screen. Two independent copies drift the moment somebody rotates a tablet.

Saved views are the page's memory and they are not tabs. Each one is a stored query somebody named, one is current, and the moment a filter moves off the saved definition the page has to say so and offer three answers — save into this view, save as a new one, reset. Keep the changed filters silently under the saved name and tomorrow morning "My open POs" is not what was saved, and nobody can tell whether the view or the data changed.

Status tabs over a register are a filter wearing a tab shape, so there is one panel and it is relabelled rather than five panels holding five copies of the same table. Switching a tab returns to page one and changes the total, and the counts on the tabs are the same query with the status predicate removed — they narrow when the search or the filters narrow, or the tab labelled 34 opens onto 6 rows and the number becomes something nobody trusts.

The count line under the h1 is a role="status" in the document from first paint, and it is where the page answers "what am I looking at". Filters, tabs and search all write to it. A second live region on the panel talks over it.

Density and column choice belong to the person, not to the visit. They are the two settings a buyer who is on this screen all day changes once, so they are persisted per user and the page comes back the way it was left; a register that resets to comfortable on every navigation is one somebody sets four times a day and then stops setting.

The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box, and the filter drawer is absolute inset-0 against that frame. As a real page it renders inside app-shell's <main>: drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the mx-auto max-w-[1600px] gutter on the band and on the body so the h1 and the panel line up, let the sticky band stick to the shell's scrolling column, and make the drawer fixed inset-0.

anatomy.description: page-header's <header> inside <main>: white, edge to edge across the column, over a border-zinc-200 rule, its content in the same mx-auto max-w-[1600px] gutter the body uses. Never overflow-hidden — the column menu and the view menu open out of it.
The breadcrumb above the title, from breadcrumbs, present here only if the topbar does not carry one. Two crumbs on a top-level register is ceremony; a module root has none at all.

The one h1, and under it a role="status" line saying what the page is showing — how many of how many, and what they are worth. Figures take tabular-nums so the band does not reflow as a filter narrows.
A <nav> of named queries under the title, one carrying aria-current, plus the strip that appears when the current view has been filtered away from.
The second row inside the band: page-header's filter row — a <form role="search">, the narrow selects, and below sm a Filters trigger carrying the active count.
One removable chip per filter in force, with Clear all as a link beside them. Visible at every width, including when the controls have gone into the drawer.
Optional, joined to the band's bottom edge with -mb-px. A filter in a tab shape: one register panel below, relabelled as the selection moves.

What the band becomes when rows are ticked: the same h1 element, a tinted count pill beside it, the scope written into the count line's own role="status", the actions that apply and the way out. The trail, the action cluster and the filter row give way to it.
data-table's panel with its toolbar dropped — the sortable header, the rows, the card list below md, and the footer. Rounded, bordered, on the page ground.
pagination's footer inside the panel: the range, the total and the page position, ends disabled rather than removed so the control keeps its width.
What fills the panel when the count is zero, in one of two shapes that must not be confused — nothing ever raised here, or nothing matching this query.
Below sm, drawer's bottom sheet holding the same controls the row holds at sm and up, with Reset and a button naming the count it would show.

behaviour: The filter band narrows the list underneath and never navigates. Every control applies on change, the chips rebuild, the count line under the h1 rewrites, and the pager returns to page one — page 4 of a two-row result shows nothing.
The primary action is in the same place on every state of the page. Nothing about the list moves it, hides it or promotes a second filled button beside it.

Selecting rows swaps the band's trail, action cluster and filter row for the selection toolbar in place, keeps the same h1 element, and rewrites the count line rather than adding a second one. Nothing stacks below the band and no row under it moves down.

The selection is an array of record ids on the page root, so it survives sorting, filtering and paging, and the toolbar states the scope as well as the size. Pressing Next is guarded rather than disabled, so the button keeps focus and the count is still there when the new page lands.
Ticking every row on the page is not selecting the query. Selecting everything that matches is a second, deliberate act with its own count, and touching any row afterwards drops the claim.
Switching a status tab returns to page one, changes the total in the footer and rewrites the count line. The trail, the h1 and the actions do not change, because it is the same register either way.

A saved view sets every filter at once. While the current filters differ from the saved ones the view reads as modified and the strip offers save, save-as and reset; picking another view discards the difference the same way Reset does.

Below sm the filter controls move into a drawer whose trigger carries the number in force, and the chips stay on the page. The drawer closes on Escape and on its own Show button, and focus returns to the trigger.
Density and the column set change the rows in place without a fetch. Hiding a column drops its header, its cells and the same field from the card layout below md.

Nothing on this page scrolls sideways at 390px. The table restacks into cards, the filter row becomes a drawer, and the only region allowed to scroll horizontally is the status tab row, because a second line of tabs reads as a different control.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1>, and the band is a <header> inside <main> rather than the banner landmark — the banner belongs to the topbar. Regions below the h1 are h2.

The count line is a role="status" rendered with the page, so a filter, a tab or a search writes a change into a region that was already there. A live region that arrives with its message already in it is announced to nobody.
The filter band is a <form role="search"> holding a labelled input, and each chip's remove button names the filter it drops — "Remove the filter Overdue", never "Remove".

Saved views are a <nav> with its own name and the current one carries aria-current="true". They are not a tablist, because there are no panels to switch, and not a radiogroup, because each view is somewhere you go and every one of them should be reachable with Tab rather than behind an arrow-key contract.

The status tabs are the tabs component in full — role="tablist" with a name, aria-selected, aria-controls, roving tabindex, arrow, Home and End all preventing default — over a single role="tabpanel" whose aria-labelledby is bound to the selected tab. One panel, relabelled, because all five tabs draw the same table of a different subset.
Sortable headers are buttons inside <th scope="col"> and the <th> carries aria-sort. The chevron is decoration; aria-sort is the answer.

Every row checkbox is labelled with its document number and the select-all says how many rows on this page it covers. The select-all is a native box carrying the indeterminate property, which is already mapped to mixed, so nothing writes aria-checked.
The selection toolbar keeps the same h1 element it replaced the rest of the band around, and its count and scope are one role="status" so a page change re-announces what the selection now spans.

A pager button that is guarded rather than disabled still says so: it carries aria-disabled while it is at a limit, so the keyboard user is told the press will do nothing instead of pressing it twice, and it keeps focus and its place in the tab order the way a disabled button cannot.

A register still loading is aria-busy on the panel with one sr-only role="status" naming what is loading, and the grey rows are aria-hidden — otherwise a screen reader walks twenty-five empty cells and is never told why.

The empty block's heading is an h2 under the page's h1, so an empty register still has an outline, and its text says which nothing this is rather than leaving the user to guess between a filter, a permission and a failure.

The filter drawer is a role="dialog" with aria-modal, a focus trap, Escape closing it and focus returning to the trigger it opened from, and the trigger names the count it carries in its own text rather than in a title.

components.name: Record page
components.description: The screen for one record: the band that identifies it and says what state it is in, a strip of the figures that matter, and the sections of detail below it — line items, approvals, documents, activity — carrying only the actions the record's current state allows.
components.when_to_use: One record opened to be read and then decided on — PO-2026-0418, GRN-4821, a vendor, an indent. The line against form-page is the reason the reader came: they came to change the record, so form-page, and its readonly variant is that same edit screen showing its own fields in read mode while nobody is editing; they came to read the record and then decide, so this. It is not a form with the inputs turned off. The figures are summarised rather than listed field by field, the line items are a table with a total rather than an editable grid, and half of this page is regions a form does not have at all — the approval trail, the documents, the activity, the linked records. A record with four facts and no sections is form-page/readonly, and building it here is ceremony. page-header is the top block of this page and not the page: reach for page-header when the band on its own is what you are placing, over a register or over a form, and reach for this when the band plus the summary plus the sections is the screen. tabs is the switching mechanism the tabs variant here uses and it is a component rather than a layout — a tab row over something that is not one record is tabs and not this. And where the next record matters as much as this one — a QC hold queue, an approval run somebody clears before the shift ends — the screen is list-detail, because there the queue never leaves the screen; a record page is what you open when you arrived from a register and the register can wait. The register itself is data-table.
rules: This renders inside app-shell, as the whole of <main>. The band and the body share one gutter and that is the only thing they have to agree on: it is written here as mx-auto max-w-6xl because a record reads better bounded than a register does, and if the application uses the register gutter of max-w-[1600px] then both the band and the body take that instead. Mismatch them and the h1 sits a few pixels off the first card.

The summary strip is card/stats' divided footer, not a row of stat-cards. A record's figures are parts of one total — ordered, received, invoiced, balance — and they add up, which is exactly what four independent tiles with gaps between them say they do not. stat-card also carries a delta, and a single record has no previous period to compare against, so three quarters of that component would be drawn empty.

Sections are stacked down the page until there are enough of them to be worth switching. Stacked, the whole record prints in one pass, Ctrl+F finds all of it, and nobody has to remember which tab the GRN was under. Tabs earn their place past about four sections or where one of them is expensive to render, and then the tabs variant is the shape — never both, because a page with three stacked sections and a tab row over two more has no answer to where anything is.

Line items are table's markup unchanged: the same header cells, the same tabular-nums and text-right on the figures, the same total in a <tfoot>, and the same stacked cards below md. The one thing this page adds is that the table is read-only. A record page that makes its lines editable has become form-page/line-items wearing the wrong header, and the two then disagree about what a line is.

An action the state has removed is gone, not disabled. A disabled Record GRN on a cancelled order is a dead Tab stop that explains nothing and invites the press it will refuse; the banner is what carries the reason, and the button is simply not drawn. Disable a control only while its own request is in flight — that is the case where the control still exists.

Cancelled and On hold are not in the locked five, and there is no sixth dot. On hold takes Approved's amber-500, because its meaning is exactly the one amber has: waiting on someone. Cancelled takes Draft's zinc-400, the inert shade: the record is over, and neither of the other candidates says that. Emerald would say it finished well, and zinc-500 would say it is still live. Both words are in the status table now — this entry was written before they were, and reached the same two answers on its own.

The rail here is first in the DOM and placed second by the grid, which is the reverse of form-page/side-rail. The reason that entry puts its rail last is that the rail is context beside a form the user is filling, and the tab order should be the form and then the context. This rail is the record's identity and standing, it is what a phone reader wants above the lines rather than below them, and it holds nothing focusable at all — so there is no tab order to get wrong, and lg:col-start-2 lg:row-start-1 is free. Put one control in it and that stops being true; move the control into the page.

One h1 and it is the record's own identity — the order number, the vendor's name, the batch code. Not "Purchase order", which names the register this came from and is the same string on 1,438 pages. Everything below the band is h2, and a subsection inside a section is h3.

A deep link to a tab selects that panel and does not move focus. The page has just loaded, so the browser is already at the top of the document and the reader has not asked to be anywhere else; pulling focus into the panel at boot skips the band that says which record they are looking at. Focus moves on a tab the reader pressed, and on nothing else.

A figure the reader may not see is absent, not blanked. No dots, no em dash, no disabled column toggle — the Rate and Value columns are simply not in the table, the money cells are not in the summary strip, and one sentence under the table says which scope is closed and who opens it. A blanked cell is a claim that there is a number there and you are not important enough for it, which is the same information leak wearing a courtesy.

A before-and-after in the activity trail needs words as well as the strike-through. line-through is announced by some screen readers as deleted text and by most as nothing at all, so the old value is followed by an sr-only "changed to" and the arrow is decorative. Without it the entry reads as "Promised delivery 02 Aug 2026 22 Aug 2026", which is two dates and no direction.

On a record that is with the reader for approval, the approval section moves to the top and the decision lives inside it. An Approve button in the band is pressed before the record has been read — it is the first thing the eye lands on and it is one press from done. Beside the trail it is one press from done only after the reader has scrolled past who has already signed and why.

anatomy.description: page-header's record variant unchanged: a <header> inside <main>, white, edge to edge over a border-zinc-200 rule, holding the breadcrumb, the one h1, the status pill and the actions. Never overflow-hidden — the action menu opens out of the bottom of it.

badge's locked pill beside the title, and the qualifier that says why anybody cares — "4 of 9 lines received" — outside the shape, because a pill that grows to a phrase stops matching the column this record occupies on the register.

One white panel divided into two to four cells, each a term and a figure: what was ordered, what has arrived, what has been billed, what is left. Two columns below sm and four from sm up, with the rules drawn as borders on the cells rather than by divide-x, which puts a rule down the left edge of the third cell the moment the grid wraps.
A card per region, h2 in its header, and the header carries the count and the one action that belongs to that region. Cards are the sections and dividers are the subsections; they do not nest.
table's markup inside a card with no body padding, the total in a <tfoot>, and the same rows as stacked cards below md. Read-only.

An <ol> on marker's rail: who signed, when, who it is with now, and who has not been reached yet. The rail stays zinc-200 the whole way down — colouring the part above the current step turns it into a progress bar whose total is written nowhere.
attachment's list in read mode: type, name, size, who attached it and when, and Download without Remove. A control that cannot act is a control that should not be drawn.
The audit region, newest first, grouped by day under an h3 per day, with the changed fields shown as an old value and a new one.

The indents, receipts and invoices hanging off this one, as a wrapped list of real links. This is the region that has no equivalent on a form and the commonest reason somebody opens the record at all.
alert's neutral card above the sections when the state needs explaining — cancelled, on hold, superseded. White, zinc border, colour only in the icon, and it says who did it and when.
The cluster in the band, ordered so the primary is last, holding only what this state allows. What the state has removed is absent rather than disabled.

behaviour: The band does not stick. On a record long enough that the actions leave the screen, the phone arrangement puts them in a bar at the foot and the desktop one repeats nothing — a record is read top to bottom and the decision is taken at the end of it.

The summary strip restacks from four cells to two below sm and never scrolls sideways. The figures are tabular-nums, so a receipt posted against the record does not change the width of the column it sits in.

Line items scroll with the page. The table becomes stacked cards below md carrying the same fields in the same order, and the total is repeated as a strip under them rather than dropped — the total is why the screen was opened.

Switching tabs changes the panel and nothing above it. The breadcrumb, the h1, the status and the summary strip are the record, not a view of it, so they stay put; the tab id is written into the query string with replaceState, so a reload lands on the same panel and Back leaves the record rather than undoing a tab.

A record that is awaiting the reader's own approval reorders: the approval section comes first, its current step is expanded, and the decision controls are inside it. Every other reader sees the same section in its ordinary place, closed, with no controls in it.

Actions follow the state. Cancelled keeps Print and Duplicate and loses Amend and Record GRN entirely; on hold keeps Release hold and loses Amend; closed keeps Print and Duplicate. Nothing is drawn disabled and nothing is drawn that the server would refuse.

A field the account may not read is not rendered — no column, no cell, no placeholder — and the sentence under the region says which scope is closed and who grants it. The rest of the record renders normally; a permission on one field does not blank the page.

Activity is newest first and grouped by day. Field changes carry the old value and the new one; entries older than the retained window are a link to the archive rather than an endless scroller on a record page.

At 390px the rail and the tab row both become something else: the rail's facts fold into the band's definition list and the summary strip, and the tab row becomes a native select with each section a real <section> and no tab roles anywhere.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1> in the band, every section an h2 and every day heading in the activity trail an h3. The heading outline is how somebody skims a record they did not open, and on this page it is the only navigation there is.

The band is a <header> inside <main>, which makes it a section header rather than the banner landmark. The banner belongs to the shell's topbar, and a second one gives a landmark list nobody can navigate.

The breadcrumb is a <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"> with aria-current="page" on the last crumb, which is a <span> and not a link. Its name differs from the sidebar's, or the landmark list holds two identical rows.

The status pill carries the word as well as the dot, and the dot is aria-hidden. A pill whose only content is colour is an empty element to a screen reader and an unreadable one to anybody who cannot separate red from grey.

Where tabs are used they carry the whole pattern from tabs — role="tablist" with a name, aria-selected and aria-controls out, aria-labelledby back, roving tabindex, and arrow, Home and End all preventing default. A row of styled buttons promises that arrows switch panels and then nothing does.

The summary strip is a <dl>: a figure with a heading above it is two paragraphs that happen to be adjacent, and read on its own "₹8,16,400" is a number with no word attached to it. Two <dd> under one <dt> is how the figure and its qualifier stay one unit.
A before-and-after in the activity trail says "changed to" in sr-only text between the two values. The strike-through and the arrow are decoration and neither of them is a direction.
The approval trail is an <ol> because the order is the record, not the layout, and every mark in the rail column is aria-hidden — the dates and the words are what say who signed and when.
The permission sentence is prose in the region it applies to, not a title attribute and not a disabled control. There is nothing to hover on a phone, and a dead Tab stop explains nothing.

At 390px the section select is a real <select> with a real label and no tab roles at all, and each section is a <section> with its own heading. Giving a select role="tab" breaks the one thing it was brought in to do.

components.name: Approval inbox
components.description: The screen an approver lives in: everything waiting on their signature in one queue, the record beside it, and the decision on a rail where the hand already is. Deciding removes the record from the queue and lands the user on the next one without a reload.
components.when_to_use: The screen an approver works in — purchase orders above a buyer's limit, goods receipts short against the challan, rate contracts, credit notes — worked one after another until the queue is empty. The boundary that decides most screens is the one against list-detail, and it is the difference between reading a queue and deciding one. list-detail is right when the queue is read: the selection moves, the detail follows, and nothing is written; its qc-hold variant is a work-one-at-a-time queue and it is the model this entry is built on, so take that one whenever the screen has no write on it. Reach for this the moment a decision is taken on the record, because a decision drags behind it the whole apparatus list-detail deliberately has none of: an action rail with the decision on it, a reason required before a refusal can be sent, the record leaving the queue when it is acted on, an in-flight state and a refusal from the server, an approval limit that can put a record beyond this user entirely, delegation, and a queue whose length changes under the user while they are looking at it. Against index-page: that is the register — every record of a kind, sorted, filtered, searched — and it is where somebody goes to find one specific order rather than to work through all of them. An approver asking what happened to PO-2026-0418 last March goes to the register; an approver clearing today's work comes here, and the two are different screens even when they list the same rows. Against alert-dialog: that is a component this screen uses rather than a screen of its own — the reason a rejection asks for, the confirmation a bulk approval takes, the refusal the server sends back — and it is composed into this layout rather than redrawn inside it. A screen that creates or edits one of these records is form-page.
rules: This renders inside app-shell, in its main column. The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[660px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box, and the confirmation dialogs are absolute inset-0 against that frame. As a real page: drop the wrapper height and border, put h-screen overflow-hidden on <body>, and make the dialogs fixed inset-0.

Act and advance is the whole component and everything else follows from it. The user reads, decides, and lands on the next record without a reload and without going back to a list. That means four things have to be decided together and none of them can be left to the browser: where focus goes when the record under it stops existing, what the live region says, what happens to the item that was just acted on, and what the screen does when the queue empties under the user's hands.

Focus lands on the record region, not back on the queue and not on the button that was pressed. Leaving it on the button is the tempting answer — the rail survives the swap, so Approve is still under the finger and the next approval is one Enter away — and it is exactly why it is wrong: a held Enter approves four orders nobody read, and these are signatures. Sending it back to the queue option is no better, because the keyboard user then has to walk the whole record again to reach the decision. Focus goes to the detail region, whose accessible name is the record heading, so the new record is announced by the mechanism that already exists and there is deliberately one Tab between the user and the next Approve.

Focus announces which record is now open; the live region announces what happened to the last one. Those are two different sentences and only one of them is deliverable by focus, which is why this layout has both and why they must not overlap. The region says the outcome and the count — "PO-2026-0418 approved. 6 left in your inbox" — and never repeats the record name that the focus move is already reading out.

Nothing is optimistic. An approval is a server write with legal weight, so the row does not leave the queue and the pill does not change until the server has said it committed. Drawing Approved on the click and reconciling afterwards means a screen that has told a plant head they signed something they did not, and there is no toast that unsays it. While the write is in flight the record stays exactly where it is, the rail goes aria-busy, the pressed button keeps its width and says what it is doing, and the other decisions on that record are disabled — the queue itself stays live, because taking the arrow keys away for the length of a slow request is taking the session away.

A refusal is said where the record is, and where the record is depends on the refusal. If the order is still in front of the user — it was amended under them, a budget check failed — the refusal belongs on that record, above the rail. If the order has already left their inbox because somebody else approved it first, there is no record left to hang it on, so it goes into a page-level alert strip under the header and stays until it is dismissed. Both say whether anything was written, because "it failed" and "it failed and nothing was written" are different facts and only one of them is safe to press again.

A refusal needs a reason and that is why it cannot be optimistic in any form. The reason is part of the write, not a note attached afterwards: a rejection with no reason returns the order to a buyer who has nothing to change, and a screen that removes the row on the click and then finds the reason field empty has already lied to the queue. Reject opens alert-dialog's reason shape — one required field, the confirm genuinely disabled until it is filled — and the row leaves only when the POST carrying that reason has come back.

An item above this user's limit has no Approve button at all. A greyed-out one with no explanation is the most-reported fault in every internal application there has ever been, and aria-disabled with a described reason is only the right answer where the user could plausibly clear the condition. Nobody clears their own approval limit, so the honest rail says what the limit is, what the order is worth, who it goes to instead, and offers escalation as its primary — the action that is actually available is the one on the rail.

Delegation is a property of the session, not a choice made per record, so it is stated once in a strip under the page header and repeated in the verb on the button — "Approve as Nilesh Patil". The limit travels with the authority rather than with the person: a delegate approving for a plant head approves up to the plant head's limit, not their own, and the rail says whose limit is in force. What is written is both names, because an audit that records only the delegate cannot answer who was accountable and one that records only the principal cannot answer who was at the keyboard.

Bulk approval is offered by the screen, never assembled by ticking rows in the queue. The queue is a listbox and a listbox is one Tab stop, so a checkbox inside an option is unreachable — that is list-detail's rule and it holds here. It is also the better design: the server is what knows which items are alike, so the offer is made from the record the user is already reading — same vendor, same rate contract, all inside the limit — and the confirmation dialog is where the checkboxes are legal and where one can be dropped. Anything that needs a reason, anything above the limit and anything amended since the queue was drawn is named as excluded rather than quietly left out.

The queue is heterogeneous and the record pane is not one template. Four document kinds arrive in one inbox and they do not share a shape, so the pane draws the record's own list of facts and its own line columns, and what stays constant is the header, the approval trail and the rail. A pane hard-coded to purchase orders is a pane that renders a credit note with four empty cells.

Every item in this queue carries the Approved pill and the amber dot, which reads backwards for one second and is correct: in this system Approved is the waiting-on-someone state, not a decision that has been taken. The pill that changes is Overdue, on anything past the approval service level, and it is the one thing in the queue that is allowed to be red. list-detail's requisition queue makes the same choice, and following it matters more than the reading.

No single-key shortcuts on any decision. A screen this keyboard-driven invites them, and an approval fired by a stray A is a signature nobody meant to give. The decisions are ordinary Tab stops on a rail the user reaches after committing to a record.

The age that matters is the age with this approver, not the age of the document. An order raised three weeks ago and forwarded this morning is one day old on this screen, and writing the document date there is how a queue acquires a column of alarming numbers that nobody can act on.

anatomy.description: The fixed-height flex column holding everything. The page does not scroll; the three regions inside it do.
shrink-0. page-header's block reduced to what an inbox needs: the one h1, and under it a role="status" count line saying how many are waiting, what they are worth and how old the oldest is.
Present only while the user is acting for somebody else. A neutral alert card under the header saying whose authority is in force and until when, with the way out of it.
The list pane. A 320–352px column at md and up, full width below it, holding the listbox and its own header with the count and the kind filter.
li role="option" with a roving tabindex: the status dot, the document number, the value, the kind and party, and how long it has been with this approver. Nothing focusable inside it.
A section labelled by the record heading, tabindex="-1" so a decision can put focus on it. Header and trail are shrink-0; only the body between them scrolls.

An aside carrying the decision. A 288px column at lg and up, a bar across the foot of the record below it — one element, not two copies. It holds the limit position, the approval trail and the decision buttons, and it never scrolls out of reach.
A role="alert" region above the rail's buttons, in the document from first paint and empty, for a server that refused a write on the record still on screen.
A second role="alert" under the page header, for a refusal about a record that has already left the queue and has nowhere else to be said.
One role="status" on the frame, present at first paint, carrying the outcome of each decision and the size of what is left.

behaviour: Up and Down walk the queue, Home and End go to its ends, and the ends clamp rather than wrap. Enter commits and moves focus into the record. The arrow keys are bound on the listbox, never on the window, so the kind filter and any search above the list keep their own caret keys.
A decision is a request. The record stays in the queue and the rail goes aria-busy until the server answers; nothing about the record changes on the click.

When the server commits, the record leaves the queue, the counts rewrite, the selection moves to the record that took its place, the record body scrolls back to its top, and focus lands on the record region so its name is read.
The live region says what was decided and how many are left. It does not name the record that is now open, because the focus move is already reading that out.

When the server refuses, nothing leaves the queue unless the refusal is that the record has already gone. A refusal about a record on screen is drawn above the rail; a refusal about a record that has left is drawn under the page header and waits to be dismissed.
A refusal requires a reason before it can be sent, and the reason is collected in an alert dialog whose confirm is disabled until the field is answered.

An item above the user's approval limit is fully readable and has no approve action at all. The rail offers escalation instead, and escalating removes it from this inbox and puts it in the approver's.

Bulk approval is offered from the record the user is on, over the items the server has grouped with it. The confirmation lists every item with a checkbox and lists what was excluded and why; the whole set is one write and one outcome.
The last decision in the queue collapses the screen to the cleared state rather than leaving two empty panes. The cleared state states what was done, over what scope, and that nothing is filtered.

Below md the queue and the record are two screens. Opening a record shows it with the decision bar pinned at the foot, so the decision is reachable without scrolling past the record; Back and Escape return to the queue with focus on the option that was opened.
accessibility: One main, one h1, and the regions under it are h2s: the queue and the record. The record heading is what aria-labelledby points at, so the region name changes with the selection and a decision that moves focus there announces the new record.

The queue is a listbox named by its heading, one option carrying aria-selected="true" and every other carrying aria-selected="false". Exactly one option holds tabindex="0" and it moves with the selection, so tabbing out to the rail and back returns to the record being decided.

No option contains a button, a link or a checkbox. A listbox is one Tab stop and a control inside an option cannot be reached; the decisions live on the rail, on a record the user has already committed to.

The action rail is an <aside> with an accessible name so it can be found and skipped in a landmark list. It is one element that changes shape at lg, not two copies behind media queries — two copies mean two sets of ids and a decision posted from the one nobody could see.
The role="status" on the frame exists before anything changes and carries only what focus does not deliver: the outcome of the decision and the size of what is left.

Both refusal regions carry role="alert" and are in the DOM empty from first paint. A region created in the same frame as its first message counts as content that was always there and is announced to nobody, which is the failure that costs most in exactly this case.

A decision in flight sets aria-busy on the rail and keeps the pressed button focused, enabled and the same width. Disabling the control that was just pressed moves focus to the body, and the keyboard user who approved an order is then at the top of the document.

Where there is no approve action the button is absent rather than disabled, and the reason is ordinary text in the rail. A disabled button cannot be focused or described, so the explanation attached to one reaches nobody.
The status dot on an option is aria-hidden and the state is a word in the option text, so the queue is readable without colour.
No decision carries a single-key shortcut, and none of them is the first focusable thing on the page.

Nothing was written." else: said = f"{doc.number} approved." queue = list(Document.awaiting(request.user)) said += f" {len(queue)} left in your inbox." response = render(request, "approvals/_inbox.html", inbox_context(request, queue)) response["HX-Trigger"] = json.dumps({"decided": said}) return response Document.awaiting(user) is the whole routing rule in one place — the user's own queue plus anything they hold a live delegation for — and it is re-run on every response, so the queue and the record can never disagree about what is left.
