components.name: Board
components.description: Records in columns by the stage they are at, where each column is one stage and moving a card between two of them is a state change on the server. The column header carries the count, and every move can be made from the keyboard.
components.when_to_use: A set of records where the stage is the thing being managed and the count per stage is a question somebody actually asks — an approval pipeline from Raised to Approved, a production board from Planned to QC, a QC hold board somebody clears before the shift ends. Both halves have to be true, and this is the layout that gets over-reached for, so start from the assumption that it is the wrong answer. A register with a status column is right far more often, and that is index-page: it sorts, filters, pages, exports, and gives the whole width to the columns being compared instead of a third of it to four stages nobody rebalances. A queue worked one record at a time is list-detail — a board shows forty cards and asks you to choose one, a queue hands you the next one and keeps the record beside it. Rows under stage subheadings is table's grouped variant, which is a board flattened: the same records and the same stages in a shape that reads down rather than across, prints in one pass, and holds fourteen columns of figures no card can carry. The board earns its place only when the horizontal split does work no vertical grouping can — when the split itself is being rebalanced, when how wide a stage has grown is the point, and when the move is a transaction rather than an edit. If nobody moves a card, this is a grouped register drawn sideways. Past about seven stages it stops working at any width and the answer is the register with a stage filter.
rules: Keyboard first, drag second, and the order is the component. The primary move is: reach a card, open its move control, choose a stage, and the card lands there. Drag is an accelerant layered over an interaction that already works without it — HTML5 drag events have no keyboard gesture anybody uses and do not fire on a touch screen at all, and this software is read on a tablet on the shop floor by somebody wearing gloves. A board whose only move is a drag is not a board with an accessibility gap in it; it is a board that half the people who need it cannot operate.

The stage list is a disclosure inside the card, not a menu anchored to it. Every column on a board is its own scroller and overflow-y-auto clips both axes, so an anchored panel is cut off by the column it opens in. dropdown's own answer to that is a fixed panel positioned from a measurement of the trigger, and such a panel has to close on scroll — on a board that scrolls in two axes while it is being read, closing on scroll shuts the panel the moment somebody looks for the column they are aiming at. A panel in normal flow inside the card cannot be clipped, is the same control at 390px as at 1440px, and gives 36px targets without a second layout.

A column is a plain ul role="list" and never a listbox. A card carries a link and a control, and a listbox is one Tab stop inside which nothing is reachable — that rule is list-detail's, and it is exactly what separates the two layouts. A queue whose rows are inert is a listbox; a board whose cards are operated is a list of ordinary elements.

The move is a server write, not a visual rearrangement, and the markup has to show the gap between the two. The card is placed in the destination optimistically, goes aria-busy with its move control aria-disabled while the request is in flight, and on a refusal returns to the column it came from carrying the reason the server gave. A board that moves the card and never reconciles is a board where the screen and the ledger disagree until somebody reloads.

Counts and totals are derived from the same array the cards render from, never held beside it. A count kept separately is wrong for the one second after a move when somebody is looking at it, which is the only second that matters. The board total is the sum across the columns and it does not change when a card moves — only the split does, and a board total that moves on a stage change is double counting.

The board region is the one place in this system where a horizontal scroll is correct, and it happens inside its own overflow-x-auto box rather than on the page. Columns are a fixed width and shrink-0: let them share the width instead and five stages give five 78px columns at 390px, none of which holds a record number. snap-x on the region and snap-start on the column means a swipe lands a whole column under the thumb rather than halfway between two.

A board card is not the card component. The column is the panel — rounded-xl, white, border-zinc-300 — and the cards inside it are rounded-lg on a bg-zinc-50 track, because a rounded-xl card inside a rounded-xl column is a card inside a card, which card's own entry calls a layout mistake.

The card carries no status pill. The column it is sitting in is its status, and a pill that repeats the column header is the first thing to delete from a board card. A pill on a different axis is another matter — a delivery that is overdue on a card in an approval column is real information, and that is what the exception line is for.

Focus after a move has to be put back by hand, and three things have to be right or it fails silently. The card is destroyed in one x-for and created in another, so the control that was just pressed no longer exists and focus has fallen to the body. The handler was called from inside the iteration being torn down, so it has to capture $refs.board into a local before it changes the stage — a deferred callback that reaches for this.$refs afterwards finds undefined, and the only symptom is that focus never moves. And the restore happens on the frame after the tick rather than in it, because at $nextTick the destination column has not been painted and the query finds either nothing or the node that is about to be removed. Take inline: "nearest" as well as block on the scrollIntoView, because the column the card landed in is often off the right edge.

Every column carries position: relative, and it is load-bearing rather than decorative. An absolutely positioned descendant is clipped by an ancestor scroller only when that ancestor is in its containing-block chain, so an sr-only span — position:absolute, one pixel, no positioned ancestor — resolves against the document and reports its static position from the fourth column, seven hundred pixels past the right edge of a phone. The board region clips it out of sight and the page still grows a horizontal scrollbar, which is the one thing this system does not allow. One relative on the column fixes every sr-only, tooltip anchor and absolute badge inside it at once.

The card is found again by an unquoted attribute selector, so every record number on a board has to be a valid CSS identifier. PO-2026-0418 and MS-4821 are; a number with a slash or a leading digit in it is not, and the query silently matches nothing.

Tab is the cost of the design. One link and one control per card is two stops, so a board of sixty cards is a hundred and twenty of them — which is why the filter bar is not decoration, why a card never carries a third control, and why the answer to a board somebody has to walk end to end is a filter rather than a longer board.

A stage over its limit is advisory and a stage that refuses is not, and they are drawn differently on purpose. Over the limit is an alert-triangle in amber-700 beside the count, and nothing else changes — no amber column, no field of colour. A stage that will not accept another card carries its destination button as aria-disabled with the reason written on the button, because a destination that has silently disappeared from the list is a board that looks broken.

The columns come from the stage list, not from the data. A stage with nothing in it still renders, with its header, its count of zero and its drop target, because the columns are the process and the process does not disappear when the work does. This is the one thing a regroup over a queryset gets wrong every time.

The board's filter belongs in the URL and the move does not. Somebody sends a colleague a board scoped to Silvassa and this week; nobody sends them a board with one card two columns further along. Write the filter with history.replaceState so a reload keeps the scope, and let the move be what it is — a POST whose answer is the new board.

The snippet root is a bounded frame — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box. As a real page it is app-shell's main column: drop the height and the border, put h-screen overflow-hidden on the shell, and let the board region take min-h-0 flex-1 so the columns scroll and the page does not.

anatomy.description: The page-header component unchanged: breadcrumb, the one h1, the scope line, and the actions. It does not scroll with the board.

One role="status" on the board root, in the document from first paint, carrying what focus cannot say — the count in the column the card landed in, a refusal and its reason, a rejection from the server.
The single overflow-x-auto box, snap-x, min-h-0 flex-1. The only horizontal scroller in the system and the reason nothing else on the page moves sideways.
A section labelled by its own h2, w-72 and shrink-0, rounded-xl white panel with its own vertical scroller. Never flex-1 — columns that share the width vanish at five stages.
shrink-0: the stage name, the count, the value at that stage, and the limit mark when there is a limit. It stays put while the cards under it scroll.
The ul, bg-zinc-50 — a band recessed inside the white column — holding one li per record. role="list", because Tailwind's reset removes the list semantics with the bullets.
rounded-lg, white, border-zinc-200. One link — the record number — one control, and the two or three facts the decision at that stage needs. No status pill: the column is the status.
The disclosure trigger, named with the record and the stage it is in now, so the announcement after a move is delivered by focus landing on it.
The panel: one full-width button per destination, the current stage absent because it is not a destination, and a refusing stage aria-disabled with its reason on the button.
One line under the facts, an alert-circle in red-600 and a sentence, for a card that is failing on an axis the column does not describe.
The strip under the region carrying the totals across every column. It is the one figure a move does not change.
The count under the h1. On a filtered board it says how many records are on screen out of how many exist, and how many filters are holding the difference.

behaviour: The move control opens the list of destinations inside the card and scrolls the card into view if the panel pushed it below the fold. Escape closes it and returns focus to the control; only one card's panel is open at a time, because the state is on the board.

Choosing a destination moves the card, closes the panel, puts focus on the moved card's move control in its new column and scrolls that column into view. The status region says which stage it went to and how many are there now.

A move in flight leaves the card in the destination with aria-busy and its control aria-disabled. A refusal puts the card back in the column it came from, attaches the reason the server gave and announces it; nothing is silently reverted.

A stage over its limit shows the mark and still accepts cards. A stage that refuses shows its destination button as unavailable with the reason on it, and pressing it announces the refusal rather than doing nothing.
Counts, values and the board total recompute from the cards on every move. The two column totals change and the board total does not.

Drag, where it is offered, calls exactly the same commit as the menu and adds nothing of its own. The column being dragged over shows it is the drop target; a drop outside a column is a no-op, and no card ever ends up nowhere.

Below sm the board stops being columns. The stage becomes a select, one column fills the width, and the counts move into the option labels so the shape of the pipeline is still readable without seeing it.

Filtering never moves a card and never changes a stage. Every column count becomes "4 of 9" and the scope line says how many records are off the board, because on a filtered board an unqualified count is a false statement.

A column with nothing in it keeps its header, its count of zero and its full height, because it is still a destination. A board with nothing on it keeps every column and puts one panel above them saying why.
accessibility: One main, one h1 in the page header, and every column an h2 under it. The heading outline is the pipeline, so a screen reader user can hear the stages in order without reading a card.
Each column is a section named by its own h2 with aria-labelledby, so a landmark or region list reads as the stage names and a card announced out of context still has one.

The card track is a plain list, never a listbox and never a grid. Cards contain a link and a button; a listbox is one Tab stop and nothing inside an option can be reached, which is why list-detail forbids controls on a row and a board requires them.

The move control is named with the record and its current stage — "Move PO-2026-0418, now in With buyer" — so when focus lands on it after a move the new stage is announced by the mechanism that already exists, and the status region is left to carry only what focus cannot.

The status region is on the board root and is in the document before anything moves. It carries the sentences focus cannot deliver: the count in the destination, a refusal and its reason, a rejection from the server. A region rendered with its message already inside it has not changed and announces nothing.
The destination buttons are in a role="group" named "Move <record> to", so the list is announced as a set of destinations rather than as three unrelated buttons in the middle of a card.

A stage that will not accept the card is aria-disabled="true" and stays focusable with the reason written inside the button. The disabled attribute would drop it out of the Tab order, so the one destination somebody is hunting for would be gone with nothing to say why.
A card in flight is aria-busy="true" and its control aria-disabled, so it is not moved twice while the first move is still being decided.
Owner initials in the corner of a card are aria-hidden with the full name in an sr-only span beside them. Two letters in a circle are a picture of a person, not a name.

Drag adds no accessibility of its own and is never the only route. Every draggable card carries the same move control, and the drop handler and the menu call one function, so there is one code path and it is the one the keyboard uses.

components.name: Schedule page
components.description: What is planned and when, drawn with time as the axis: promised deliveries across a month, production against each line, a shift roster. Position carries meaning — further right is later, and a block twice as wide takes twice as long.
components.when_to_use: The screen a planner opens to find out whether Tuesday is over-committed — delivery dates promised across a month, production planned against each machine, a shift roster, a maintenance calendar. The first boundary to draw is against calendar, because half of this screen looks exactly like it and is not it. calendar is a date picker: a month grid whose whole job is to return one date or one range into a field, whose cells are options, whose selected day is a value about to be posted, and which closes the moment the answer is given. Nothing on this page is being picked. The cells carry records, the grid is a view of data rather than a control, there is no field under it and no value to commit — a day here is somewhere you go, not something you choose. A screen that puts a month on it so that somebody can fill in Required by is calendar/picker inside form-page, and reaching for this entry because the month grid looked similar hands the user a schedule they cannot type a date into. The trap is sharpest at calendar/marked, which draws dots on days and is still a picker: its dots are a hint about the day you are about to select, and its cells are still buttons that answer a form. If the grid returns a value, it is calendar. Against index-page: the same deliveries as a register — sortable, filterable, pageable, exportable, with the promised date as one column among nine — and that is the better answer whenever the question is which rather than when. Which orders are late, which vendor is worst, what is outstanding against a cost centre: register. Whether Tuesday can take another truck: this. Against board: columns by stage, not by time. A board's axis is how far a record has got, its columns are a process, and moving a card between two of them is a state change on the server; here nothing moves between columns, a block moves along the axis because a date changed, and the axis is a measurement rather than a set of buckets. Where a Thursday block is not later than a Wednesday one but merely different, the layout is a board and this one is lying about its own geometry.
rules: Position is the message, and everything else follows from that. A block's left edge is when it starts and its width is how long it lasts, so a block cannot wrap to a second line, cannot be reordered for tidiness, and cannot be given a minimum width that would make a two-hour job look like a four-hour one. Every rule below is that one rule meeting a case where it is inconvenient.

The geometry is a percentage of the track and not a count of columns. A block is absolutely positioned inside a relative lane with left and width in per cent, which is the same style attribute progress writes its fill with. Snapping blocks into a grid of fixed cells is the version that ships first and it rounds every start time to the nearest cell — 06:20 becomes 06:00, three of those in a row become an hour of production that does not exist, and the screen stops being a measurement.

The month grid gives up the proportional axis on purpose, and that is the one place it is allowed. At a month's scale the unit is the day: a delivery is promised on the 18th, not at 46.9 per cent of the 18th, and drawing a stripe across three cells to mean a three-day job would need the grid to be a matrix rather than a table of days. What a month grid answers is how many and on which day; the hour is what week, day and resource are for, and the view switcher is how the planner gets from one question to the other.

Monday first, matching calendar, and for the same reason: every Indian office runs Monday to Saturday and a Sunday-first grid puts the weekend at both ends of the row. Saturday is a working day and is drawn white like any other; Sunday is the recessed fill. A plant holiday is a third thing again and it is not the national calendar — 15 August closes every plant in the country and the annual maintenance shutdown closes this one, so both are marked and only one of them is a public holiday. A schedule that renders the gazetted list and calls it the factory calendar promises deliveries into a shutdown.

A block is the chip token and nothing new: bg-zinc-200, ring-1 ring-inset ring-zinc-300, hovering to zinc-300. Colour lives in the 6px dot exactly as it does in badge, so a month of blocks reads as a month of work with six late ones in it rather than as a heat map. A field of red behind a block is the defect the alert rule already names, and on a screen where forty blocks are visible at once it is worse than anywhere else.

A block truncates and never wraps, and what survives the truncation is decided rather than left to the browser. The record number is first and always fits; the vendor name is what goes, then the times, then the quantity, and the order is the same on every view so a planner learns it once. A block narrower than its own number shows the dot and no text, carries the whole record in its accessible name, and hands the pointer to hovercard — an unreadable half-number is worse than a bare bar, because a bar does not look like an answer. There is no minimum width, ever: a block widened to fit its label draws forty minutes as two hours, which is the one thing this layout may not do.

Two things at one time have to be visibly at once. Overlapping blocks on one lane split the lane's width and sit side by side, so the overlap is a shape on the screen rather than a sentence somewhere else. Stacking them into separate rows is the arrangement that hides the one fact the planner opened the page for.

Three different nothings, and they must not look the same. A day inside the published plan with nothing on it is white and empty — silence means nothing is booked. A day past the planning horizon carries one zinc-500 line saying so, because an empty cell and an unplanned cell are the difference between a free Wednesday and a Wednesday nobody has looked at. A non-working day is the recessed fill with its reason written in it. Draw all three as blank cells and the planner books a truck into a shutdown.

Over-commitment is a mark beside a figure, never a coloured lane. A line booked past its shift shows the hours as booked of available and an alert-triangle in amber-700, which is board's limit rule unchanged, and the block that runs past the end of the shift is clipped at the edge of the lane with its right corners squared so the clip reads as an overrun rather than as a block that happens to end there.

A day holding more than fits shows the first three and a control that expands the cell in place. An anchored panel was rejected twice over: a panel opened inside a grid cell is clipped by whichever scroller the grid sits in, which is board's reason for putting its stage list in normal flow, and at 390px there is nothing to anchor one to. Expanding in place grows the week row, which is honest — that week does have more in it.

The resource grid is the only region here that scrolls sideways, it does it inside its own overflow-x-auto box, and it exists only from md up. Below that the same rows are a stacked list with the times written out, which is table's sticky-column rule and this layout does not get to opt out of it: a matrix that scrolls sideways on a phone is indistinguishable from a layout that broke.

Everything on the grid is a link and nothing is dragged. Moving a delivery is a date change on a record with a reason attached to it, which is a form and not a gesture; a schedule whose only way to reschedule is dragging a block is a schedule that cannot be operated with a keyboard, on a tablet, or by anyone who needs to say why the date moved. The block opens the record and the record is where the date is changed.

The period, the view and the scope all belong in the URL. A planner sends a colleague the Silvassa extrusion week of 17 August, and every one of those three has to survive the paste; write them with history.replaceState if they are changed without a reload. Which day is expanded does not go in the URL — it is not a fact about the schedule.

The snippet root is a bounded frame — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box. As a real page it renders inside app-shell's <main>: drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the mx-auto max-w-[1600px] gutter on the band and on the grid so the h1 and the first column line up, and let the sticky ruler stick to the shell's scrolling column.

anatomy.description: page-header's <header> inside <main>: white, edge to edge over a border-zinc-200 rule, its content in the same mx-auto max-w-[1600px] gutter the grid uses. Holds the trail, the one h1, the scope line and the page's actions.
The role="status" under the h1 saying what is on screen — how many are planned in this period, how many are late, what they are worth. Rewritten by the period, the view and every filter.
Previous, the period label, next, and Today. calendar's chevron buttons unchanged, with the label as an aria-live region so paging is announced rather than silently redrawn.
Month, Week, Line and Day as a <nav> of anchors on button-group's segmented track, the current one carrying aria-current="page". Four URLs, not four panels.
The row or column of labelled hours that names the axis. Sticky against the grid's own scroller, and aria-hidden — the hours are decoration, and every block carries its own in its name.
The relative track one resource or one day owns. Blocks are positioned inside it in per cent; it never shrinks below the height of the blocks stacked in it.
One scheduled thing: the chip fill, a status dot, the record number, and as much else as the width allows. A link to the record, never a drag handle.
The "+2 more" button on a day that holds more than fits. Expands the cell in place; the same button collapses it.
The booked-of-available figure on a resource row, with an amber-700 alert-triangle when booked exceeds available. Advisory — the schedule still accepts the work.
bg-zinc-50 with its reason in it — Sunday, a public holiday, a plant shutdown. Three different reasons and the same fill, because the difference is in the words.
The part of the grid past the planning horizon, carrying one line saying nobody has planned it yet. Distinct from a planned period that happens to be empty.
The dot key under the grid, from calendar's marked variant: what each status dot means, once, rather than a tooltip per block.
What the grid becomes at 390px: one day at a time, the time in a gutter, the blocks as rows, and the gaps written out as sentences.
One removable chip per filter in force, on the recessed band under the band, with the count of what is hidden in the scope line.

behaviour: Paging the period redraws the grid and rewrites the scope line, and does not move the view, the scope or the vertical position. Today returns to the period containing today and puts focus nowhere — it is a jump, not a selection.
A block is a link to its record. Opening one leaves the schedule where it was; nothing on this page edits a date in place, because a date that moves needs a reason recorded against it.

A day holding more blocks than fit shows three and a control. Pressing it expands that cell, grows the week row and swaps the control to Show less; only one day is expanded at a time, and the expansion is not in the URL.
Overlapping blocks on one lane split its width and both stay legible. The lane grows to hold whatever is stacked in it rather than clipping the second one.

A block that runs past the end of its lane is clipped at the edge with its right corners squared and says by how much in its own text. The capacity figure on the row goes to booked-of-available and takes the amber mark.

A delivery promised on a non-working day is drawn on that day rather than moved to the next working one. Moving it silently is how a plant discovers on the morning of the shutdown that four trucks are on their way.

Filtering hides blocks and never moves one. Every count on screen becomes n of m while any filter is in force, the scope line says how many are hidden and by how many filters, and the figures revert to the plain form when the last chip goes.

The resource grid scrolls sideways inside its own box from md up, with the resource column sticky against the left edge. Below md it is a stacked list, and nothing on the page scrolls sideways at any width.
At 390px the grid is gone and the day is an agenda: one day, a time gutter, the blocks as rows in order, and the gaps stated as sentences rather than drawn as space.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1> in the band, and every region below it an h2 — the month, each resource lane, the agenda for a day. The heading outline is the shape of the plan.

The month grid is a real <table> with th scope="col" for the weekdays, the same as calendar, and the difference is inside the cell: calendar's cell is a button that returns a value, and this one holds a <ul role="list"> of links to records. Row and column position is available without sight either way.

The geometry is decoration and every block says so. A lane is not readable, so each block carries its resource, its start and its end in an sr-only span inside the link — a span rather than an aria-label, so the visible text stays a prefix of the accessible name and the name a speech user says out loud is the one written on the screen. The one block that takes an aria-label instead is the one too narrow to show any text at all, where there is no visible label for the name to contain.
The ruler is aria-hidden. Reading twelve hour labels before the first block is noise, and the hours are already in every block's name.

The period label is aria-live="polite" so paging is announced. The scope line is a separate role="status" that is in the document from first paint, and the two never speak at once — paging does not change the scope and filtering does not change the period.
Today carries aria-current="date" on the day number, which is a fact about the calendar and not about any record on it.
A non-working day says why in real text inside the cell, never by fill alone. A recessed cell with nothing in it is a day that reads as free to everyone who cannot see the fill.
The overflow control names what it would reveal and what day it is on — "Show 2 more on 18 August" — because "+2 more" repeated four times down a month is four controls with the same name.
A block that is clipped by the edge of its lane says so in its text, not by being cut off. A visual clip is not information to a screen reader and the overrun is the whole point of that block.

Each resource lane is a <section> named by its own h2, and its capacity figure is inside that section, so a block announced out of context still has a resource and the row it belongs to still has a name.

Every chip's remove button names the filter it drops — "Remove the filter Extrusion", never "Remove" — and clearing all of them moves focus to the scope line, which is tabindex="-1" for exactly that and is also the sentence saying what happened.

variants.html:
The scheduled block

One lane, 06:00 to 22:00. Every block below is the same record at a different duration.

What the text does

  • A fortnight, or the whole lane

    MS-4838 06:00 – 22:00 · 16.0 h Injection 120T · 9,500 crates · Meera Joshi

    Number, times, duration, resource, quantity, owner. Everything the record has that a planner reads at a glance.

  • Half the lane — eight hours

    MS-4838 06:00 – 14:00 · 9,500 crates Injection 120T, Meera Joshi

    The owner and the resource drop out of the block; the lane already names the resource and the record page holds the rest.

  • Two hours

    4838 MS-4838, Injection 120T, 06:00 to 08:00, 9,500 crates, Meera Joshi

    The prefix goes before the digits do. MS- is the same on every block on the screen; 4838 is the one part that identifies this one.

  • Forty minutes

    The dot and nothing else, with the whole record in the accessible name. Widening it to fit the number would draw forty minutes as two hours, which is the one thing this layout may not do.

What the edges do

  • Started before this lane began

    MS-4835 Started 21:00 yesterday · ends 11:30

    Square on the left, rounded on the right, and the start date written in. A rounded left edge at 06:00 says the job started at 06:00.

  • Runs past the end of the shift

    MS-4838 14:00 – 23:30 · runs 1.5 h past shift end

    The overrun is in the text as well as in the clip, and the lane it sits on carries the amber mark on its booked-of-available figure.

  • Two on one lane at one time

    MS-4835 · 06:00 – 14:00 MS-4841 · 12:00 – 20:00

    The lane grows and the two blocks keep their true left and width, so the overlap is a shape. Squeezing both into one row hides the two hours that are the whole problem.

components.name: Compare page
components.description: Several vendors' quotations against one enquiry, side by side, so a buyer can award the order. Line items down, vendors across, rates in the cells and the totals along the bottom — the comparative statement that is attached to the requisition and shown to whoever signs it.
components.when_to_use: One enquiry, several offers, and a decision that ends with all but one of them dropped. Reach for this when the columns are alternatives rather than records — four vendors against twelve lines, three freight quotes, two revisions of the same vendor's offer — and when what leaves the screen is an award. The neighbour that looks identical is reconcile-page, and the difference is what the two screens are for: reconciliation puts two sets of records that both already exist beside each other and makes them agree, so every difference it draws is an error somebody has to clear and both sides survive the screen; comparison puts alternatives beside each other and picks one, so every difference it draws is a fact about an offer and only one column outlives the screen. If nothing is being chosen, this is the wrong layout. table is wrong for a different reason: a table sorts, and a comparison has no meaningful sort — sorting a matrix by one vendor's column reorders the line items under every other vendor and destroys the thing the reader was reading across, which is why nothing on this page has a sortable header. A register of the quotations themselves — who quoted, when, for how much, still open or expired — is data-table inside index-page, and that is where a quotation is found rather than where it is weighed. One quotation on its own is record-page.
rules: Rows are line items and columns are vendors, and neither axis may be reordered by the reader. A sort control is the first thing somebody asks for and it is the one thing this page must not have: the value of a matrix is that line 7 is line 7 in every column, and a sort applied to one vendor's rates breaks the correspondence the whole screen is made of. Reordering the lines is legitimate only when it is done to the enquiry, before the quotations were sought, and then it is the same order everywhere.

Both axes stick at once, and that is the structural problem of the entry. table/sticky-header pins the head, table/sticky-column pins the first column, and doing both in one scroller costs more than the sum of the two. border-separate border-spacing-0 on the table, because preflight collapses borders onto the table and a collapsed border does not travel with the cell that sticks. Every rule then moves onto the cells, so a 12 by 6 matrix carries the row rule on 72 <td>s instead of on 12 <tr>s. Every sticky cell needs an opaque fill of its own, which means every one of them also stops taking the row hover and has to be given it back with group-hover. And there are two corner cells rather than none: the top-left cell is sticky on both axes and the bottom-left cell is too once the foot sticks, so both need z-20 against z-10 on the three planes around them. The corners are where this ships broken, because a reviewer scrolls one axis at a time and the defect only appears when both are scrolled at once.

The matrix scroller carries position: relative, and it is load-bearing rather than decorative. Every sr-only span on this page — the caption, the words behind an em dash, the reason a cell is excluded — is position: absolute with no positioned ancestor, so its containing block is the document and it reports its static position from the sixth vendor column, six hundred pixels past the right edge of a phone. The scroller clips it out of sight and the page still grows a horizontal scrollbar, which is the one thing this system does not allow. One relative on the scroller fixes every one of them at once, and it is measured at 390px on a page with the sr-only text in it, because with the spans removed the defect disappears and the fix looks unnecessary.

The scroller carries tabindex="0" and a name. A div with overflow-auto is not focusable in Chromium, so a keyboard user cannot pan a matrix that scrolls in two axes at all — the content is on screen, reachable by every other means, and simply unreachable by the arrow keys. Firefox makes scrollable regions focusable and Chrome does not, which is why this passes review on one machine.

L1 per line is arithmetic and the award is not. The lowest rate on a line is a fact the page can compute; who gets the order is decided by freight, duty, the terms of payment, the delivery date, whether the quotation is still valid and whether that vendor has ever delivered on time. A screen that marks the smallest number and stops has told the buyer something true and let them believe it was the answer, so the terms band and the landed figures are not an optional extra region — they are what stops the mark being read as a recommendation.

The L1 mark is a graphite pill and a weight, never a colour behind the cell. Three reasons and none of them is taste. Colour in this system says what a record is doing, and cheapest is not a state; green means finished and borrowing it for lowest spends a colour that meant something. A field of colour behind a figure is what the colour rule forbids outright, whatever the hue. And on a twelve-line matrix there are twelve marks scattered across four columns, so a tinted cell reads as a pattern in the grid rather than as a set of separate decisions, which is exactly the failure the status pill exists to avoid.

Absent is not zero and the total must not pretend otherwise. A vendor who did not quote three lines has a total for nine lines, and that number is smaller than everyone else's for a reason that has nothing to do with price. The foot states the line count under every total, a partial total is excluded from the mark on the total row, and the reason is written where the figure is — not in a footnote under the table, which is below the fold on the screen this decision is actually made on.

GST is shown and is not compared. A registered buyer recovers it as input credit, so a comparison ranked on a figure that includes it ranks on money nobody spends; freight and non-creditable duty are the two that genuinely change the landed cost and therefore the answer. The page carries all three, ranks on basic plus freight plus duty, and labels the tax row as recovered so nobody adds it back by hand.

An alternative make is quoted against the enquiry, not against the other vendors. A rate for a grade nobody asked for is not a lower price for the same thing, and it cannot carry the L1 mark until somebody with the authority to accept the substitution has accepted it. The cell keeps the figure, says what was offered instead, and is excluded from the line mark and from the comparable total.

table-fixed with every column width declared, on every variant. Under auto layout the widest vendor name decides the width of its own column, so four columns of identical figures come out four different widths and the digits stop lining up across the row — which is the one thing a rate matrix is for. Fixed widths also mean the L1 pill appearing in a cell cannot widen the column, so switching the comparison from basic to landed moves the mark without moving a single figure.

Vendor names wrap in the header and are never truncated. A truncated vendor name is a different vendor as far as anyone reading it out is concerned, and the column heading is the one place on this page where the reader has to be certain which offer they are looking at. Rates and totals take whitespace-nowrap for the opposite reason: ₹15,60,370 broken between the symbol and the digits stops being a figure.

Six vendors is the ceiling and it is a width budget, not a preference. A rate column wide enough for ₹1,72,120 and an L1 pill is 176px, the line-item column is 256px, and a sixth vendor puts the matrix at 1,312px — already a sideways scroll on the 1,366px laptops these are worked on. The answer to a seventh quotation is to drop the ones that are out of the running before the comparison, which is a decision a buyer makes anyway, not a narrower column.

The award bar states what it is about to do before it does it, in the units of the record: how many purchase orders, against which vendors, for how much, and whether the L1 offer is being passed over. A split award that raises three orders instead of one is a fact the person signing has to be told on this screen, because the saving that justified it is smaller than it looks once three deliveries and three sets of paperwork are counted.

An award that is not L1 needs a reason and the reason is a field, not a checkbox. This is the internal control the whole screen exists to serve: a comparative statement is filed with the requisition and read by audit a year later, and "lowest not accepted" with nothing after it is what turns a routine file into a question nobody can answer. Guard the button on the field having content, never disable it — a disabled button beside an empty box explains nothing.

The page renders inside app-shell, and its own root here is a bounded preview frame. As a real screen, drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the max-width and the padding, and let the matrix keep its own scroller: the matrix is the one region on this page allowed to scroll sideways, and the page behind it never does.

anatomy.description: The page-header component unchanged: breadcrumb, the one h1 — Comparative statement — the enquiry's status pill, and the actions. Never sticky; the award bar at the foot is what has to stay reachable.

A white strip of the facts every column is quoted against: the enquiry number, what it is for, the plant, how many quotations arrived out of how many were invited, and when the enquiry closed. Without it the columns are four prices for nothing in particular.

The segmented track that chooses the basis of the comparison — basic rate or landed cost. It moves the mark and the emphasis and changes nothing in the cells, so the rates a vendor actually quoted are on screen under either basis.

The div that owns the sideways scroll: overflow-auto, overscroll-contain, tabindex="0" and a name, with a negative focus offset because it sits flush inside a clipped panel. The only region on the page that scrolls in x.
The top-left <th>, sticky on both axes and z-20. It names the row axis — Line item — and it is the cell that is painted over from one side or the other when the layering is wrong.

One <th scope="col"> per quotation: the vendor's name at 13px in sentence case, the quotation number and its date under it. Right-aligned over right-aligned figures, bottom-aligned so the quote references line up when a long name wraps.
A <th scope="row"> carrying the item name, its code and the enquired quantity with its unit. It is the frozen column, so it carries an opaque fill and the row hover has to be put back on it.
The quoted rate per unit on the first line and the extended line value under it in 12px zinc-500. Both tabular-nums, both nowrap, right-aligned so the column reads as a column.

A small graphite pill reading L1 to the left of the figure, with the figure stepped up to zinc-900 and font-semibold while the unmarked cells sit at zinc-600. The key sits under the matrix and says what L1 means on this page.

The rows that are not numbers — payment terms, promised delivery, quotation validity, warranty, past on-time performance, whether there is a live rate contract. Left-aligned in a matrix built for right-aligned figures, and carrying no L1 mark on any row.

A <tfoot> holding the totals, the derived landed rows and the line count under each. A total is never one more row in the body: a partial total in the body reads as a line item and is announced as one.

The strip at the foot of the scrolling column: the shape of the award, what it will raise, the reason field when the award is not L1, and Award beside Cancel. Opaque and top-bordered, like every other action bar in the system.

behaviour: Nothing on this page sorts. The header cells are labels, not buttons, and there is no aria-sort anywhere on the matrix, because a sort applied to one vendor's column reorders the lines under all of them.

The matrix scrolls in both axes inside its own box. The head stays while the lines scroll, the line column stays while the vendors scroll, and where a foot is sticky it stays as well; the page behind the matrix never moves sideways at any width.

The L1 mark is recomputed from the rates on screen, so it cannot disagree with the figures beside it. Two vendors at the same rate are both marked — L1 is a rate, not a rank, and marking the first one in DOM order would make the award look decided by the order the quotations happened to arrive in.

Changing the basis from basic to landed moves the mark and the emphasis and touches nothing else. Every quoted rate stays on screen under both, and the row the mark is sitting in is the one the ranking is being read from.

A vendor who did not quote a line gets an em dash and the words in the accessibility tree; its total is drawn with the number of lines it covers, and it takes no mark on the total row however small the number is.
A line quoted against an alternative make keeps its figure and is excluded from that line's mark. It stays excluded until the substitution is accepted, which is a decision made off this page.

Choosing a whole-order award selects one vendor for every line. Choosing a split award replaces the matrix with one decision per line, and the running total under it is the sum of the choices rather than any vendor's quoted total.

The award bar restates the award in the record's own units on every change — how many orders, to whom, for how much — and says when the L1 offer is being passed over. The reason field appears with that sentence and the button is guarded on it, never disabled.

The matrix keeps its panning box at every width rather than disappearing below md, because a frozen line column and a pannable grid is what makes a narrow desktop window work and there is no card form of a comparison to fall back to. What a phone ships is a different arrangement, not a smaller grid: one vendor at a time, chosen from a select, with that vendor's rate against every line and the L1 rate beside it as the reference, and the totals and the award action on the phone in full.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1> in the page header, and every region below it an h2 — the matrix, the terms, the award. The heading outline is what lets anybody skim a comparison without reading four columns of figures.

The matrix carries a <caption>, sr-only, naming the enquiry and saying what the rows and the columns are. Without it a screen reader entering the table is told the number of rows and columns and nothing about which axis is which.

Vendor headers are <th scope="col"> and line headers are <th scope="row">, both, without exception. A rate is meaningless without both of its coordinates, and a figure four columns along announced on its own is the failure the two scopes exist to prevent.

The scroller is a role="region" with an accessible name and tabindex="0", so it appears in the tab order and the arrow keys pan it. Chromium does not make an overflow container focusable on its own, so without this the matrix is operable by mouse and by nothing else.

The focus outline on the scroller takes the negative offset — focus-visible:-outline-offset-2 — because it sits flush inside a panel that is overflow-hidden for its rounded corners, and a positive offset draws two thirds of an outline with the sides clipped away.
A cell nobody quoted is an em dash for the eye and the words "Not quoted" in an sr-only span. An em dash alone is announced as nothing, which is indistinguishable from a cell the page failed to fill.

The L1 pill is real text and its meaning is written once under the matrix. It is not aria-hidden and it is not an icon: the mark is the only thing separating one figure from three identical ones, so it has to survive being read out.

The basis control is a role="radiogroup" of role="radio" buttons with a roving tabindex, and its aria-checked is the announcement. There is no live region over the matrix: a basis change rewrites every figure in the foot, and a live region announcing all of them makes a control nobody presses twice.

The award summary is an <output> so it is a live region by default and the restatement is heard as it changes. The reason field is an ordinary labelled textarea with its message paragraph, and the button that needs it is guarded rather than disabled, so it keeps focus and can say why it refused.

The terms band is part of the same table with its own <tbody> and a <th scope="colgroup"> naming it, not a second table below. Split into two tables the vendor columns lose their headers in the second one, and a payment term is announced with no vendor attached to it.

components.name: Reconcile page
components.description: Two sets of records that ought to agree, with the difference between them written out as a figure and the controls that make them agree — pairing, explaining and posting. The variance is the content; the rows that already agree are a count.
components.when_to_use: Two populations of records that are supposed to say the same thing and somebody accountable for the fact that they do not: a purchase order against a goods receipt against the vendor's invoice, a bank statement against the ledger, a physical stock count against the system quantity. The test is that both sides already exist and both are true — reconciliation is an agreement between records that have already been written, and the work is finding the pairs and explaining the gaps. compare-page looks almost identical and is the opposite job: several vendors' quotations laid out side by side so somebody can choose one, where the columns are candidates rather than facts and the outcome is a decision rather than an entry. If the columns are things you are choosing between, that is compare-page; if they are things that have already happened and disagree, it is this. A column that sums at the foot of one table is not a screen at all — that is table's totals variant, a region inside a page. And where the variance is a fact somebody is reading about one record rather than the work in front of them — an order that says 4 of 9 lines received — it belongs on record-page beside the rest of the record, not on a screen of its own. index-page is the register scanned and filtered, list-detail is the queue worked one record at a time with the record beside it; this is neither, because the unit of work here is a pair rather than a record.
rules: The variance is the whole page and the agreement is a count. Two columns of matching rows are not information — the four lines that disagree are the reason anybody opened this screen, so they render first, at full size, and the twelve that agree collapse to one strip saying how many and what they came to. The rejected alternative is one table of all sixteen lines with the four scattered through it, which turns a screen that is scanned into a screen that has to be read, and the cost of missing one of them is a payment.

Print the arithmetic, do not imply it. Ordered, received, invoiced and the difference are four columns, and the difference is one of them rather than something the reader works out from the other three. Two people subtracting the same two figures in their heads get two answers often enough that the whole reconciliation is worth nothing, and the one who is wrong is the one who signs.

The direction of the subtraction is written into the column header — invoiced less received — because a signed figure with no stated direction is read both ways. A positive variance means the vendor billed for more than arrived; without the header sentence half the readers take it to mean the receipt was short, which is the same number and the opposite dispute.

Matching is a claim somebody is accountable for, not a gesture. The primary interaction is: select a record on one side with the arrow keys, choose from the candidates on the other, press the button that makes the pair. Drag is an accelerant layered over that and never the thing itself — HTML5 drag has no keyboard gesture anybody uses and does not fire on a touch screen, and a matching screen that can only be dragged cannot be operated by the accounts clerk on a tablet or by anybody using a keyboard. A pair is undone with an Unpair button until it is posted, and posting is a separate act with its own confirmation.

A variance row carries no stretched row link, and that is the one place this page deliberately does not copy table's linked-rows. A row here is not a record — it is two records and the difference between them — so a single anchor over the whole row has to pick one of them and lies about the other. The identifiers are separate anchors inside the first cell, which is two tab stops a row and is the honest cost of a row that is a pair.

A quantity column across mixed units does not total. MT, kg and nos do not add up, so the foot carries an em dash and the reason sits under the table. This is table/totals' rule and the answer is the same here, only more load-bearing: on a reconciliation a plausible wrong total in the foot is read as the finding.

An unmatched record is not a variance and the two must not be drawn as one thing. A receipt with no invoice against it means the invoice has not arrived, has not been posted, or has not been found, and only the last of those is work for this screen. Each side therefore states its own count and its own value and the two are never subtracted from each other — the figure that has to reach zero belongs to the bank reconciliation, where both sides really are the same account.

A match is an allocation with an amount, not a link between two ids. Store it as a link and neither of the two cases that actually turn up can be expressed: one invoice covering three receipts, and one receipt split across two invoices. Both are the same table read from opposite ends, both leave a remainder that has to be shown rather than rounded away, and a screen built on one-to-one pairing has to be rewritten the first week it meets a part shipment.

Three verdicts, and they wear the locked dots rather than a new palette: In tolerance takes emerald-600, Needs a reason takes amber-500, Blocked takes red-600. That is Closed, Approved and Overdue reading as finished, waiting on someone and the alarm state, which is what those three dots already mean. It is a reuse of the status table under different words and it is flagged for a person, on the same footing as record-page/states mapping On hold and Cancelled.

A line that cannot be posted offers no control at all. There is no reason box on a rate above the contract rate, because no reason makes it postable — what it needs is a credit note from the vendor or an amendment to the order, and neither is done from this screen. Giving it a reason field invites somebody to type a sentence and press a button that then refuses, and the refusal arrives after the work.

The post button is aria-disabled, never disabled, and the reason sits in a sentence the button is described by. disabled drops the one control somebody is hunting for out of the tab order with nothing to say why, and a browser moves focus off a disabled element to the body. The handler returns early instead, so the press is real and the refusal is announced.

Say when a difference is ordinary. A bank posts on value date and a ledger on voucher date, so the same payment sits on two dates one day apart, and an unannotated date column makes a clerk chase a variance that does not exist. The same goes for a cheque drawn and not presented: it is carried forward, it is not a difference, and the working has to distinguish the two or the reconciliation never closes.

Every figure carries tabular-nums and Indian digit grouping — ₹12,45,000, two-two-three above the last three digits. toLocaleString('en-IN') does it in the browser; on the server it is a project filter, because intcomma groups in threes and ₹1,245,000 is wrong by a factor of ten to anyone reading it at speed. Columns line up on the right so a variance stands out of a column without the digits being read.

An sr-only label carries its whole sentence in one string — a bare text node, or one x-text — never a run of nested spans. sr-only is position:absolute in a 1px box with overflow hidden, so an inline element inside it lays out past that box and reports a rect well beyond the right edge of a 390px screen. It is clipped and nothing scrolls, so it never shows up as a bug, but it trips every overflow audit the project will ever run. One string is also one accessible name rather than four fragments.

At 390px the table is not a table. A variance is four figures and a subtraction, so each line becomes a card whose arithmetic reads top to bottom as a small ledger with the difference ruled off under it, and the verdict moves from a column to a line under the figures. The agreeing lines move behind a segmented switch rather than into a second section, because a section four cards further down is not something anybody finds on a phone.

The page renders inside app-shell's main column and starts at <main>. The variants that need a bar stuck to the foot or a dialog over the page are shown in a bounded frame — h-[680px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box; as a real page, drop the height and the border, let the bar stick to the shell's scrolling column, and make the dialog fixed inset-0.

anatomy.description: page-header unchanged: breadcrumb, the one h1, which two documents are being reconciled, and the actions. Not sticky — the posting bar at the foot is what has to stay reachable.
The headline figures directly under the header: what each side says and the difference between them, at 20px, before any row is drawn. It is the answer to the question the page was opened with.
One line beside the band counting the lines into agree, in tolerance, needs a reason and blocked. Every number on it is derived from the same array the rows render from.

The exceptions, at full size. Ordered, received, invoiced, the difference in quantity, the difference in value, and the verdict. Header cells are table's, the numeric cells are right-aligned and tabular-nums, and below md it is stacked cards.

One line under the item name where the row is failing on an axis the columns do not carry — a rate above contract, a charge with no order line behind it. An alert-circle in red-600 and a sentence, never a field of colour.
badge's pill shape with the locked dot: emerald-600 in tolerance, amber-500 needs a reason, red-600 blocked. The word is in the pill, so the column reads without colour.
A tfoot on the recessed zinc-50 band. Each figure named by a th scope="row" in the column it totals, and the quantity column carrying an em dash because its units do not add.
The lines that match, collapsed to a count and their value, with a link that opens them. It is deliberately the smallest thing on the page.
One side of the two-sided view: a section with its own h2, its own count and its own value in the header, and the rows under it. The two panes are never subtracted from one another.
A fieldset of radios naming the record on the other side, each carrying the reason it is a candidate — same vendor, same value, dated two days apart — and a last option that means none of them.
The pairs made and not yet posted. A plain list, one Unpair button a row, and a line saying that nothing here has been written.
A receipt or an invoice with the amount of it allocated to the record on the other side, as a real input, with the remainder recomputed under the rows as an output.
shrink-0, opaque, top-bordered, stuck to the foot of the scrolling column: what is about to be written, in figures, and the one button that writes it.
An alertdialog that restates the figures — how many matches, what goes to the ledger, what is held back — and carries the amount on its confirm button.
One role="status" on the page root, in the document from first paint, for the changes focus does not announce: a pair made, a pair undone, a remainder that reached zero.

behaviour: The exceptions render first and the agreeing lines are a count. Nothing reorders on its own — the order is the order of the invoice, so a line found on the paper copy is found on the screen.

Every total, count and remainder is derived from the same array the rows render from, so the foot and the body cannot disagree. On a server-paged reconciliation the figures come from the server over the whole query and the label says which of the two it is.

Matching runs from the keyboard end to end. Arrow keys walk the unmatched list, Enter moves focus into the candidate set, the candidates are real radios, and one button makes the pair. Drag, where a project adds it, calls the same commit and adds nothing of its own.

A pair moves the record out of both unmatched lists and into the pairs list, moves the selection to the record that takes its place, moves focus with it, and says in the status region what was paired and how many are left.

The helper that reveals a selection focuses and scrolls and schedules nothing; whoever calls it decides when. Moving the selection is one tick. Making a pair is the frame after the tick, because the row is destroyed in one x-for iteration and created in another. Undoing one parks focus in the queue before it touches the arrays, because the button that was just pressed is the node about to be removed and a browser resets activeElement to the body the moment the focused node leaves the tree — restoring afterwards is a race against a teardown on a schedule nobody controls. All three failure modes measure as correct: the element is found, focus() is called, and the keyboard is on the document.

A pair is reversible until it is posted. Unpair returns both records to their lists at the index they left from and moves focus onto the restored one, because the button that was pressed no longer exists and focus would otherwise fall to the body. After posting there is no undo on this screen — a posted match is reversed by a journal, which is a separate approval, and the confirmation says so before the press.

A variance inside tolerance posts silently. One outside it will not post until a reason is chosen, and the posting bar says which line is holding it. One that cannot post at all offers no control and is excluded from the posting figures rather than blocking them.
Editing an allocation recomputes the remainder as it is typed. While the remainder is not zero the post button is aria-disabled and the sentence it is described by names the amount outstanding.

Posting is a separate act. The bar states what is about to be written, the dialog restates it in figures and carries the amount on its confirm button, and the submit is guarded rather than disabled while the request is in flight — the bar goes aria-busy and the button keeps focus and its width.

A reconciliation with nothing left is the clean state, and the view may only choose it when no filter is in force and the unscoped unmatched count is zero. It prints what was reconciled and what is carried into the next period, because a period closing does not mean nothing is open.
At 390px the exception table becomes one card a line, the two unmatched panes stack, and the agreeing lines move behind a segmented switch. Nothing scrolls sideways at any width.
accessibility: One main, one h1, and every region below it an h2 — the exceptions, the agreement, each side of the unmatched view, the pairs. The heading outline is the shape of the reconciliation and it is how anybody reads the page without a mouse.

The difference band is a description list: the label is the dt, the figure is the dd, and the sentence saying which way the subtraction runs sits with the figure rather than in a heading three lines above it.

Numeric cells are right-aligned and tabular-nums, and the identifying cell of a wide row is a th scope="row", so a variance eight columns along is announced with the line it belongs to rather than on its own.

A figure in the foot is named by a th scope="row" in the same row. A bare number at the bottom of a reconciliation is announced as a number with no word attached to it, which on this page is the worst place in the application for that to happen.

The unmatched list is a listbox with one Tab stop and a roving tabindex, exactly one option carrying aria-selected="true" and every other option carrying aria-selected="false". Nothing focusable goes inside an option; the controls that act on the selection live in the candidate set beside it.

The candidates are a real fieldset of radios named by a legend that carries the record being matched, so the group is announced as the destinations for that receipt rather than as four unrelated buttons. The last radio means none of them, because the only way to say none is an option that says so.

The guarded post button is aria-disabled="true" and stays focusable, with aria-describedby pointing at the sentence that names what is holding it. disabled would take the control out of the tab order with no explanation attached to anything.

The remainder is an <output> with aria-live="off", because it recomputes on every keystroke and an output is a live region by default. What announces a remainder reaching zero is the status region, once.

The status region is on the page root and is in the document before anything changes. It carries what focus cannot say — a pair made and the count left, a pair undone, a refusal from the server. A region rendered with its message already inside it has not changed and announces nothing.

The verdict is a word in the pill and the dot is aria-hidden, so a column of verdicts is readable without colour. The exception line states the reason in a sentence for the same reason: the red icon beside it is decoration and carries no label.

The confirmation is role="alertdialog" with aria-modal, a focus trap, and Escape closing it back onto the button that opened it. It does not dismiss on a backdrop click, because the question it asks has to be answered.
