The fragment has to carry that id itself, or the swap after this one has nothing to aim at. verdict_dot_class and age_dot_class come off the model and return one of the locked five — bg-zinc-500, bg-amber-500, bg-red-600, bg-emerald-600, bg-zinc-400 — so the pill shape is written once in the template and only the dot changes. In tolerance is emerald-600, Needs a reason amber-500, Blocked red-600. with_candidates() is what stops this page issuing one query per row. It annotates each receipt with the invoices from the same vendor within the tolerance window, ordered by how close they are, and match_note is the sentence saying why each one is a candidate — same vendor, same value, dated two days apart. Working that out in the template means a query inside a loop and a page that is fine on the demo data and unusable on a month of it. reconciliation_totals() returns invoiced, received and difference over the whole invoice and the same three over the exception lines only, so the band at the top and the foot of the table cannot disagree about which population they describe. {% endcomment %}

components.name: Import page
components.description: The screen that takes a spreadsheet into the system: the file and the rules stated before it is picked, the column mapping, the review of what the system understood, the failures grouped by kind, and the write itself with a report at the end.
components.when_to_use: A file of records the user hands over once — an item master, a vendor list, opening stock, a rate contract price list, a month of ledger entries. The overlap that matters is form-page's wizard variant, and it is real: both are staged screens with a review at the end. The line is what is being staged. form-page/wizard steps through fields the user types, so the review is a summary of their own answers and the failure mode is field validation. An import steps through stages of a machine's understanding of a file somebody else wrote, so the user is supervising a translation rather than entering data — which is why the middle stage is a mapping grid that has no analogue in a form, why the review is a table of the system's guesses rather than a recap of the user's, and why the failure mode is a data-quality report about 37 rows out of 1,240 rather than a list of controls that are wrong. If you can name every field on screen at design time, it is form-page. Against attachment: that is a document stapled to a record — a signed challan, a test certificate — which is kept, versioned and downloaded for the rest of the record's life. The file on this page is consumed and thrown away; what survives is the rows it created, and the staged copy is deleted a week later. If the user will ever want the file back, it is an attachment and not an import. Where the user goes to see what the import produced is index-page, and the last thing this screen does is send them there. A screen that shows one array of records with a search box and a pager is data-table; a table of rows with a sortable header and nothing around it is table.
rules: This renders inside app-shell, like every signed-in page. The variants start at the Alpine wrapper and their first structural element is <main>; the shell owns the skip link, the nav landmark and the keyboard shortcuts.

The errors are the screen. A clean import is four clicks nobody remembers; what people live through is row 418's UOM reading Kgs when the master says KG, a duplicate item code, a date Excel turned into 45,904, and a vendor that does not exist yet. Every decision in this entry — grouping failures by kind rather than listing them by row, stating the rule once per group instead of once per row, offering the rejected rows as a file — comes from that stage being the one the screen is actually for.

An import is a write, and a half-finished write is the worst outcome, so the page says which of the two contracts it is honouring and says it in the same words on every stage. All-or-nothing: nothing appears in the master until every row has posted, and cancelling discards what has been written. Partial: the good rows post and the rest come back as a file. A user who cannot tell which they got runs the import again, and the second run is the defect.

Partial is never the default and never silent. It is a radio the user chooses at the review stage, against a stated count — post the 1,203 and skip the 37 — because a master that quietly imported 97% of a price list is harder to notice than one that refused, and the 3% it dropped keep last month's rate until somebody spots it.

Rows are matched on a key and the key is named on screen. Item code here; a GRN number, a vendor code, a ledger voucher elsewhere. It is what decides whether a row is a create or an update, and it is what makes a second run of the same file safe to describe: it will update the rows it made rather than duplicating them. Without a named key, "will this run twice" has no answer and the result screen cannot make a promise.

The mapping grid is the stage with no analogue in a form. One row per column in the file, their header and a sample value on one side, a select of your fields on the other, the system's guess already chosen, and a real answer for a column you do not want — Do not import — rather than leaving it blank and hoping. A blank select and a deliberate exclusion look identical and mean opposite things.

Say how each guess was made. Matched on the header name and Guessed from Rate/Kg are different levels of confidence, and a grid that shows eight confident-looking selects invites the user to press Continue without reading any of them. The guessed ones are the only rows anybody needs to check.

The preview shows values as they will be stored, with the file's own text under anything that changed. KG under Kgs, 04 Sep 2026 under 45904, 39012000 under 3901 2000. A preview that echoes the file back confirms the upload and nothing else; the whole question at that stage is whether the translation is right.

Fixing in place is offered only where the fix is a value translation the system can apply to the whole file and remember for the next one — Kgs means KG for this vendor, now and in September. Per-cell editing is offered for the handful of cells where the file is right and the formatting is not. Everything structural goes back to the spreadsheet: 37 hand-edits are 37 ways for the staged copy to differ from the file the vendor sent, and next month the same file arrives with the same 37 rows. The other answer is defensible and this entry does not pretend otherwise — for one typo in 1,240 rows, sending the user back costs them the whole mapping again, which is why a second upload resumes at the review stage with the mapping already applied.

A commit in flight has a known denominator, so it is progress and not spinner: 742 of 1,203 rows. The bar takes no aria-live — a value repainting every few hundred milliseconds queues announcements faster than they can be spoken — and milestones go into a separate role="status" that was in the document before the run started.

What the user may and may not do during the write is written on the screen, not implied by which buttons are grey. They may leave the page. They may not upload the file again. Cancel means something specific under each contract and the sentence changes with it.

The result screen is the one that has to be unambiguous, so it carries four figures and not one: created, updated, not posted, and the total it was given. 1,203 posted is ambiguous on its own — it does not say whether the other 37 were skipped, rejected or never read.

The rejected rows come back as a file with the same columns the user sent plus a Problem column, because the correction happens in the spreadsheet and a list on a web page cannot be pasted back into one.

One h1 and it does not change between stages. The stage nav says where you are; a page whose title changes from Import items to Import complete is a different document arriving under the same URL, and the heading outline stops being usable as a landmark.

The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box, and the cancel dialog is absolute inset-0 against that frame. As a real page it is the shell's <main>: drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the max-width and the padding, let the footer bar stick to the viewport, and make the dialog fixed inset-0.

anatomy.description: page-header's block: the trail, the one h1, and a line naming the file and its row count once it exists. Never sticky, and never restated per stage.

An <ol> of four stages carrying aria-current="step", the same shape form-page/wizard uses. Stages passed are buttons back, stages ahead are disabled, and below sm the whole thing is one line of text over a thin rail.
One sentence, in the footer bar of every stage, saying whether the rows post together or separately. The same words each time — a paraphrase reads as a different promise.
attachment's zone unchanged: a real file input hidden with sr-only, its label as the peer carrying the focus outline, both drag handlers prevented and the depth counted rather than flagged.
What the file has to be, before the picker rather than after it — the types, the size, the header row, the required columns and a template to download.
One row per column in the file: their header with a sample value, a select of your fields with the guess chosen, and how the guess was made. Below md it is one card per column.
table's markup with the stored value on the first line of each cell and the file's own text under it wherever the two differ, plus an Action column saying create or update.
A <section> per kind of failure: an h3 with the count, the rule stated once, a small table of row numbers and offending cells, and the fix. Not one row per line of the file.
The radio pair that picks the contract when there are failures — post nothing, or post the good rows and report the rest — each with its consequence written under it.
progress's bar over a known total, the two figures under it, aria-busy on the region, and the list of what may and may not be done while it runs.
Created, updated, not posted and the total, the rejected-rows download, whether this can be undone, what a second run of the same file would do, and the route into the register.
Opaque, top-bordered, stuck to the bottom of the scrolling column: the contract line on the left, Back and the stage's primary on the right.

behaviour: Each stage validates before it advances and the primary names what it will do — Continue to mapping, Review the 37 problems, Post 1,203 rows — rather than saying Next four times.

A required field with nothing mapped to it blocks the mapping stage. The primary carries a real disabled attribute, because the reason is a fact rather than a policy, and it points at the sentence naming the field with aria-describedby; both come off together the moment the field is mapped, since a description that is display:none is read to nobody.
Two columns mapped to the same field is an error and is shown on both rows, not on whichever one was touched last.
The problem list filters by kind through a select rather than by row through a search box. Row numbers are how a failure is found in the spreadsheet, not how it is understood.

Fixing a value re-validates the whole staged file rather than the row it was typed into, and the new counts are announced from a role="status" that was already on the page. A fix that repairs 14 rows and reports only the one on screen is a fix nobody trusts.
The commit runs against a known total. The bar moves, the panel is aria-busy, milestones are announced every tenth, and nothing else on the stage is interactive except Cancel.

Cancel during a commit opens an alert dialog that states what is discarded in figures, because the answer differs by contract: under all-or-nothing the 742 rows already written go, under partial they stay.
The result stage is reached by a redirect, so refreshing it re-reads a finished run instead of importing the file a second time.
A second upload of a corrected file resumes at the review stage with the same mapping applied, so a user sent back to the spreadsheet does not pay for the mapping twice.
Nothing scrolls sideways at 390px. The mapping grid becomes one card per column, the preview and problem tables become stacked rows, and the footer buttons go full width in DOM order.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1>, and it survives every stage. Panels below it are h2 and problem groups inside them h3, so the heading outline reads as the stages of one task rather than as five unrelated pages.

The stage nav is an <ol> inside a named <nav>, not a tablist. These are stages of one job rather than views of one record, so the current one carries aria-current="step"; a tablist would promise arrow-key movement between panels that do not exist.
Every stage change moves focus to the new stage's heading, which is tabindex="-1" for that reason. Focus left on the button that has just changed what it means tells a screen reader nothing happened.

The file input is a real input hidden with sr-only rather than display:none, and the focus outline is drawn on its label with peer-focus-visible. A display:none input cannot be focused and the keyboard never reaches the picker at all.

Every select in the mapping grid carries an aria-label naming its source column, because the same grid is rendered twice — a table above md and cards below it — and one for/id pair cannot serve two copies of a control. A <th scope="col"> establishes the column for anything reading the table as a table and contributes nothing to the accessible name of a control that has been tabbed to.

The count of what will and will not post is a role="status" that is in the document from first paint, so re-validating writes into a region that was already there. A live region that arrives with its message already inside it is announced to nobody.

The commit bar is role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax and a name pointed at the heading above it, plus aria-valuetext because the reading is rows rather than per cent. It takes no aria-live and no tabindex — it reports, and Cancel beside it acts.
aria-busy sits on the panel that is waiting and comes off the moment the run stops, whether it stopped by finishing or by failing.

The cancel dialog is role="alertdialog" with aria-modal, a focus trap, Escape closing it and focus returning to the trigger, and it states the figure it is about to discard in its body rather than in its title.
A problem group is a <section> with its heading as the accessible name and the rule in a paragraph the group's table is described by, so the rule is read once on entry instead of once per row.
The rejected-rows download is a link with a name saying how many rows and what format — "Download the 37 rejected rows as XLSX" — because Download three times on one screen names nothing.
Figures carry tabular-nums everywhere, so a count that falls from 37 to 21 after a fix does not reflow the line it sits in.

components.name: Search page
components.description: The whole-page answer to a query typed into the global search: the query echoed as the one h1, the results grouped by record type with a count on every group, the facets that narrow them, and the states the page is in when there is nothing to show yet or nothing to show at all.
components.when_to_use: Where the global search lands when somebody presses Enter — a whole page at a URL, with the query in it, bookmarkable and sendable to the person who asked. The first line to draw is against command-palette, and it is the line between an accelerator and an answer. The palette is the ⌘K overlay: it opens over the page you are already on, it is a shortcut to a record you know exists, it shows about ten rows because that is what fits above a software keyboard, and it is gone the moment you pick one. Reach for it when the user knows what they want and wants to be there in three keystrokes. Reach for this page when the palette was not enough — when the query matched more than an overlay can hold, when the user wants to narrow by type, plant, status, date or value, or when the answer is a set of records they are going to read rather than one record they are going to jump to. The palette links here rather than truncating silently: its last row is "See all results for …", and this page is what that row opens. The second line is against index-page, and it is the difference between searching and filtering. Typing into the box at the top of the purchase order register is a filter — one record type, the register's own columns, the register's own sort, and the result is still the register. This page searches every register at once and does not know which one the answer is in, which is the whole reason it groups; the moment the user does know, index-page is the better screen and its filter is the better control, which is why every group heading here links to it. The third is combobox, which is searching to fill in a field: the typing is a search, but the outcome is a value posted with a form and nothing about it is a page. A query that could not be answered at all — the index is down, the request timed out — is error-page, not the empty variant here.
rules: A result is a record and not a document. This is not web search and there is no snippet: a purchase order row carries the number, the vendor, the value, the date and the status, because that is what the buyer recognises the order from, and it is the same set of facts the register would have shown them. So the row shape is designed per record type — five row shapes, not one generic row with a title and two grey lines under it. A generic row is cheaper to build and it costs the user the one thing they came for, which is to tell at a glance which of the fourteen orders is theirs.

Grouping beats ranking, and it is the opposite call from the one command-palette makes on the same facts. Type 4821 into a procurement system and the number is an item code, a GRN, part of a PO number and a substring of somebody's GSTIN. The palette ranks those into one list because it has ten rows to spend and no room for headings, and it pays for that by writing the kind onto every row. A page has a screen: fourteen purchase orders, three items and one vendor is a more useful answer than eighteen rows in score order, because the user almost always knows which kind of thing they are after and a heading with a count answers that before they read a single row. The heading is also the control — it is where the narrowing starts.

Groups are ordered by the best match inside them, never by size. An exact hit on one item code outranks 186 orders that merely quote it, and a group of one goes first when its one is the answer. Sorting by count puts the noisiest register on top on every query, and sorting by a score that can tie makes the page reshuffle between two searches that looked the same. The tiebreak is a fixed register order, so equal scores never swap.

Three rows per group, and the count is the rest of the answer. With five kinds on one screen the point of a group is its shape and its size, not its contents; the fourth row costs the group below it its heading, and a page whose fifth heading is under the fold is a page that has hidden a whole register. Where a group is truncated, the header carries the link — "See all 186" — and that link is the route to the scoped page.

One group with 400 results is the normal case and not an edge. An item code is on every order line ever raised for that item, so searching one gives 186 purchase orders and always will. The page does not page inside a group and must not: a pager under one heading with four more groups below it is a control that moves rows nobody is reading. It truncates, states the true count, and hands the whole thing to the scoped page, which has one type, one sort, one pager and room for the register's own columns.

Where the field that matched is not on the row, the row says which field it was. A vendor whose name has nothing to do with the query, sitting in the results because the digits are inside its GSTIN, reads as noise and takes the credibility of the whole page with it; the same row with "matched on GSTIN 24AACCS4821K1ZP" under it is the most useful row on the page. The clause is grey and it is a fact, not a highlight — nothing in this system paints a fill behind matched characters.

The query is the URL and the whole query is in it. /search/?q=MS-4821&type=order&plant=silvassa, always a GET, so Back works, a narrowed result is a link somebody can send to the buyer who asked, and the export of a result set cannot disagree with the screen. Facet state that lives only in the browser is the defect: the page looks right and cannot be shared, and the second person to look at it sees a different answer.

Every result row is a real anchor and the whole row is the target — one stretched after:absolute after:inset-0 link in the identifying cell, with any second link inside the row lifted above it on relative z-10. This is exactly where the page differs from the palette, and it is the reason the palette has to link here: nothing inside role="option" may be focusable, so a palette row is a div and a handler, with no middle-click, no open-in-a-new-tab and no status bar saying where it goes. A search result is something people open in six tabs.

A query that is exactly one document number does not redirect. The temptation is real — one obvious answer, so send them to it — and it costs the two most common reasons anybody types a number into a search box: to find out whether the record exists at all, and to see what else refers to it. Redirecting drops them inside a record they did not choose to open, makes Back part of the workflow, and hides the fourteen receipts and invoices that were the actual question. The palette may navigate on Enter because a person picked a row; the page may not, because nobody picked anything. The exact hit gets its own region at the top instead, and it is not repeated in the group below it — a record drawn twice on one page is a record somebody opens twice.

The empty result is the variant that earns this entry. Nobody complains about a search that works. It says what was searched — five registers, by number, code, name and GSTIN, and not the text of notes, line descriptions or attachments — because "no results" leaves somebody retyping the same string, and it offers the loosened query with its real count rather than running it silently. A search that quietly widens is one whose result count nobody can reproduce, and the user cannot tell whether the seven rows in front of them are what they asked for.

Nothing matched and nothing you may see are different answers and the page must give the second one. A permission-filtered search genuinely returns zero rows, and rendering that as "no such record" teaches somebody that the order they raised was never saved. The page names the registers that were not searched and who opens them — a person and a role, never "your administrator" — and it never says how many hidden records matched. Naming a closed register is a fact about the account; naming the number of rows inside it is a fact about the data, and a search box that answers "MS-4821 matched 3 records you may not see" is an oracle anybody can query one string at a time.

There is no create action anywhere on this page, in any state. That is empty-state's rule about a filtered register, and it is sharper here: the whole premise of a search is that the record might exist, so a New order button under "nothing matched" is the shortest path to raising the same order twice. The way out of an empty result is a wider query, not a new record.

A facet's own counts are computed with that facet's predicate removed and every other predicate in force. Tick Silvassa with the counts computed naively and Vapi reads 0, so the facet you just used is the one facet you can no longer use. This is a server fact and not something the browser works out — the counts arrive with the results and the page draws them.

A facet that does not apply to every group is not drawn until the type is chosen. A value band over a mixed result silently drops every vendor and every item from the answer, because they have no value to be in a band, and the count under the h1 falls by a hundred for a reason nothing on screen explains. The band appears the moment the type facet narrows to orders or invoices, and it goes again when it widens.

A facet value at zero keeps its place and stops being a control. Removing it makes the list a different shape on every query, so nobody can find the value they set last week, and the value that vanished is indistinguishable from one the register never had. Rendering it as a disabled checkbox is worse again — a dead tab stop that explains nothing. It becomes plain grey text with its 0 beside it, which is the whole explanation, sitting where it always sits.

Loading draws the facets for real and the results as a flat run of grey rows with no headings. The group shape is precisely the thing that is not known yet, so three headings with rows under them is a promise the answer will probably break — and a skeleton that reflows on arrival is worse than a spinner, because a spinner never promised a layout. The facet rail is drawn because it is largely the same rail every query gets; its counts are blank rather than stale, since last query's numbers beside this query's box are wrong in a way nobody can see.

A bare /search shows recent searches and recently opened records, and the recent searches carry no counts. "MS-4821 — 303 results" recorded last Tuesday is a number that has since changed and that nobody can check, and it is read as current. The query and when it was run is all that is true. These are the palette's recents made browsable: the same list, longer, at a URL, with real links in it.

The query language is optional and, where it exists, an unrecognised key is text and never an error. value:10l typed by somebody who read half the help is searched as the literal string, the page says so and names the fields that do exist, and the results still arrive. A search box that returns a parse error for a typo is a search box people stop using; the recognised keys are echoed as removable chips whose only source of truth is the box itself, so removing a chip edits the string and there is no second copy of the query to drift.

Below lg the rail cannot be a rail. The facets become a bottom sheet whose trigger carries the number in force, and the one facet everybody uses — record type — is promoted out of the sheet into a row of pills that scrolls sideways in its own box. The chips never go into the sheet: they are the answer to what is applied, and a phone that hides the filters without saying which are on is a search that looks broken and cannot be diagnosed.

The h1 is the query that produced this page and not what is currently in the box. They diverge the moment somebody starts typing a new search, and that is right: the heading names the answer on screen, and rewriting it as the caret moves would relabel the results under the reader with a query that has not been run. The box is the next query; the h1 is this one.

On a page template the preamble is an HTML comment and carries no template tags at all, which is the one place the two comment forms are not interchangeable. Django wants the extends tag first and tests that against the first non-text node, so a comment tag above extends raises where raw text does not — and an HTML comment is not a Django comment, so a comment tag written inside one as prose opens a real comment block and swallows the template to the next endcomment. Below the extends line the rule inverts and every block of prose is a real comment tag, because a multi-line hash comment is not a comment and renders from its second line on.

The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box, and the facet sheet is absolute inset-0 against that frame. As a real page it renders inside app-shell's <main>: drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the mx-auto max-w-[1600px] gutter on the band and on the body so the h1 and the results line up, and make the sheet fixed inset-0.

anatomy.description: page-header's <header> inside <main>: white, edge to edge over a border-zinc-200 rule, its content in the same mx-auto max-w-[1600px] gutter the results use. Holds the box, the h1 and the two status lines and nothing else.

input's search markup — bordered wrapper, the icon inside it, type="search", enterkeyhint="search", a clear button that only exists while there is a value and hands focus back when it acts. It carries the query that produced the page, not a placeholder.
The one h1, and it is the query: Results for “MS-4821”. Scoped to one type it becomes Purchase orders matching “MS-4821”. Group headings below it are h2.
A role="status" in the document from first paint, saying how many results in how many registers. Facets, scoping and a new query all rewrite it; it never arrives with its message already in it.
What was searched and what was not — the registers this account may read, named. Present on every state, because the answer means something different depending on it.
An <aside> at lg with its own h2, one fieldset per facet, every value carrying its own count. Below lg it is a sheet behind a trigger that carries the number in force.
One removable chip per facet value in force, with Clear all as a link beside them, in data-table's exact shape. Visible at every width, including when the controls have gone into the sheet.
One white card per record type: an h2 with the type's name, the true count, and where it is truncated the link to the scoped page. Three rows, and the group is the unit that gets ordered.

Designed per record type and carrying the register's own facts. A stretched anchor over the whole row, a status dot in a line box where the record has a state, and a grey clause naming the field that matched when the match is not visible on the row.
The region above the groups when the query is one document number: the record itself, drawn as its identifying band rather than as a row, and not repeated in the group below.
empty-state's shape in the results column — one graphite well, the headline naming the query, what was searched, and the looser query offered with its real count. No create action, in any state.
The recessed band under an empty result naming the registers that were not searched and the person who opens them. It carries no count of what is hidden.
skeleton's row shape with no headings over it, standing in the results column while the query is in flight, aria-busy on the column and aria-hidden on the pulse wrapper.

behaviour: Enter in the box navigates to a new URL carrying the query; it does not filter what is on screen. Every facet, every scope and every page of a scoped result is a parameter on that URL, so Back returns to the previous answer and the current one can be sent to somebody else.

Results are grouped by record type and the groups are ordered by the best match inside them, tiebroken by a fixed register order. Every group states its true count, shows the first three rows, and where there are more the header links to the scoped page.

A group heading is where narrowing starts. Following it scopes the page to that one type: the h1 changes, the facets change to the ones that type has, the register's own sort appears, and a link back to all results sits above the h1.
A query that is exactly one document number promotes that record to its own region above the groups and does not navigate to it. The record does not appear again in the group below.

Facet counts arrive with the results. Ticking a value re-runs the query, rewrites the count line, rebuilds the chips and returns a scoped result to its first page. A value at zero is drawn where it belongs, as text, and cannot be ticked.
A facet that only applies to some record types is drawn only while the type is narrow enough for it to mean something, and disappears again when the type widens.

Nothing matched shows what was searched, offers the loosened query with the count it would return, and offers the two searches this page cannot run itself. It never runs the looser query silently and never offers to create the record.
Where the account cannot read a register, the page says which register and who grants it, on every state, and never how many rows are behind it.

While a query is in flight the box keeps its value, the facets stay drawn with their counts blank, and the results column is a flat run of grey rows with no headings — the group shape is what is being waited for.
A bare /search shows recent searches with when they were run, and recently opened records in the same row shapes the results use. No recent search carries a count.

Below lg the facets are a sheet, the record type is a row of pills scrolling in its own box, and the chips stay on the page. The sheet closes on Escape and on its own button, and focus returns to the trigger.
Nothing on this page scrolls sideways at 390px. The only region allowed to is the record-type pill row, because a second line of pills reads as a different control.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1>, and the h1 is the query. Group headings are h2, the facet rail's own heading is an h2, and the empty state's headline is an h2 as well — an empty search page still has an outline.

The query box precedes the h1 because it precedes it on screen and the two orders must not disagree. It is a <form role="search"> holding a labelled input, and the label says what is searched rather than repeating the word Search.

The count line is a role="status" rendered with the page, so a facet, a scope or a new query writes into a region that was already there. A live region that arrives with its message in it has not changed and is announced to nobody.

The result list inside a group is a <ul role="list"> — the role is written because the divide and the padding remove the list semantics in Safari — and each row is one <li> with one stretched anchor naming the record.

The stretched anchor is the row's accessible name and it names the record, not the row: PO-2026-0418, never "view". A second link inside the row sits above the stretched one on relative z-10 so it is separately reachable, and the row lights up on has-[a:focus-visible] so the keyboard sees what the pointer sees.
A status dot is aria-hidden and the state is a sr-only word at the front of the meta line, so nothing on this page is carried by colour alone.

The facet rail is an <aside> with an accessible name, and each facet is a <fieldset> with a real <legend>. The count is inside the label rather than beside it, so the checkbox is announced as "Purchase orders, 186" and not as "Purchase orders" with a loose number after it.
A facet value at zero is not a control at all. It is text in the same position, so it is read in place and is not a tab stop that does nothing.
Each chip's remove button names the facet it drops — "Remove the filter Plant: Silvassa", never "Remove" — because six buttons called Remove is what gets read out otherwise.

While the query is in flight the results column carries aria-busy="true", the pulse wrapper carries aria-hidden="true", and one sr-only role="status" outside that wrapper says what is being searched. Three jobs, and collapsing any two loses one.

The facet sheet is a role="dialog" with aria-modal, a focus trap, Escape closing it and focus returning to the trigger, and the trigger carries the number in force in its own text rather than in a title.
The empty state's explanation is text and not an aria-label, and the looser query is offered as a real button whose name contains the query it would run.

components.name: Focus page
components.description: One task on the whole screen with the application chrome removed: a bag scanned into a GRN at the gate, a bin counted at a rack, a sample passed or failed at the QC bench. Large targets, type one step up, and a scan field that never gives up the keyboard.
components.when_to_use: A tablet bolted to a trolley or held in a gloved hand, a barcode gun in the other, and one action repeated a few hundred times a shift — receiving bags into GRN-4821, counting rack B-14, passing or failing a sample at the bench. Three things have to be true together: the operator is standing rather than sitting, the screen does exactly one thing, and the input is a scanner or a gloved thumb rather than a keyboard and a mouse. This is one of the only signed-in screens in the library that does not render inside app-shell, and the exemption is narrow on purpose. The shell owns the skip link, the nav landmark, the command palette and the keyboard shortcuts, so dropping it is only paid for where the chrome is actively harmful — where a 68px rail is 68px of target taken off a screen read at arm's length, and where a link to another part of the application is a route to losing a count nobody has posted yet. Every other signed-in screen is app-shell, including the ones that feel simple; the test is not "this page is focused", it is "the operator has one hand free and must not be able to wander off". The same figures typed at a desk are form-page — a keyboard, a mouse, the 13px scale and a validation summary — and that is the right screen for the supervisor amending the GRN an hour later. A QC checklist worked through in full and countersigned is questionnaire; this entry is one of its questions, at a bench, at bench scale, and a run of eighteen of them belongs back in questionnaire where they can be read as a column. A queue somebody walks while keeping the queue on screen is list-detail.
rules: This is the exception to the rule that every signed-in screen is app-shell, and the exception has to be paid for rather than assumed. Dropping the shell drops the skip link, the nav landmark, the off-canvas trap, the palette and the shortcuts, so the screen supplies by hand the two of those it genuinely needs — a <main> landmark and exactly one route out — and deliberately supplies none of the rest. If a screen wants the shell back for anything at all, it wanted app-shell.

Type goes up one step across the whole screen, and that is a decision rather than drift. Nothing here is smaller than 13px: the default is 16px where the rest of the library runs 13px, secondary lines are 14px where the library runs 12px, section headings are 16px, and the one value the operator reads at arm's length — the scanned code, the counted quantity, the running total — is 24px, the top of the scale. An 11px uppercase label under a work light on a tablet propped a metre away measures as accessible and cannot be read, so this screen has no 11px and no 12px type on it at all.

Targets go up with the type. Controls are h-12 at the smallest, h-14 for anything the operator reaches for repeatedly and h-16 for the one thing the screen is for, against the 36–44px the shape token gives the rest of the library. 44px is the floor for a finger on a phone held still; it is not the floor for a gloved thumb on a trolley that is moving. Keypad keys and answer tiles are bigger again, because they are hit without looking.

The h1 is the smallest heading on the screen and that is deliberate. On a page with no chrome the title is the least useful thing on it — the operator knows which station they are at — so it takes the 20px section step and the task takes the 24px page step. The heading outline is still correct: one h1, regions under it as h2.

The scan field holds focus by taking it back on blur, and the blur handler reads relatedTarget before it does. A barcode scanner is a keyboard: with focus anywhere else the scan lands in the wrong control or in no control at all, and the operator finds that out three racks later. Anything the operator is allowed to move the keyboard into carries data-hands-off — the manual-entry box, Finish, Exit — and everything else is pulled back on the next animation frame. The alternative, a document-level keydown handler that redirects characters into the field, was rejected: it swallows the operator's own typing, it cannot tell a scanner from a keyboard, and it breaks the moment a dialog opens.

The first focus of the page is taken on $nextTick, not in x-init directly. x-init on a component root runs before Alpine has walked its children, so $refs.scan does not exist yet and the call is a silent no-op — the screen loads looking ready, the operator scans, and the first read of the shift goes nowhere. It is the same class of defect as focusing a control that is still display:none, and it fails in exactly the same way: measurably correct, visibly nothing.

inputmode="none" on the scan field is load-bearing, not an omission. Focusing a text input on a tablet raises the on-screen keyboard, so a field that always has focus means a keyboard permanently covering half the screen; the hardware scanner types into it regardless of what the input mode says. The manual-entry route flips to inputmode="text" because there the soft keyboard is the point.

Loudness on this screen is size, not colour. A refusal is a 24px sentence in black on white with one red icon beside it, exactly the alert shape the rest of the library uses — a red field behind the message would be visible from further away and would say less, and it is the first thing forced-colours mode repaints. The audible half of a refusal belongs to the scanner, which beeps differently for a good read and a rejected one; the page does not make sound.

A rejection recovers without the operator touching the screen. The field is already empty and still holds the keyboard, so the next scan replaces the message — nothing has to be dismissed. A refusal that needs an OK press costs the operator a hand they do not have, and after the third one they leave a finger resting on the button and stop reading.

Keypad keys prevent default on mousedown so the pointer never moves focus off the quantity field. That is the pointer half only: a tap on a touch screen still moves focus, which the field's own blur handler takes back, and a Tab to a key is a deliberate keyboard move that is left alone.

A run counter is derived from the answers, never incremented. Going back to amend rack 11 must not decrement the total, because rack 11 still holds a figure — the count moves only when a rack gains or loses one. A counter that steps down on Back and up again on Record drifts every time somebody checks their work, and the drift is invisible until the numbers are reconciled at the end of the shift.

A stock count hides the system figure until the operator has committed theirs. Shown first, the count stops being a count and becomes a confirmation of the number already on screen, and the variance the whole exercise exists to find is the one thing it can no longer produce.

Nothing destructive sits within a thumb's width of the commit target. The commit is the full width of the column at the bottom edge where the hand already is; Back, Exit and anything that discards are at the top of the screen or separated by a rule, because two 64px targets 8px apart on a moving trolley is one mis-tap.

Offline, the screen states what is true rather than what is comforting: how many scans are held on this tablet, that none of them is in the GRN, and that closing the tab loses them. It also states what stopped working — the item lookup, so a bag that would have been refused is now accepted into the queue and may be refused when the queue goes up. A queue that lives only in memory has to say so on screen; if the deployment persists it, that sentence changes and nothing else does.

There is exactly one route out and it is guarded. With no sidebar and no breadcrumb, Exit is the only in-app navigation on the screen, so it is the only place the unsaved-work dialog has to live — and beforeunload covers the tab being closed, which on a shared tablet is how work is actually lost. With nothing in hand Exit does not raise the dialog at all, or people learn to press Discard without reading it.

The snippet root is a fixed-height frame — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box, and the exit dialog is absolute inset-0 against it. As a real page it is h-dvh on a bare document that does not extend the app-shell base: drop the wrapper border, make the dialog fixed inset-0, and let the middle band be the only thing that scrolls.

anatomy.description: The one band of chrome: which station this is, which document is open, whether the tablet is on the network, and Exit. It is a <header>, because with no shell nothing else claims the banner landmark, and it is never a topbar — it carries no navigation and no search.
The h1, at the 20px step. It names the document being worked on and nothing else; the line under it carries the item, the lot and the unit.
One 64px field at 24px, permanently focused, inputmode="none". The gun types the code and presses Enter. It is the only control on the screen that takes the keyboard by default.
The named way to type instead — a button carrying data-hands-off that swaps the scan field for a keyed one at inputmode="text". Escape returns the keyboard to the scan field.
The permanent role="alert" panel under the field whose text is replaced on every scan. Accepted, refused, or held — one icon, one 24px sentence, one line saying what to do next.

The last few reads, newest first, so the operator can check the gun is reading the right label without waiting for the total. Server rows are real markup; scans made since load are prepended above them.
The figure and the progress rail at the foot: how many of the known total are done. Derived from the answers, so amending one does not move it.
A 3-by-4 grid of 64px keys for a quantity typed with gloves on. Keys prevent default on mousedown so the pointer never takes the keyboard off the field they write into.
questionnaire's three-tile answer at bench scale — equal columns, a real radio inside each, the tint painted by has-[:checked]. Position carries the verdict, so Fail is always the middle target.
The full-width 64px primary at the bottom edge. It states what is about to be written above itself, and nothing destructive is within reach of it.
What is held on the tablet while the network is down: the count, the oldest entry, and the sentence saying none of it is saved.
The alert-dialog raised by the only route off this screen, naming exactly how much uncommitted work is in hand and offering to post it rather than only to keep or discard it.

behaviour: The scan field is focused on load and takes focus back whenever it loses it, unless the keyboard moved into a control marked data-hands-off. The re-focus runs on the next animation frame, so it does not fight the click that caused the blur.

Enter is the scanner's terminator, not a submit. It reads the field, records the code, clears the field and leaves focus where it is; the form is never submitted by the gun, because a navigation would take the keyboard with it.
A refused scan clears the field, leaves the running count alone and says so. The next scan replaces the message, so recovery costs no touch; nothing has to be dismissed and nothing times out.

The manual route swaps the scan field for a keyed one rather than adding a second field beside it. There is one field on screen at a time, so there is never a question of which one the gun is typing into. Closing it returns focus to the scan field after a tick and a frame, because a control that is still display:none cannot be focused.

A keypad key writes into the quantity field without taking the keyboard off it. The pointer is prevented from moving focus, and a tap that moves it anyway is pulled back by the field's own blur handler.

A stock count reveals the system figure and the variance only after the operator commits their number, and the reveal is a status region rather than an alert — it is the answer to something they just did, not an interruption.

Going back in a run reopens the previous position with its recorded figure already in the field and says that recording again replaces it. The completed count does not move, because the position it went back to still holds a figure.

Offline, scanning keeps working and the queue grows. Anything that would need the server — the item lookup, posting the document — is unavailable and says why in a sentence beside it rather than only by being dead.

Exit is the only in-app navigation on the screen. With uncommitted work it raises the guard; with nothing in hand it leaves immediately. beforeunload covers the tab being closed, and a successful post clears the flag before it navigates.

Only the middle band scrolls. The station strip and the commit bar are fixed at the two edges, so the commit target is in the same place whether the echo list has two rows or forty, and nothing on this screen scrolls sideways at 390px.
accessibility: One <main> and one <h1>, both supplied by this screen rather than by the shell. The station strip is a real <header> so the banner landmark exists, and the commit bar is inside <main> because the action belongs to the task and not to the frame.

The scan field has a real visible <label>, never a placeholder standing in for one. The placeholder says what the field is waiting for and disappears the moment anything is in it, which is exactly when a screen reader user most needs the name.

The outcome panel is a permanent role="alert" whose text is replaced on each scan, not a panel that is inserted and removed. A live region that arrives with the page announces nothing, and one that is created and destroyed announces unreliably; replacing the string inside a region that was already there is what actually reads.
The reveal after a stock count is role="status", not role="alert". It answers something the operator just did, and an assertive interruption would talk over the control they are still standing on.

The progress rail is role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax and a name pointing at the figure already on screen. It is not a live region — announcing the total after every scan is a sentence read three hundred times a shift.

Every bound number is paired with the server's figure written into the element underneath it. A count that exists only as x-text is a hole in the sentence until Alpine boots, and on a tablet at an unloading bay that is not instant.

Answer tiles are real radios inside their labels, so the tile is the target and the label text is the option name. The criterion is referenced with aria-describedby from every option rather than from the fieldset, because focus lands on one radio and only that radio's description is read.

A quantity field driven by a keypad is still a real input with inputmode="numeric", so a keyboard user types into it directly and the keys are an alternative rather than the only route. Each key is a button with its own accessible name; the backspace key is named rather than left as an icon.

A control that is genuinely unavailable is disabled and carries the reason as text beside it. A dead button on a screen with no other affordances tells the operator nothing at all about what to do next, and there is no menu here for them to go looking in.

The exit dialog is role="alertdialog" with aria-modal, x-trap.noscroll and Escape bound, and it returns focus to the control that opened it. It is the only modal this screen has, and with no shell there is no focus trap anywhere else to inherit.

components.name: Settings page
components.description: The configuration screen: a permanent nav of sections down one side and the section being changed beside it. One h1 for the whole screen, an h2 per section, and a Save that belongs to the section rather than to the page.
components.when_to_use: Where a user goes to change one thing out of the forty that live there — company and plant details, the financial year, numbering series for POs and GRNs, approval limits, tax defaults, users and roles, and the master lists every other screen picks from. The line against form-page is what the user came to do. A form page is one record somebody came to fill in and submit: one Save, one dirty state, one exit, and when it is done they leave. Settings is a place. The nav never goes away, the Save is per section, a setting that takes effect the moment it is touched sits beside one that does not, and the accident this layout exists to catch is clicking a different section with changes still pending. Against tabs the test is the count and the address: tabs are two to seven sibling views of one record inside one document, switched by a widget that owns the arrow keys and marks itself with aria-selected. Past about six sections that row wraps, scrolls or turns into a select and stops being scannable — and a settings section is a URL, so its nav is a list of real links marked with aria-current="page" and the browser owns the keys. Against sidebar: sidebar is the application's own navigation and this screen renders inside it. The section nav is the second level and has to read as the second level. Do not assemble it out of sidebar, and do not lift the settings sections up into the application sidebar, where they push every operational destination below the fold. A screen that lists records somebody works through is data-table, and one switch on one record is toggle on that record's page.
rules: It renders inside app-shell like every other signed-in screen, which is the whole design problem: two levels of navigation on one page. The section nav is deliberately the quieter of the two — a bare list with a 2px rule down its side, no icons, no fills, no counts, sitting on the page rather than in a panel of its own. Give it the sidebar's tinted current row and its icon column and the screen has two panels both claiming to be the navigation, at which point the user reads the nearer one as the application and gets lost between them.

Saving is per section and the button says which section it commits — Save approval limits, not Save. One Save over a nav of forty sections promises to write things the user cannot see and has never looked at, and the first time it does that in a numbering series nobody trusts the screen again.

The section footer is always on screen and never appears on the first keystroke. A bar that materialises when the form goes dirty adds 52px to the pane under the pointer at the exact moment somebody is typing in the last field. What arms is the line inside it, not the bar itself.

The dirty guard is per section and armed by input and change, exactly as form-page arms it. What is different is where it fires: the likely accident is not closing the tab, it is clicking Tax defaults while Approval limits has an edit in it, so the guard has to intercept the nav click as well as beforeunload. A guard that only covers the browser navigation catches the rare case and misses the common one.

Two promises on one screen, and they are never interleaved. A switch writes when it is touched; a field writes when Save is pressed. Put them in one run and the user cannot tell which gesture applies to which row, so they go in separate blocks under separate h3 headings with a divider between them, and the block of switches says once that there is nothing to save. When a section holds both, the Save moves out of the card footer to the end of the block it commits — a Save button sitting under a run of switches promises to save the switches.

Sections the user may not open are absent from the nav, not disabled in it. A greyed row advertises a section, refuses it, and gives no reason; and it is the one component in the page that a screen reader cannot reach to be told why. The filtering is the view's job — the template guard is the second lock, not the first, because the section still has a URL somebody can type.

Every section is a URL and the nav is real links. That is what lets an error message elsewhere in the application say where the rule lives — "orders above ₹5,00,000 need a second approver, set in Settings, Approval limits" — and link straight to it. A tablist cannot be linked into, and a settings screen that cannot be linked into gets explained in a wiki instead.

The numbering series preview is computed in the page from the same four fields the server concatenates, so the string the user is about to commit is the string they read. It is an <output>, never a disabled input, and the half that cannot be undone is gated by an acknowledgement with the actual next number printed in it rather than by a dialog that says Are you sure.

How many role columns a matrix can carry belongs to checkbox, not to this entry: checkbox/matrix up to three, checkbox/wide-matrix past that, with a frozen capability column and both axes pinned. This section shows the split-by-module arrangement, which is the other way to spend the room a settings pane has and reads better when the modules are genuinely separate concerns. Either is right here. What is never right is a second copy of the same boxes restacked for a phone, because two renderings of one checkbox is two values for one permission and after a save the hidden one is wrong — checkbox/wide-matrix-phone is a separate variant for exactly that reason.

Below lg the nav stacks above the pane in DOM order, which is honest for nine sections and nothing more. At 390px a permanent side nav cannot be permanent: the index and the section become two screens, and the Back control is a real link because in production those are two URLs.

The destructive section is last in the nav, below a rule, and it is a white card like every other section. The colour is in the icon and in the button, and the consequence is written out in figures — 34 orders, 61 invoices — because that sentence is what stops the click, not a red panel behind it.

The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box, and any dialog is absolute inset-0 against that frame. As a real page it is the shell's <main>: drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the max-width and the padding, and make the dialog fixed inset-0.

anatomy.description: page-header unchanged: the one h1, which says Settings and not the name of the open section, and a line under it naming the company and the financial year everything on this screen is scoped to.

A <nav> with its own accessible name holding a list of real links, one per section, marked with aria-current="page". A 2px zinc-700 rule and font-medium mark the open one; there is no fill, because the fill is what the application sidebar uses and there are two navs on this screen.
A search input above the nav on a deployment with more than about fifteen sections. It hides rows in the nav and never touches the pane, and it reports how many of the total are left.
The single column beside the nav holding exactly one section. A <section> labelled by its own h2, with tabindex="-1" so the keyboard follows a nav click into it.
card's shape: header with the h2 and one line saying what the section governs, body, footer. Blocks inside it are h3 and divided with border-zinc-100 — cards do not nest.
Always present. Left, who changed the section last and when, and the role="status" line the save answers into. Right, Discard then Save, and the Save names the section.

The run of toggles that write when they are touched, under their own h3, with one line saying there is nothing to save and one role="status" line under the run. Never mixed into the run of fields above it.

The per-section dirty flag, the alert-dialog it raises when a nav link is clicked with changes pending, and the beforeunload that covers the tab closing. Three answers, and focus lands on Keep editing.
The last item in the nav, below a rule. An ordinary white card whose rows carry the consequence in figures and a bordered red-text button; the typed confirmation lives in alert-dialog, not here.

behaviour: Clicking a section navigates. The pane swaps, focus moves into the new section's heading, the nav marks it with aria-current="page", and the scroll position of the pane resets while the nav does not move.
Each section commits on its own. Save writes that section and nothing else, the footer status line says so in words, and the last-changed line and its timestamp are rewritten from the response.

The dirty flag is set by input and change bubbling out of the section's own controls. While it is set, a click on any other section link is intercepted and the guard dialog opens with three answers — keep editing, discard and switch, save and switch — and beforeunload covers the tab closing.

A switch writes on change and answers into the status line under its block; it is never wired to the section's Save. A failed write reverts the switch to the value the server still holds and says which setting did not stick, naming it.

The numbering preview recomputes on every keystroke in the prefix, the separator and the width, and shows the next document number that would actually be issued. Changing the running number arms an acknowledgement that prints that number; Save stays refused until it is ticked.
The nav filter hides rows and updates a count. It never filters the pane, never changes which section is open, and clearing it restores the list with the open section still marked.
A permission matrix is a Save section, not a live one. Twenty-four boxes that each post on change is twenty-four requests nobody can reconcile, and no way to say what the state was before.

Below lg the nav stacks above the pane. At 390px the index and the section are two screens: choosing a section replaces the index, Back replaces the section, and focus is placed deliberately on both moves.
A section the signed-in user may not open is not in the nav and not in the pane. Nothing on the screen says it was removed, because a gap that announces itself is an invitation.
accessibility: One <main> and one <h1>, and the h1 is Settings. The open section's name is the h2 inside the pane and the blocks inside that section are h3 — the heading outline is how anybody skims a screen whose content changed without the page title changing.
Two navigation landmarks on one screen both need names, or the landmark list reads "navigation, navigation" and neither can be chosen. The shell's is Main and this one is Settings sections.

The section nav is links with aria-current="page", never role="tab" with aria-selected. They are two different promises: aria-current marks where you are among destinations, aria-selected marks which panel is showing, and a link wearing role="tab" tells a screen reader that arrows will switch panels and that Tab will jump into one, after which neither happens.

The pane is a <section> with aria-labelledby pointing at its own h2 and tabindex="-1", and it takes focus after a section change. Without it a nav click leaves the keyboard in the list and the next Tab walks the remaining thirty-nine sections instead of entering the one that was opened.

The save answers into a role="status" line inside the section footer. A save that changes nothing visible — a limit that was already 5,00,000, a tick that was already on — is announced by nothing at all otherwise, and the user presses Save again.

A toggle that writes on change carries its own role="status" line naming the setting, because reverting a switch after a failed write is script setting checked, and a programmatic change to checked is announced by nothing.

Every checkbox in a permission matrix carries an aria-label naming both axes — "Approve over ₹5,00,000 — Approver". Row and column headers are announced when a screen reader walks a table and not when somebody tabs through the controls inside one, which is how this screen is used.

The guard dialog is role="alertdialog" with aria-modal, is trapped, and puts focus on Keep editing. Discard is never the focused answer: the dialog exists because something is about to be lost, and the safe answer is the one under the fingers.

The numbering preview is an <output> with aria-live="off". It recomputes on every keystroke and an <output> is a live region by default, so left on it reads the whole document number back one character at a time while the user is still typing the prefix.

On a phone the index and the section are two screens, and both moves place focus: choosing a section focuses its heading, Back focuses the row that was opened. A screen swap with focus left behind is a page that did not move for the person using it.

Deactivate and reset

Three acts that cannot be reversed from this screen. Each one is separate and each one is guarded on its own.

Deactivate Vapi plant

Stops new orders, GRNs and issues being raised against VAPI-02. The 34 open orders, 61 unpaid invoices and ₹27,10,400 of committed value stay in the ledgers and stay readable. The plant is never deleted — a plant with ledger history against it cannot be.

Reset the GRN series

Sets the running number back to 1 for FY 2026–27. GRN-4821 and everything before it keeps its number, so the register will hold two receipts numbered GRN-0001 once the first new one is posted.

Revoke every API key

4 keys are in use, the oldest issued 11 Feb 2025. The weighbridge feed and the Tally export both authenticate with one of them and stop within the minute.

Every act on this page is written to the audit trail with your name against it.

Deactivate Vapi plant

9 users work only at this plant and lose the ability to raise anything from tomorrow morning. Reactivating is a support request, not a button.

components.name: Onboarding page
components.description: The screen that tracks a deployment being configured: every task that has to be finished before a document can be raised, grouped, with what is done, what is blocked and on what, who owns each one, and what the page becomes once it is finished.
components.when_to_use: The first weeks of a deployment, where the company, the plants, the financial year, the numbering series, the tax defaults, the chart of accounts, the item and vendor masters and the opening balances all have to exist before a single purchase order can be raised, and somebody has to be able to see how far that has got. The line against form-page — and specifically its wizard variant — is who owns the clock. A wizard owns the user until it finishes: one record, one sitting, one Save, and the steps are sequential because step 3 needs step 2's answer. This is none of those. The tasks take days, half of them are somebody else's job, one is waiting on a trial balance that has not arrived, and the person who opens the screen on Friday is not the person who opened it on Tuesday. So the state is on the server, the progress is on the page, and any task can be opened in any order. Built as a wizard, the second person to touch it starts again at step 1 and the first person's work is invisible. Against settings-page: every setting on this screen lives in settings-page permanently, and that is where it is changed for the rest of the deployment's life. This page is a view over those same sections for the first month — it adds the order, the ownership, the dependencies and the progress, and nothing else. It is not a second home for a setting. The moment setup is complete it stops being a destination: the nav entry goes, the URL keeps working, and what is left is the record of who set what up and when. A checklist parked at 100% for three years is clutter with an audit trail attached, which is what the complete variant is about. Against import-page: several of these tasks are not forms at all — item masters, vendor masters and opening stock open the import screen — so this page links out to it and marks itself done from what the import posted. Do not rebuild an import here. And this is not a product tour: no coach marks, no tips, no dismissible overlay pointing at a button. A tour teaches an interface; this tracks work that people are already doing.
rules: It renders inside app-shell like every signed-in screen. The variants start at <main>; the shell owns the skip link, the nav landmark and the keyboard shortcuts, and the nav item that points here is the thing the complete variant takes away.

It is a checklist and not a wizard, and the whole markup follows from that. Every task is reachable at any time, nothing is behind a Next, and the state is server state on the company rather than per-user state in a browser. A checklist kept in localStorage tells the second person that nothing has been done, and the first person that it has, and neither of them finds out.

A blocked task is a link with a reason, never a disabled row. Disabled takes it out of the tab order, gives no reason and is the one control on the screen a keyboard cannot reach to be told why — and the reason is the only useful thing the row has. So the blocker is named in a sentence under the row, outside the row's own anchor so the link to it is a real link and not a link inside a link.

Two kinds of waiting, and they are not the same problem. A dependency is a fact the system knows and clears by itself — a lock mark in zinc-500, the neutral shade, because nothing is wrong. A person who has not answered is a state somebody set, so it carries a name, the date it was asked and the amber-700 warning mark, because it will not clear unless somebody chases it. Give both the same mark and the screen cannot tell you which of the six stalled tasks a phone call would fix.

Work time and waiting time are never added together. Two hours of typing and four days of waiting on a trial balance do not sum to anything anybody can plan against, so the header carries three separate figures — what you can start now, what is waiting on a person, what is waiting on a task — and the estimate on a row is only ever the typing.

A skipped task is not an unfinished one and the arithmetic has to show it. Seventeen tasks, two skipped, fifteen counted, nine done. The skipped ones keep their row, keep who skipped them and why, and can be brought back, which puts them back in the denominator. Print both figures or the progress bar becomes something to game.

Skipping asks for a reason and refuses to proceed without one. In November somebody asks why there are no customer masters, and "skipped" with no sentence beside it is indistinguishable from an oversight. The reason is short free text and it is shown wherever the skip is shown, including on the completion record.

Anything waiting on a skipped task is stranded and the screen says so. A skipped task never finishes, so a dependency on one never clears — that is the one place where skipping is not free, and it is the state the blocked variant spends a whole card on.

A task the server can detect is marked done from the fact, not from a tick. Item masters is done when the item table is not empty; opening stock is done when the first stock entry posts. A manual tick over a detectable fact goes stale the first time somebody deletes the rows again, and then the checklist is lying about the database it sits on.

Each task is its own URL with its own h1. Unlike import-page, where four stages are one document and the h1 must not change, a task here arrives in an email — "Meera has assigned you Approval limits" — and a page whose h1 says Set up Konspec has not told the person who opened that link what they are looking at.

A row that also carries a Mark done button cannot be one big link, because a form inside an anchor is not valid HTML and browsers repair it by moving the form out. Where the completion posts from the list, the row is a flex container with the title as the link and the form beside it; where it does not, the whole row is the link.

Every task shows who it is on, and unassigned is a state with its own block rather than an empty cell. The task nobody owns is the one that is still not done at go-live, and it is invisible in a list sorted by anything else.

The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box. As a real page it is the shell's <main>: drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the max-width and the padding, and let the phone variant's footer bar stick to the viewport.

anatomy.description: page-header's block: the one h1, and a line naming the company, the plants, the financial year and the go-live date everything on this screen is scoped to. No status pill — setup is not a record and none of the five locked statuses describes it.

A white card holding progress's bar over the counted total, the two figures written out, and the sentence that reconciles them with the number of tasks that exist. Its heading is what the bar is named by.

Three figures under the bar, never one: what can be started now with a time on it, what is waiting on a person, what is waiting on a task. Adding them together produces a number that describes nothing.
One named task at the foot of the summary card with the route into it, so the answer to "what do I do now" is on screen before any group is read.

card's shape, one per stage of the setup — company and plants, money and tax, master data, opening balances, people. An h2, one line saying what the group governs, the count done, and the task rows in a divided list.

marker's checklist item as a row: the state mark with its sr-only word, the task name, a meta line carrying who and when or who it is on, and the typing estimate on the right. The mark is the only colour on the row.
The sentence under a blocked row, outside the row's anchor, naming what it waits for as a real link and saying whether it clears by itself.
On optional tasks only, and absent rather than disabled on the rest. It opens a reason field in place and the reason is required; a skipped row afterwards carries who, when, why and Bring it back.

On the complete screen: the date this page leaves the navigation, what the URL becomes afterwards, the route to settings-page where the settings actually live, and a control for the person who wants it gone today.

behaviour: Any task can be opened at any time, including one that is blocked — the task page states the blocker and offers the route to it rather than refusing to render. Nothing on this screen enforces an order; the dependencies describe one.

A dependency clears itself. When the task it waits on is completed the blocked task becomes startable on the next render, with nobody going back to tick it, and the row's mark and sentence change together.

Marking a task done posts to the server and the progress figures, the bar and the group count are all rebuilt from the response. Nothing is kept in the browser, so a second person on a second machine sees the same page.
A task the server can detect is completed by the fact rather than by the button: the item import posting 1,240 rows finishes Item masters, and the button is not offered on those rows at all.

Skipping opens a reason field in place, requires it, and on success the row keeps its place in its group with the skipped mark, the reason and Bring it back. The denominator drops by one and the percentage is recomputed from the new one.
Reassigning a task is a change other people are told about — it appears in the resume variant's list of what happened while you were away, with who moved it and when.

The change list on the resume screen is measured from the user's last acknowledged visit, and that marker moves when they press Mark as read and at no other time. Moved on render, a three-second visit on a phone erases the record of four days somebody needed to read.

Below sm the group cards keep their rows and the estimate moves from the right of the row into the meta line. At 390px finished groups collapse to a single summary row and the next task moves out of the summary card into a bar pinned to the foot of the screen.

When the last counted task is done the page swaps to its completion state: the checklist becomes a record, the retirement date is set, and the navigation item is removed on that date rather than immediately, so the person who finished at 18:00 can still find it the next morning.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1>. On the list screens it names the setup; on a task screen it names the task, because that is the page a link in an email lands on. Group cards are h2 and blocks inside a task are h3.

The progress bar is role="progressbar" on the track with aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin and aria-valuemax counted in tasks rather than per cent, aria-labelledby pointing at the heading already on screen, and an aria-valuetext that says what the skipped tasks do to the figure. Read as "60%" it hides the two tasks that were taken out of the denominator.

Every state mark is an aria-hidden icon paired with an sr-only word at the front of the task name — Done, Blocked, Waiting on somebody, Skipped, Not started. Hiding the icon without putting the word back deletes the only carrier of the state, and leaving it audible reads out fifteen icon names down one list.

A blocked row is a real link and never disabled. The blocker sits in a paragraph after the row, outside its anchor, so the link to it is reachable — an anchor inside an anchor is repaired by the parser and the inner one stops existing.

The count of what is done is a role="status" that is in the document from first paint, so a completion or a skip writes into a region that was already there. A live region that arrives with its message inside it is announced to nobody.

The skip reason field is a real labelled control, is focused when the panel opens, and its Cancel returns focus to the Skip button that opened it. Focus after a reveal needs a frame as well as a tick: at $nextTick the panel is still display:none and .focus() on it is a silent no-op.

Buttons that act on a named task carry the name in their accessible name — Send Nilesh Patil a reminder, Skip Opening customer balances — because Skip and Remind repeated down a screen name nothing, and a screen reader's control list is where they are read.
The avatar circle beside a person's name is aria-hidden, since the name is written beside it; otherwise it is announced as "NP Nilesh Patil".

The timeline of what changed while you were away is an ordered list, its rail and dots aria-hidden, and the dates carry the sequence in words. The rail is a picture of the order, not the record of it.

Nothing on this page is a coach mark, a tooltip on load or a focus trap. It is an ordinary document with links in it, which is what makes it survive being abandoned and reopened by somebody else four days later.

    Optional and done, which counts exactly like any other finished task. Optional describes whether it may be skipped, not how it is counted once it is not.

A skipped task is not an unfinished one

  • It leaves the denominator, so 9 of 15 rather than 9 of 17, and both figures stay on the page.
  • It never appears in what is next, and it never appears in the work-left estimate.
  • Anything waiting on it waits for ever. A skipped task never finishes, so the dependency never clears — that is the one cost, and it is why the screen names what is stranded.
  • It can be brought back at any time, which puts it into the denominator again and the count down with it.
