components.name: Audit page
components.description: The whole system's audit trail as a page: who changed what, when, and what the value was before. Queried across records, actors, fields and dates, grouped by day, newest first, and append-only — nothing on this screen edits anything.
components.when_to_use: Somebody is asking a question about the past that no record answers on its own — why a rate does not match the contract, whether an approved order was amended after it was approved, who released the QC hold in March, what a leaver touched in their last fortnight. The line against record-page and its activity variant is who is asking and where they started. record-page/activity is one record's history shown as a region of that record's page: the reader already has the record open, the trail is bounded by it, and there is no query — it is the last thing you read before deciding about that record. This is the system's trail, queried across records, actors, record types, fields and dates, and an auditor does not start from a record. They start from a question, and the filter apparatus is the component: the same event that appears as one line under a purchase order appears here beside events on four other records because they share an actor and an afternoon. Both exist and neither replaces the other — the record variant here is the same events as record-page/activity with the whole query apparatus over them, and it is what the "See the full trail" link at the foot of that region opens. Against index-page: that is a register, and the rows in a register are things — orders, vendors, receipts — which can be created, opened, edited and acted on in bulk. The rows here are events, which happened, and cannot be any of those; that is why this page has no selection, no row actions and no create, and why saying so is worth a paragraph. Against table: that is the rows and a sortable header with no page around them, and it is what a register is built from — an audit trail is not sorted by column, because the only order it has is time and it is descending. Where the question is "what does this record look like now" rather than "how did it get here", the answer is record-page.
rules: This renders inside app-shell, as the whole of <main>. The gutter is mx-auto max-w-5xl — wider than a record because an entry carries an actor, a record, a timestamp and a pair of values on one line, and narrower than a register because there is no column set to compare across.

The old value is the component. "Akshay Prabhu updated PO-2026-0418" is a receipt for an audit trail rather than one; the entry that answers the question is the one carrying ₹58,400 and ₹61,200 and the timestamp between them. Every entry that changed a field renders both values, and an entry that cannot produce the old value is a defect in what was written, not a case to design around.

Append-only has consequences on screen, and they are the unusual ones in this library. There is no selection column, no row menu, no bulk bar and no create — not disabled, absent. Every other list here grows those the moment it is real, so a reviewer will ask where they went: an event happened, and there is nothing to do to it. What the page does instead is filter, group and export, and those three are where the whole design budget goes.

Time is the only order and it is descending. The day is the unit people argue in, so the day heading is a full-bleed recessed band with one list under it — marker/grouped's shape — rather than one card per day. A card per day is what record-page/activity does because it draws at most a handful of days; a page that can draw forty of them turns into forty bordered boxes with two lines in each, and the column of marks restarts at every one.

Today and Yesterday are said in words and the date is said beside them, never instead. "Today" alone is wrong the moment the page is left open past midnight, printed, or screenshotted into a ticket, and a trail whose headings depend on when it was read is not evidence.

The timestamp is a real <time datetime> in a fixed-width gutter, so a column of times reads down the day. Relative time — "2 hours ago" — is a gloss and never the record: it is written after the absolute time, not in place of it.

A multi-field change is a grid, not a run of sentences. Field, old, new as three tracks means nine changed fields read as three columns instead of nine paragraphs, and the arrows line up down the middle. The column headings are drawn once above the band and only from sm up, because the strike-through and the arrow already say which value is which.

A value that was empty is the word "not set" and not an em dash or a blank cell, and clearing a value shows the old value struck through against the word "cleared". A blank on either side is indistinguishable from a field the export dropped.

The strike-through and the arrow are decoration. line-through is announced as deleted text by some screen readers and by most as nothing at all, so an sr-only "changed to" closes the old value. Without it the entry reads as two figures and no direction — this is record-page's rule and it is repeated here because half the entries on this page are that shape.

Colour is rationed harder here than anywhere else in the library. Most entries take the zinc-500 dot, and the palette is spent on the three that are worth stopping at: a refusal is red-600, something finished is emerald-600, and a change made after the record was approved is an amber-700 alert-triangle. Colour every entry by its verb and the column is a barcode by the twelfth row.

Nothing on this page is a live region and nothing polls. An audit trail that announces itself while somebody is reading it moves the page under the cursor, and the entry they were mid-way through is now four rows down. The reload is the refresh, and the load-more control is the only thing that adds rows.

The export is an audited event and the dialog says so before it runs. An auditor who takes a file away has done something the trail has to hold, and the scope of what they took — the count, the range, the filters in force — is exactly what the entry records. Stating it in the dialog is also the last chance to notice that the range is wrong.

The retention window is a fact of the page, not a footnote. The scope line in the header carries the earliest date the trail holds, and a query that reaches past it is a different empty state from a query that found nothing.

anatomy.description: page-header's shape unchanged: a <header> inside <main>, white over a border-zinc-200 rule, holding the breadcrumb, the one h1, the scope line and Export. No create button, because nothing on this page creates anything.
One 13px line under the h1 stating the query in figures — how many entries, between which two dates, over which record types, and that the order is newest first. It is the sentence the export copies.

index-page/filters' band unchanged: a search box, one select per axis — actor, record type, field, date range — and the chips underneath saying which ones are in force. Below sm the controls fold into a drawer and the chips never do.
One white rounded-xl panel holding every day. It has no heading of its own; the day bands inside it are the h2s.
marker/grouped's recessed band: bg-zinc-50, border-y border-zinc-100, an 11px uppercase h2, and one <ul> under it pointing back with aria-labelledby. Today and Yesterday are named and dated.

A mark, a timestamp gutter, the sentence naming the actor and the record, a meta line, and the diff band where a field changed. No hover fill, no link on the row itself — the record inside the sentence is the link.

A <dl> in a bg-zinc-50 well: field, old value struck through, new value after a decorative arrow. Three grid tracks from sm up, stacked below it, with the column headings drawn once and only where the grid is.
What an entry shows instead of a diff — the count of rows exported, the document printed, the permission that was refused, the session and the address. One line, same 12px, same well.
The count line and the pager, or the Load more control where the trail is being appended to. It is a role="status" and it is what says how much of the trail is on screen.
dialog/form's panel: the scope restated in figures, the format, and the sentence saying the export will itself be written to the trail.

behaviour: Nothing on the page mutates anything. There is no selection, no row menu, no inline edit and no delete, and no control is drawn disabled to stand in for one — the only writes this screen can cause are the export, which is itself an entry, and the filters, which are a GET.

Filters compose and the count line says what they add up to. Actor, record type, field and date range are one query; the chips are the answer to which of them is doing something, and each drops on its own because the usual cause of an empty trail is one filter set an hour ago and forgotten.

Changing a filter re-runs the query and rewrites the count line in place. The count is a role="status" that was in the document before the first keystroke, so the new figure is a change a screen reader reports rather than a block that arrives already speaking.

Load more appends the next batch under the last entry and never above it. A batch that starts on a day already on screen continues that day's list instead of drawing the heading twice, and the count line is rewritten and focused when the last batch lands, because the control that was pressed has been replaced by a sentence.
The day headings are the page's outline and they are stable. Appending never renumbers or reorders anything already drawn; the trail only ever grows downwards.
Export states its scope in figures before it runs, writes the file, and writes an entry recording who took what. The dialog is the only place on the page where a button causes a write.

At 390px the timestamp gutter moves above the sentence, the filter controls go into a drawer, and a change touching more than two fields collapses to a count with a disclosure — nine fields as twenty-seven stacked lines is an entry nobody can read past.

Deep-linking a query is the point. Every filter lives in the querystring, so the trail an auditor was looking at is a URL they can put in the finding, and Back returns to the query rather than undoing a chip.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1> in the band naming the trail, and every day heading an h2 with the day's list pointing back at it with aria-labelledby. The heading outline is the whole navigation this page has.

The day heading is a real heading and never a list item. Written as an <li> it is announced as item 1 of 12 and every count in the group is off by one; dropped between two <li>s without one it is lifted out of the list entirely.
The timestamp is a <time datetime> carrying the full local date and time, so the 14:22 in the gutter is unambiguous to anything reading the markup rather than the heading above it.

The diff is a <dl>: the field name is the <dt> and the two values are two <dd>s under it, which is what keeps them one unit. An sr-only "changed to" closes the old value, so the pair is announced as "Rate, line 3 — fifty-eight thousand four hundred, changed to sixty-one thousand two hundred".

Every mark in the gutter is aria-hidden and every arrow in a diff is aria-hidden. The colour of a dot is a summary of a sentence that is already written out beside it; where the dot is the only thing carrying a warning, the warning is written in the entry as well.
The count line is role="status" with tabindex="-1", so it both reports a new figure and is somewhere to put focus when the control that was pressed is removed from the page.

Each chip's button is named for the filter it drops — "Remove the filter Field: rate" — because six buttons called Remove is what gets read out otherwise. Clear all is a link beside them, not a second filled button.

The export dialog is aria-modal with a focus trap, its heading names it, and the scope figures are inside the dialog rather than only on the page behind it — a dialog that says "Export?" over a scope the reader can no longer see is a confirmation of nothing.

The permission and retention empty states are prose in the region they apply to, naming the scope that is closed and the person who opens it. Not a title attribute and not a disabled control, both of which explain nothing on a phone.

components.name: Docs page
components.description: The manual inside the application: the standard operating procedures, the approval limits, the definitions a screen assumes you already know. The only screen in this library that is mostly prose, so the measure, the heading rhythm and what a link looks like inside a sentence are the component.
components.when_to_use: Reach for this when the content is the page — how a capital indent is raised, what the approval limits actually are, what a QC hold means and who may release it, the numbering scheme somebody looks up once a quarter. Everything in it is arranged for reading rather than for working: one measure, one heading rhythm, a section nav down the left and an on-this-page rail down the right. Three neighbours sit close enough to be reached for by mistake, and each of them is a different question about the same document. record-page is the screen for an SOP that is itself a record in a document-control module — the revision awaiting approval, the change request against it, the distribution list, the eleven people who have signed it — because there the SOP is a row with a state and a set of actions on it. This entry is how that same document reads. They are two screens for one object and not one screen in two modes, and the tell is whether the page carries buttons that change the document: if it does, it is record-page. form-page owns help text that belongs to a field. A sentence explaining what goes in Cost centre lives in that field's help slot, where the person filling it in is already looking, and moving it into a manual is the first step of a form that needs a manual. accordion is an FAQ, or any set of sections that collapse to their headings inside some other page: a component in a page, where this is the page — and note that a manual may not be built out of one, because find-in-page walks rendered text and does not reach an x-show panel, so a term inside a closed section does not exist as far as the browser is concerned. Be blunt about the failure mode this entry attracts: documentation written because a screen was confusing is a bug report, not a document. A page explaining which of two buttons to press is a defect logged against the screen carrying those two buttons; writing it up here fixes nothing, and it hides the defect behind something that looks like a deliverable. What belongs here is what no screen can say on its own — the policy, the sequence that crosses four screens, the reason a limit is what it is.
rules: It renders inside app-shell like every other signed-in page. The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[720px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box; as a real page, drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the cap and the padding, and let the rails stick against the shell's own scrolling column.

The measure is max-w-xl, 576px, which is the reading measure container already derived and writes as an exact string twenty-two times. Everything in the article body lives at it — paragraphs, lists, callouts, figures and tables alike — rather than the text capping and the furniture running wider, because a table set 100px wider than the column beside it reads as a mistake and the eye has to find the left edge twice. The consequence is a rule about content: a block that genuinely cannot live at 576px is not prose. A fourteen-column matrix is a register and belongs on an index-page with a link to it from here.

The body is text-[14px]/6 and not the default text-[14px]/5. Rule 19 fixes the seven sizes and allows prose, and only prose, a looser leading than the default pairing; this is the screen that allowance was written for. 24px of leading on 576px of 14px type is what makes 400 words readable in one sitting, and marker's own anatomy already assumes it — "h-6 for the 24px leading of prose" is in that entry before this one existed. Everything on the page that is not a sentence stays at the default pairing: the rails, the meta lines, the captions, the table.

The heading scale runs out below h3 and the entry says so rather than inventing a step. h2 is text-[20px]/7 font-semibold tracking-tight, h3 is text-[16px]/6 font-semibold, and h4 is text-[14px]/5 font-semibold — the same size as the body, separated by weight, by the tighter leading and by the space above it, because the next size down from 16 is the body size and there is nothing between them. There is no h5. A document that needs one is two documents.

The rhythm is asymmetric and the asymmetry is the whole of it: the space above a heading is larger than the space below it, so a heading belongs to what follows rather than floating between two blocks. mt-10 above an h2, mt-8 above an h3, mt-6 above an h4, and the first block after any heading takes mt-3. Paragraph to paragraph is mt-4. A list under the sentence that introduces it takes mt-3 — tighter than two paragraphs, because the list is the object of that sentence and not a new thought — and the paragraph after the list goes back to mt-4. Four numbers, and they are read as three pairs.

Prose here is text-zinc-900. On every other screen in this library prose describes a control or a record and correctly takes the secondary zinc-600; on this one the prose is the content, so it takes the primary colour and zinc-600 is left to the things around it — the lead under the h1, the captions, the rails, the source line under a quotation. A whole manual set in secondary text reads as a caption for something that is not there.

The lists are marker/prose unchanged — list-disc space-y-1 pl-5 marker:text-zinc-400 for a set, list-decimal pl-6 marker:tabular-nums marker:text-zinc-500 where the order is the point. Only the text colour changes, for the reason above. Nothing here hand-rolls a bullet: ::marker already does everything a prose list needs, and the rest of the marker entry is for the cases it refuses.

An inline link is the Link token and nothing else: text-zinc-900 underline underline-offset-2. In a paragraph already set in zinc-900 the underline is the only thing separating a link from the words on either side of it, which is the point of the token and also its one constraint — a link that is a whole sentence underlines the sentence and the paragraph reads as struck through. Link two or three words, and never the words "click here", for the reason the print variant gives.

A cross reference is written as the document number. "See SOP-QA-011, QC hold and release" and not "see this page", because the manual is printed and pinned to a noticeboard often enough that a reference which only works as a link is a reference that is missing from every copy on the floor. The number is what survives the printer, the photocopier and the WhatsApp photograph of the sheet.

Inline code is the exact span the library already writes thirteen times: rounded bg-zinc-200 px-1.5 py-0.5 font-mono text-[12px]/4 text-zinc-600. It is a tinted shape carrying no ring, which is the one place rule 12 is not applied in this system, and this entry copied it rather than fixing it — thirteen occurrences that agree are the convention, and changing them is a separate decision. 12px of mono against 14px of Inter is about right optically; do not scale it to 13 to match.

There is no code block and no <pre> in this entry. Nothing in an internal manual for this domain is a program, and the one shape that looked like it needed one — a numbering format — is inline code inside a sentence. A manual that genuinely has to show a block of code needs a pattern this system does not have, and that is a flag rather than something to improvise on a docs page.

Nothing in the library sets italic type, so a quotation earns its shape from a 2px left rule in the Edge colour and the secondary text colour, with the source on a line under it rather than in a <cite> — which browsers italicise by default and would be the only italic in the system. The rule is border-zinc-300 rather than the border-zinc-200 a nested edge would take, because it is a mark and not an edge, in the same way the current item in the section nav takes a graphite rule against a zinc-200 track.

Do not write scroll-mt on the headings. The system carries one base rule for this, [id] { scroll-margin-top: 88px }, because app-shell's topbar is 56px of sticky white and a fragment that lands under it reads as a link that did nothing. This page is the reason that rule exists — it has more fragment targets than the rest of the application put together — and a page that sprinkles scroll-mt-22 onto the elements that happen to be targets today covers the ones it can see and none of the ones somebody adds next week.

The page cap follows the number of columns, which is container's own rule that the cap follows the widest thing the page has to hold. max-w-6xl where the section nav, the article and the on-this-page rail are all on screen — 220 plus 576 plus 200 plus two gaps and the gutter is 1,092 and the next cap up is 1,152. max-w-5xl for the two-column arrangements, a procedure with a step rail or an article with a section nav. max-w-4xl where the article stands alone with a document control block over it, and max-w-3xl where it stands alone without one. Copy the cap from the variant you copied the arrangement from; a three-column cap on a one-column page leaves 400px of white beside a 576px measure and reads as a layout that failed to fill.

Nothing a :class ternary toggles may also appear in the static class attribute, and the scroll-spy rail is where this entry learned it. Alpine removes the classes it added and cannot remove the ones the markup wrote, so an item rendered current by the server keeps its graphite rule for the rest of the session and the rail ends up marking two headings at once. The fix is not a second binding — it is that the resting state has to be reachable without a class at all: the marker is a 2px <span> with no background of its own, which is transparent until the ternary paints it, and the resting text colour is inherited from the <ul> rather than written on the link. That also fixes the case where Alpine never boots, which the border-l-2 the section nav uses would have rendered in currentColor — a dark rule against every item in the list.

Neither rail is a panel. The section nav and the on-this-page rail are both bare lists on the page ground with a 2px graphite rule marking the current item, exactly as settings-page writes its section nav and for the same reason: the application sidebar to the left of this screen is already a white panel claiming to be the navigation, and a second one on the page means the user reads whichever is nearer as the application. Three columns of navigation-looking things is the failure this rule prevents.

The two rails carry different aria-current values and the difference is real. The section nav marks the document you are reading with aria-current="page". The on-this-page rail marks a position inside that page with aria-current="location", because every one of its entries is the page you are already on and a rail full of aria-current="page" says the document is five different documents.

Below xl the on-this-page rail is a second copy of the same list rendered inline under the lead, and the two copies are hidden against each other with xl:hidden and hidden xl:block. That is table/responsive's idiom — two renderings of one thing in the DOM, one of them display:none, which is out of the accessibility tree rather than duplicated in it. The trap that comes with it does not apply here and would if the rail ever grew a control: a form field with a name posts even while its rendering is hidden.

A controlled document says which revision it is on every screen and on every sheet, and the answer is never relative. "Updated 3 months ago" is decoration on a document somebody has to be able to place in time — an auditor asking which revision was in force on 12 May 2026 needs the effective date in figures, so the absolute date is the record and the relative phrase, if it is shown at all, sits beside it in brackets.

A superseded revision says so in the flow of the document, above the lead, and not in a dismissible banner. It is not a notice about the application, it is the first fact about the text underneath it, and it has to survive being printed, dismissed and scrolled past. The link on it goes to the current revision, and the document number stays the same in both — what changed is the revision, which is why the number alone is never enough to identify what somebody read.

A step in a procedure carries its own id and its own anchor, and the anchor is a visible link rather than something revealed on hover. "I am stuck on step 4" is how this content is actually used, over a phone, by somebody with one hand on a keyboard, and a link that only appears under a pointer does not exist on a touch screen and cannot be reached by a keyboard at all.

The print rules are document-page's, unchanged and not re-derived: everything that is not the sheet carries print:hidden, backgrounds are not allowed to carry meaning because Chrome and Firefox drop them, rules stop at border-zinc-300, corners go square with print:rounded-none, nothing inside the sheet is sticky, and the @page rule lives once in the project stylesheet because @page is an at-rule and not a utility. What an SOP adds to that list is one line: an uncontrolled-copy note in the sheet footer beside the revision, because the whole point of a revision number is that the paper on the noticeboard may be older than the screen.

anatomy.description: page-header unchanged: the breadcrumb into the manual, the one h1, and a meta line carrying the document number, the revision and the effective date. Never sticky — the on-this-page rail is what keeps the reader oriented.
The manual's tree down the left: a bare list on the page ground, a border-l-2 zinc-700 rule on the current leaf, groups seeded open to the page being read. Sticky from lg, above the article below it.
The one white card holding the whole document. Its h2s are the document's sections and not card headers, so the card has no header of its own and the h1 stays outside it in the page header.
max-w-xl inside the card. Everything in the body sits at it, and the white to the right of it at wide viewports is the measure doing its job rather than a layout that failed to fill.
The first paragraph, in zinc-600 at the body size. There is no size between 14 and 16 that is a paragraph, so the lead is separated by colour rather than by scale.
A nav of the h2s in this document, aria-current="location" on the one in view. Sticky from xl on the right; below xl the same list renders inline under the lead.

alert's markup unchanged — white card, zinc-300 edge, the only colour in the icon — carrying a note, a caution, or a plant difference. A callout is a sentence that had to be seen, never a paragraph somebody put in a box for emphasis.

One <li> of the procedure: a numbered well at the leading of its heading, an h3, the body, and a visible anchor link. break-inside-avoid, because a step split across two sheets is two half-instructions.
The bordered <dl> a regulated SOP carries: number, revision, effective date, supersedes, owner, approver, next review. Two columns from sm, one at 390px, and every value tabular-nums.
A table of what changed in each revision and who approved it. Three columns, because a table in prose has at most three.
A screenshot or a diagram with a numbered caption under it at 12px. Numbered because the prose refers to it by number, and a caption that only describes cannot be referred to.
Who last reviewed the page and when, when it is next due, and the route for saying something on it is wrong — which is where a confusing screen gets reported.
document-page's A4 sheet with the SOP on it: the control block as a header, the steps, the signature block, and a footer carrying the revision and the uncontrolled-copy note.

behaviour: The on-this-page rail follows the reading position. An IntersectionObserver watches the h2s and the last one to cross the top third of the viewport becomes current; the rail marks it with aria-current="location" and a graphite rule, and clicking an entry is an ordinary fragment link the browser handles.

Nothing in the article body collapses. Every word of the document is rendered, because find-in-page walks rendered text and Ctrl-F is how half the readers of a manual navigate it — a section folded behind a disclosure does not exist to the browser's own search.

The section nav's groups are seeded open to the section being read, rendered by the server rather than defaulted in Alpine, because moving between two pages of the manual is a full page load and a map that starts empty folds the tree up underneath the reader on every one of them.
Opening one group in the nav does not close another. A manual is walked across sections as often as down one, and the single-open rule saves two rows of height and costs a click on every journey.

The nav filter hides rows with the hidden attribute and then hides any group left with nothing under it, in a second pass. A group label standing over nothing is what makes a filtered tree look broken.

Search runs over the manual and nothing else, and each result says which document and which section it came from. A result on a superseded revision is labelled as one rather than hidden, because it is often what somebody was sent a link to.

A step is a fragment target. Following a link to one lands the heading clear of the topbar through the [id] scroll-margin rule, and the reader sees the step number they were given rather than the step under it.

At 390px the three columns become one. The section nav is replaced by a link to the manual's contents and a search field, the on-this-page rail becomes a native <details> under the lead, and the body keeps its leading — the measure is wider than the screen, so at that width it is doing nothing.

Printing removes the chrome and leaves the document. The nav, the rail, the search field and the toolbar carry print:hidden; the steps take break-inside-avoid; and the sheet footer prints the revision and the date the copy was taken, because a printed SOP is uncontrolled the moment it leaves the screen.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1>, and it is the document's title in the page header. The h2s below it are the document's sections and the h3s are the steps or the subsections inside them — that outline is the manual's table of contents, and it is what a screen reader user navigates a 2,000-word page with. Heading level is structure and has nothing to do with type size, which is why the h4 here is the same 14px as the paragraph under it.
Both rails are <nav> elements with names — "Manual sections" and "On this page" — so they are two distinguishable landmarks in the list rather than two unnamed regions, and either can be skipped.

aria-current="page" belongs to the section nav and aria-current="location" to the on-this-page rail. Every entry in the rail is the page the reader is already on, so marking one of them as the current page contradicts the nav on the other side of the article.

The scroll-spy writes aria-current as the string "location" or the string "false" and the graphite rule is bound to the same expression, so the mark a sighted reader sees and the one a screen reader hears cannot disagree.

Every step and every h2 is a fragment target and none of them carries scroll-mt. The page relies on the system's one base rule, [id] { scroll-margin-top: 88px }, so a target added later is covered without anybody remembering to add a class to it.

A step's anchor is a real link with a real name — aria-label="Link to step 4" — and it is visible at rest. An anchor revealed on hover is unreachable from a touch screen and from a keyboard, which are the two ways this content is actually read.

A callout is a bordered block with its own text; the icon inside it is decorative and unlabelled, so the sentence has to state the severity itself. "Do not release the hold until the lab result is on the record" says what the amber triangle says.

The superseded notice is text in the reading order, above the lead and inside the article, rather than a colour or a banner over the page. It is the first thing said about the document, and it must be the first thing read.

The figure is a <figure> with a <figcaption>, and the caption is numbered so the sentence that refers to it has something to refer to. A screenshot standing in for an instruction needs the instruction in the prose as well — an image is not a step.

The table in prose carries a caption saying what it lists, <th scope="col"> on every heading and <th scope="row"> where the first cell names the row. It has no hover state, because nothing in it is a target.
The search field is labelled, its result count goes to a status region, and the empty case names what was typed. A list that silently empties reads as a search that crashed.

Raising a capital indent

SOP-PUR-004 · Revision 3 · Effective 01 Apr 2026 · Owner: Materials, Silvassa

Procurement

  • Onboarding a vendor
  • Raising a capital indent
  • Approval limits
  • Amending an order
  • Closing an order short

Quality

  • Inward inspection
  • QC hold and release

All 204 pages

A capital indent commits money that is not in the plant's operating budget, so it takes a budget code before it takes a vendor. This page covers indents raised at Silvassa and Vapi. For revenue purchases — consumables, spares, packing material — see SOP-PUR-002, Raising a purchase indent.

On this page

  • When an indent is capital
  • Raising it
  • Who approves it
  • After approval

When an indent is capital

An indent is capital when what is bought is expected to last more than one financial year and is carried on the fixed asset register. The test is the asset register and not the value: a ₹40,000 die that is capitalised is a capital indent, and ₹6,00,000 of packing film is not.

Three things make an indent capital regardless of what it costs:

  • Plant and machinery, including a rebuild that extends the life of an existing machine.
  • Moulds, dies and tooling held against a part number rather than consumed in a run.
  • Anything installed in the building — a compressor line, a weighbridge, a fire panel.

If none of the three applies and the item is still expected to last three years, ask Accounts before raising anything. Getting this wrong is expensive to unwind: the indent has to be cancelled and raised again under the other series, and the budget consumed in between shows against the wrong head until the month is closed.

Raising it

Open Materials → Indents → New and choose Capital as the type. The type cannot be changed after the indent is saved, which is the one field on the form worth reading twice.

A capital indent without a budget code will not route to anybody.

It saves as a draft and sits there. Nothing tells you, because nothing has been submitted.

The budget code is on the capital budget sheet the plant head circulates in April. It is eight characters — plant, year, head, serial — and it is written SIL-27-PM-04 on the sheet and typed without the hyphens.

What to attach

Two quotations for anything above ₹2,00,000, and three above ₹10,00,000. A single-source purchase needs a note saying why, signed by the plant head, attached to the indent and not sent separately.

Who approves it

The indent routes on its value, and the value is the whole indent rather than the line. Splitting one purchase across two indents to stay under a limit is the thing internal audit looks for first.

Approval limits for a capital indent, by value
Indent value Approver Also needs
Up to ₹2,00,000 Plant head —
₹2,00,001 to ₹10,00,000 Plant head, then Finance Two quotations
Above ₹10,00,000 Director Three quotations, board note

Limits are set once a year and are the same at both plants. They are listed again, with the delegation in force while an approver is away, in SOP-PUR-006, Approval limits.

After approval

An approved capital indent becomes a purchase order raised by the buyer holding that category. The indent stays open until the order is closed, so a partially received machine keeps its indent open and the budget stays committed against it.

At Vapi the budget code is allotted by Accounts, not by the plant head.

Everything else on this page is the same at both plants.

Last reviewed 12 Jun 2026 by Anil Kulkarni · Next review 01 Apr 2027

variants.html:
QC hold and release

SOP-QA-011 · Revision 5 · Effective 01 Jul 2026

A hold stops material moving. It is not a rejection and it is not a note on the record — while a lot is on hold nobody may issue it, and the store cannot override that from the issue screen.

What a hold does

Placing a hold writes a block against the lot in the batch ledger. The lot keeps its quantity and its location, so it is still counted in stock and still valued, and every issue against it fails with the hold reference rather than with a generic error.

A hold is placed by Quality and by nobody else. A buyer who believes material is wrong raises a re-inspection request against the lot, which is what puts it in front of Quality.

Three kinds of hold

The kind is chosen when the hold is placed and decides who may release it:

Inward hold
Placed automatically on every lot received against a material with an inspection plan. Released by the inspector who passes the lot.
Quality hold
Placed by an inspector on a lot already in stock, usually after a complaint from the line. Released by the QA head.
Customer hold
Placed against finished goods when a customer has raised a claim. Released by the QA head with the claim reference on the record.

Releasing a hold

A release needs a result on the record. Not a phone call, not an email to the store — the lab result or the inspection has to be entered against the lot first, because the release records which result it was made on and that link is what an audit follows.

  1. Open the lot in Quality → Holds.
  2. Check that the result you are releasing against is listed under the hold.
  3. Choose Release and enter the reason.
  4. The block clears on the next issue attempt, which is immediate.

A hold that has to stay while part of the lot is used is not a partial release. Split the lot first — Quality → Holds → Split — and release the child lot. Releasing and re-holding leaves a gap in the ledger during which the whole lot was issuable.

Who may release each kind of hold, and what the release needs
Hold Released by Needs
Inward Inspector Inspection result
Quality QA head Lab result
Customer QA head Claim reference

If the material has already moved

Material issued before a hold was placed is traced through the batch ledger and recalled by the QA head. That is a different procedure and it is SOP-QA-014, Recall of issued material.

Material that does not conform to specified requirements shall be identified and controlled to prevent its unintended use or delivery.

IATF 16949:2016, clause 8.7.1 — the requirement this procedure exists to meet.

The caption is numbered because the sentence above refers to it by number. A caption that only describes the picture cannot be referred to from anywhere else in the document, and a printed copy has no other way of pointing at it.

Booking a goods receipt

SOP-STO-002 · Revision 7 · Effective 01 Jul 2026 · Owner: Stores, Silvassa

Nine steps, about fifteen minutes for a single-vehicle receipt. Do them at the gate, in this order, before the vehicle is released — a GRN booked after the lorry has gone cannot be corrected against the weighbridge.

Before you start

  • The vehicle is on the weighbridge and the gross weight is recorded.
  • You have the vendor challan and, for a taxable supply, the e-way bill number.
  • The purchase order is approved and not closed.
  1. 1

    Check the challan against the order

    The challan carries the order number. If it does not, or it carries one that is closed, the vehicle does not come off the weighbridge until the buyer confirms which order it is against.

  2. 2

    Open the order in Receipts

    Stores → Receipts → Against an order. The screen scans a barcode as well, which is faster at the gate and is the same form either way.

    Open the receipt screen

  3. 3

    Enter the vehicle and the challan

    Vehicle number, challan number, challan date and the e-way bill. The e-way bill is required above ₹50,000 of taxable value and the form will not post without it.

  4. 4

    Weigh in and record the tare

    The net is gross less tare and the system computes it. Do not type a net weight over it: the two figures are what the vendor is paid on and a typed net that does not reconcile is found at the monthly weighbridge audit, by which time the vehicle is four weeks gone.

    A difference over 0.5% against the challan needs a shortage note before the GRN posts.

    Step 7 covers it. Do not adjust the weights to make the difference go away.

  5. 5

    Enter the received quantity per line

    Count what is on the vehicle, not what the challan says. The two columns sit beside each other on the screen for that reason.

  6. 6

    Post the GRN

    The number is allotted on posting — GRN-4821 — and it cannot be reused. A GRN posted in error is reversed and a new one raised; there is no delete.

  7. 7

    Raise a shortage note if there is a difference

    Short, excess or damaged, on the GRN itself, while the vehicle is still on site. The driver signs the shortage note and the copy travels back with the vehicle.

  8. 8

    Put the material away against the bin

    Material against an inspection plan goes to the quarantine bay and stays on inward hold until Quality passes it. See SOP-QA-011, QC hold and release.

  9. 9

    Release the vehicle

    Gate out against the GRN number. The gate register and the GRN reconcile nightly and a vehicle released without one is the exception the security supervisor is asked about the next morning.

Last reviewed 04 Jul 2026 by Sunita Rane · Next review 01 Jul 2027

variants.html:
Closing an order short

SOP-PUR-009 · Revision 2 · Effective 01 Apr 2026

An order is closed short when the balance quantity will never be received — the vendor cannot supply it, the requirement has gone, or the material has been bought elsewhere.

Before you close it

Closing short releases the committed value back to the budget and stops the order appearing in the pending-receipt register. It does not cancel anything already received and it does not touch an invoice that has been booked.

A short close is reversible for seven days.

After that the order is archived and reopening it is a request to Materials.

Tell the vendor before you close, not after. The order is what they are producing against, and a closure they hear about from the accounts department two weeks later is a claim.

Do not close an order short to make the pending register look clean at month end.

The commitment is what the plant is planning cash against. A closed order that is still coming is a payment nobody has provided for.

Where the balance is genuinely still expected but late, the answer is a revised delivery date on the order, which keeps the commitment and moves it out of the overdue count.

Who may close

The buyer who raised the order, up to a released value of ₹1,00,000. Above that it is the plant head, on the same screen, and the released figure is shown before the confirmation.

At Vapi a short close above ₹50,000 also needs the Finance controller.

Silvassa has no second approval on a short close. Everything else on this page is the same at both plants.

Both routes record who closed it and why, and the reason is printed on the order's own document. It is read by the vendor, so write it as something a vendor can read.

Amending an order

SOP-PUR-007 · Revision 4 · Effective 01 Apr 2026

Nothing in the manual matches “”.

  • Onboarding a vendor
  • Raising a capital indent
  • Approval limits
  • Amending an order
  • Closing an order short
  • Booking a goods receipt
  • Short and excess receipts
  • Material issue
  • Inward inspection
  • QC hold and release
  • Rejections and debit notes
  • Document numbering
  • Glossary

An order is amended when a term on it changes after it has been approved — the quantity, the rate, the delivery date or the freight. Every amendment raises the revision number and reissues the document to the vendor.

What may be amended

Anything except the vendor and the plant. Changing either of those is a new order, because the first one has already been sent to a vendor who may have started against it.

  • Quantity, up or down, on a line that has not been fully received.
  • Rate, which re-routes the order for approval if the new value crosses a limit.
  • Delivery date, which is the amendment that does not need re-approval.

components.name: Document page
components.description: The record as a sheet of paper: a purchase order, a GST tax invoice, a delivery challan, a goods receipt note. Laid out on A4, printed from the browser, and built so that what comes out of the printer is the same document that was on screen.
components.when_to_use: A record that leaves the building — the purchase order a vendor is sent, the tax invoice an auditor will ask for later, the delivery challan that travels with the lorry, the goods receipt note the store files. The screen where that record is worked on is record-page: the header, the status, the tabs, the timeline and the buttons that change it. This is the artefact record-page produces, and the two are not one screen in two modes — record-page is arranged for the buyer amending the order, and this is arranged for a transporter at a gate, a vendor's accounts clerk and an assessing officer three years later, none of whom has a toolbar, a hover or a second click. Reach for card when the thing is a panel grouping one region of a screen; a card is furniture and this is the whole page. Reach for table when rows are read, sorted and paged on screen — a printed line table has different rules, it may not restack into cards, it repeats its own header across sheets and its totals may not be orphaned, and those rules live here rather than in table. The test is where the pixels end up: if the answer is a printer, a courier or a PDF attached to an email, it is this.
rules: It renders inside app-shell like every other signed-in page, and the shell is chrome. Everything that is not the sheet — the toolbar, the copy selector, the back link — carries print:hidden, and what is left on the paper is the document. app-shell's own rail and topbar do not carry print:hidden today, so a document printed from inside the shell as it stands comes out with the navigation down the left of it. That is a gap in app-shell and closing it is a decision for a person, not something this entry patches from the outside.

Backgrounds do not print. Chrome, Firefox and Edge drop every background fill unless somebody ticks Background graphics in the print dialog, and nobody ticks it. So nothing on the sheet may carry meaning in a fill: structure is borders and rules, the recessed table header keeps bg-zinc-50 for the screen but earns its shape from a border-y that survives without it, and the status dot — a 6px background circle — is not drawn on a document at all. A document says Approved in a word. This is the one screen in the system where the locked status pill is the wrong component.

A watermark is the same defect twice over. DRAFT set diagonally in pale grey is a background effect in a colour chosen to be faint, so it prints as nothing on a laser and as a smear on an inkjet, and the sheet that comes out looks exactly like the real one. The draft variant states it in a ruled band of type above the letterhead, where it cannot be dropped and cannot be missed.

Rules that have to survive paper stop at border-zinc-300. The Divider token, border-zinc-100, is a 4% grey and is simply not there on a printed sheet; border-zinc-200 is marginal and is used only for the row rules inside a line table, where the rows are close enough together that the eye supplies the rest. Hierarchy comes from weight — border-b-2 under the letterhead, border-t-2 over the totals — and not from a darker colour, because the system has no ink-weight border token. That is a real gap and this entry left it open rather than inventing one.

Physical size is @page, and @page is not a utility. A4 is 210 by 297mm: the sheet is max-w-[210mm] with min-h-[297mm] so the screen preview is the shape of the paper, and print:min-h-0 because the printable area is 297mm less the page margin — a 297mm minimum on paper pushes a blank second sheet out of every one-page document. The margin itself, @page { size: A4; margin: 14mm 12mm }, cannot be written as a Tailwind class and belongs once in the project stylesheet. The preview variant carries the rule to copy.

Do not trust a breakpoint to mean paper. A4 portrait is 794 CSS px at 96dpi, so md: applies while printing and lg: does not — but the Scale field in the print dialog changes the layout width, and at 50% the same sheet lays out at about 1588px with every lg: rule switched on. Where the printed shape has to differ from the screen, write print: and let it win. A table that only becomes a table at md is a stack of cards on somebody's paper.

The line table is the one region here allowed to scroll sideways at 390px, inside its own overflow-x-auto box, and it is cancelled again with md:overflow-visible print:overflow-visible. Both halves matter. A preview that restacks the lines into cards is a preview of something that will never come out of the printer, which is the whole reason the exception is taken. And an element with overflow other than visible is monolithic in paged media, so a line table left inside a live scroller is clipped at the first page break instead of splitting across sheets. The same trap makes overflow-hidden rounded-xl — the card idiom every other panel in this system uses — wrong on a document. The exception used to cost an affordance — at 390px the line table simply looked cut off at the right edge. The framework has an answer for that now and this entry takes it: the scroller carries relative, tabindex='0', role='region' and a name, so it is reachable and announced, and a line under it says it scrolls. relative is not cosmetic there: an sr-only span inside a scroller with no positioned ancestor resolves against the document and widens the page, which is a 390px overflow with no visible cause.

A table splits across sheets by itself and repeats its <thead> while it does, because display: table-header-group is the browser's own default for a real <thead>. It stops the moment the table is wrapped in a flex or grid container, a transform, or a scroller. break-inside-avoid goes on every <tr>: a row split across the fold is not a shorter row, it is two rows carrying half a figure each.

Nothing that adds up may be orphaned. break-inside-avoid on the tax summary, on the amount in words, on each signature block and on the foot. A totals block that lands on a sheet of its own with no lines above it is a defect the reader cannot detect, because it reads as a total of what is on that sheet.

Page numbers and carried-forward subtotals are the view's job, not the browser's. counter(page) inside an @page margin box is not implemented in Chrome, and no CSS anywhere can sum the lines that fell on the sheet before. So a document that needs "Page 2 of 3" and a brought-forward figure is paginated on the server into one <section> per sheet, each ending in break-after-page — that is multi-page. Where neither is needed, do not paginate: let the table flow and repeat its own header, which is purchase-order.

Nothing inside the sheet is sticky. position: sticky is meaningless on paper and actively wrong on the way there — a sticky header prints on the first sheet and leaves a gap on the rest. The toolbar above the sheet is sticky, and it is print:hidden.

Corners are square. rounded-xl is the panel affordance of a screen; a printed form is ruled boxes, and one rounded box among them reads as a screenshot pasted into a document. The sheet keeps rounded-xl on screen, because there it is the edge of the paper, and drops it with print:rounded-none.

Secondary text on the sheet stops at zinc-600. zinc-500 and lighter are screen-chrome colours: at 11px through an office laser they read as grey mush. The one place zinc-500 is used here is a footer line nobody has to read.

Figures carry two decimal places and Indian grouping — ₹5,26,080.00. The registers drop the paise because in a column of forty they are noise; on a tax document they are the amount, and dropping them makes the sheet disagree with the ledger by up to fifty paise a line. Every figure keeps tabular-nums, and an identifier — GSTIN, HSN, e-way bill, PO number — is never truncated, because a shortened identifier is a different identifier and somebody will read it into a phone.

The values are the server's. Nothing on the sheet is computed in the browser, which is the line between this and form-page: a rail that recomputes is helping somebody fill a form, and a document that recomputes is a second implementation of the tax engine whose output the vendor and the assessing officer read. The only Alpine on these variants is in the chrome — which copies to print, and the button that calls print().

anatomy.description: The zinc-100 page the sheet sits on, so the preview reads as paper on a desk. print:bg-white print:p-0 — on paper there is no desk, and a ground that survives printing is a full-bleed grey rectangle nobody asked for.

One A4 page: max-w-[210mm], min-h-[297mm] on screen, print:min-h-0 print:rounded-none print:border-0 print:p-0. The border and the rounded corner are the edge of the paper drawn for the screen; on paper the edge is the paper.
Who is issuing the document — name, address, GSTIN, CIN, telephone — under a border-b-2. The mark beside it is a bordered square, not a filled one, because a filled square prints as white.
The document type as the h1, the number under it, the date and the revision. Top right, because that is where every clerk who handles the sheet looks first.
Two square bordered boxes side by side: who it is addressed to and where the goods go. Each carries the GSTIN and the state code, because the state codes are what decide the tax split.
A <dl> of the four or five terms that qualify the whole document — required by, payment terms, freight, buyer reference. One bordered band, two columns on a phone and four from sm.

A real <table> inside overflow-x-auto md:overflow-visible print:overflow-visible. <thead> repeats across sheets by itself; every <tr> takes break-inside-avoid; the foot totals the column it sits under and leaves a mixed-unit quantity column as an em dash.
The legally controlling figure, spelled out, in a bordered box with break-inside-avoid. It is text in the reading order, never decoration and never aria-hidden.

The build-up from taxable value to the round-off and the total, as its own small table beside the words. break-inside-avoid: a tax block split across sheets is a tax block that has to be added up twice.

Original for Recipient, Duplicate for Transporter, Triplicate for Supplier — a word in a bordered box at the head of the sheet. Text, because a tint would print as nothing and all three copies would then be identical.
Two, at the foot, each break-inside-avoid: who prepared it and who signs for the company. The rule to sign over is a border-t, never a run of underscores, which is read out as punctuation.
The computer-generated note and "Page 1 of 1". The date and URL a browser prints down the margin come from the print dialog, not from here, and nothing in the page can remove them.
The screen chrome above the sheet: back, Print, Download PDF, which copies. print:hidden, and it is the only part of the page carrying state.

behaviour: Nothing on the sheet moves. It has no disclosure, no sort, no hover state and no tooltip, because every one of those is a promise that the paper cannot keep. Everything that moves is in the toolbar above it.

Print calls window.print() on the page that is already on screen. It does not open a second window and it does not re-render the document into a hidden frame — the sheet the user checked is the sheet that has to go to the printer, and a second render is a second chance for the two to disagree.

Download PDF is a server route that returns a file, not window.print() renamed. The browser's Save as PDF and a server-rendered PDF are different documents with different fonts and different page breaks, and a vendor who receives one and an auditor who receives the other will find the difference.

The copy selector adds hidden to a copy rather than filtering it out of the record. Unticking Triplicate takes it off the paper and off the screen at once, so the count in the toolbar and the sheets below it cannot disagree.
Each copy and each sheet ends in break-after-page except the last one, which ends in nothing. break-after-page on the final section prints a blank sheet at the end of every job.

At 390px the toolbar wraps to two rows, the sheet fills the width, and the line table scrolls sideways inside its own box. Everything below the table — the amount in words, the tax summary, the terms, the signatures — is full width and reachable without scrolling, because those are the parts somebody checks on a phone.

A document produced from a record that is not approved prints as a draft: the band at the head, no signature block, and the number shown as not yet allotted. It is a state the record can be in, not a preview mode the user chooses.

The browser's own page header and footer — the URL, the date, the page numbers down the margin — are switched off in the print dialog and nowhere else. No CSS in this page can remove them, so the sheet carries its own page numbering rather than relying on the browser's.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1> naming the document and its number, and an h2 on every region — Vendor, Deliver to, Order lines, Tax summary, Terms. Several of those h2s render at 11px uppercase; heading level is what a screen reader plans the document with and has nothing to do with size.

Where one page carries three copies, the h1 belongs to the page and each copy is a <section> with an accessible name whose own headings start at h2. Three h1s on one page is three documents and the outline says nothing about which is which.

On a paginated document the h1 is on the first sheet only. Continuation sheets carry a compact head at h2 naming the document and the sheet number, which is how a paper continuation sheet has always been headed.

The line table has an sr-only <caption> saying what it lists and against what, <th scope="col"> on every heading, and <th scope="row"> on the foot total. A bare figure at the bottom of a table is announced as a number with no word attached to it.

The copy marking is text. It is the only thing separating three otherwise identical sheets, so it cannot live in a fill or a border colour — neither of which is available to a screen reader or to a laser printer.

The amount in words stays in the reading order at full contrast. It is the figure that controls if the digits and the words disagree, and it is the line a reader who cannot scan a column of numerals uses.
The rule above a signature caption is a border, never a run of underscores. A row of underscores is announced as punctuation, one character at a time.
The letterhead mark is aria-hidden. The company name is beside it in text, and a bordered letter K adds nothing to what is already said.

Toolbar controls are real buttons with names that say what they do — Print this order, Download as PDF — and they wear focus-visible:outline-3 focus-visible:outline-offset-2 focus-visible:outline-zinc-700/15 like everything else. Print is a button, not a link: it changes nothing and goes nowhere.
Nothing on the page is autofocused. The document is there to be read from the top, and an autofocused Print button turns a stray Enter left over from the previous screen into a print job.

components.name: Label sheet
components.description: Labels that come off a printer and get stuck onto things: a bin label on a rack, a batch label on a drum, a pallet tag, a QC hold sticker. Either a grid of them on an A4 sheet of die-cut stock or one at a time on a continuous roll, sized in millimetres because the stock in the printer is.
components.when_to_use: The output is adhesive stock a machine will scan and a person will stick onto something — a rack beam, a drum, a pallet, an incoming carton. The line against document-page is the medium and it is not a matter of degree: a document is A4 paperwork a person reads, signs and files, sized so a clerk can read a tax figure, and its failure is a wrong number; a label is stock a scanner reads, sized to the die-cut in the printer, and its failure is a symbol that will not scan or a sheet that peels two millimetres out of register across a whole shipment. Reach for document-page whenever the artefact carries terms, totals or a signature. Reach for focus-page for the other half of this workflow — the shop-floor screen that scans these labels back in at the gate or the rack, which is a task on a screen and prints nothing. Reach for card when the thing is a bordered panel grouping one region of a screen: a card is furniture measured in rem that reflows with the viewport, and a label is a physical object measured in millimetres that must not reflow at all. The test is whether a millimetre matters. If it does, it is this.
rules: It renders inside app-shell like every other signed-in page, and the shell is chrome. The toolbar, the stock selector, the offset controls and the page heading all carry print:hidden; what is left is the stock. app-shell's own rail and topbar do not carry print:hidden today, which document-page already flagged — a sheet printed from inside the shell as it stands comes out with the navigation down the left of it, and on label stock that lands the navigation across the first column of labels. Closing it is a decision for a person, in app-shell.

The print rules are document-page's and this entry does not restate them: chrome carries print:hidden, backgrounds do not print so nothing may carry meaning in a fill, break-inside-avoid on anything that must not split, and @page is hand-written CSS rather than a utility. Three things a label needs that a sheet of A4 does not are extensions of those, not replacements — the size is exact rather than capped, there is no secondary text colour, and the printer has to be told not to scale.

Every dimension a label has is exact and written in millimetres. 63.5 × 38.1 mm across a 210 mm sheet with a 7.25 mm side margin, a 2.5 mm column gutter and a 15.15 mm top margin is not a layout choice, it is the die-cut in the stock, and the three numbers have to add back to 210.0 or every label in the third column runs off its backing. What may flex is what is inside the label: the type wraps, the description clamps, and a long item name loses its tail. What may not flex is the box. A label sized in rem, in percentages, or as a fraction of its container is a label that is correct on the screen it was designed on and wrong on the stock.

There is no secondary text colour on a label. document-page stops at zinc-600 because zinc-500 is grey mush through an office laser; a thermal printer is worse than an office laser — it is one bit deep, so it has no grey at all and dithers zinc-600 into a checkerboard that at 11px reads as a smudge. Everything printed on a label is zinc-900 and the hierarchy is size and weight. zinc-600 survives in this entry only in the screen chrome, which never reaches the stock.

The label box takes overflow-hidden, which is the class document-page rules out on a document, and the reason the two disagree is the reason for the rule rather than an exception to it. There, overflow other than visible makes an element monolithic in paged media and a long line table is clipped at the first page break instead of splitting across it. Here monolithic is exactly what is wanted: a label that splits across two pages is two half labels on two pieces of stock. The scroller that holds the sheet on screen is the one place the old trap still bites, so it is cancelled with print:overflow-visible — a job of four sheets inside a live scroller prints the first one and stops.

The barcode is not drawn. A scannable Code 128 or QR symbol needs a font or a library and this stack has neither, and a barcode invented out of divs is worse than no barcode: it looks right in a review, it reaches the printer, and it fails at the gate at six in the morning with a lorry behind it. Every variant reserves the symbol's area at its exact printed size, with a border that survives onto the paper, and puts the human-readable value under it in the position a real label puts it. A sheet that comes out with empty ruled boxes on it is obviously wrong and gets caught in the first print; a sheet with a blank gap where a symbol should be looks fine. Whether the library takes a barcode dependency, and in which layer, is a decision for a person.

The human-readable line under the symbol is not a caption, it is the fallback, and it is what somebody keys in when the scanner will not read a scuffed label. So it is never truncated, never smaller than the label's own body size, and it carries the whole identifier. Descriptions truncate; codes do not. That is document-page's rule about identifiers, applied to the one line on the label most likely to be typed by hand.

Alignment is a workflow and not a setting. No printer agrees with anybody's stock on the first try, and the drift is a millimetre or two of feed rather than anything the operator did wrong, so the align variant is a real screen: a registration pattern printed onto the stock, an offset in millimetres in each axis, and a statement of what the operator does with the result. The offset applies on screen as well as on paper, because a preview that does not carry the correction is a preview of a different sheet.

The offset moves the grid with a margin rather than a transform. A transformed element is monolithic in paged media for the same reason an overflowing one is, so a translated grid takes its whole sheet with it and a two-sheet job breaks at the first page. A negative top margin is the one mechanism that shifts a block in both directions without fragmenting it.

The registration marks are drawn with type. A corner mark has to be black to be lined up against a die-cut edge, and the border tokens stop at border-zinc-300, which is about 16% grey and dithers on a thermal printer into something that cannot be registered against anything. document-page hit the same wall and took weight instead of inventing a darker token; this entry takes a plus sign, because a glyph is ink at full strength and needs no token at all. The label outlines beside them stay border-zinc-300 and are the secondary aid, not the mark.

Sheet stock gets part-used. Eight labels come off a sheet on Tuesday and the same sheet goes back in the drawer, so the print on Friday starts at position nine. The skipped positions are rendered as real empty cells and never dropped from the grid — remove them and every label after them moves up one position, which is the whole defect the start position exists to prevent. On screen they carry a bg-zinc-50 fill and their position number so the operator can check the count against the sheet in their hand; on paper they are simply blank, which says the same thing, because the sticker is already gone.

The print dialog has to be told not to help. Scale must be 100% and Fit to page must be off, or a 63.5 mm label comes out at 60.4 mm and no offset will fix it; margins must be None, because the stock's own margins are already in the markup and the dialog will add its own on top. Background graphics stays off, which is why nothing here depends on a fill. None of that is settable from the page and all of it is on the screen next to the Print button, because it is the difference between one wasted sheet and a box of them.

The outer four millimetres or so of a laser page are physically unprintable whatever the margin says. Die-cut stock leaves 7.25 mm at the sides and 15.15 mm top and bottom for exactly that reason, so the labels are safely inside it — but a label design that runs ink to its own edge loses it on the outer column, and a full-bleed label is a thing this stack cannot produce.

There is no h1 on a label. document-page puts the h1 on the paper because a purchase order has a title block; a 38 mm label has room for a location and a symbol and nothing else, so the h1 names what is about to be printed, sits above the stock, and carries print:hidden with the rest of the chrome. It is still exactly one per page.

The values are the server's. Nothing on a label is computed in the browser — not the quantity, not the expiry, not the check digit that a real symbol carries. The Alpine on these variants is in the chrome: the start position, the offset, the quantity, and the count of what will come out.

anatomy.description: The zinc-100 page the stock sits on, so the preview reads as stock on a desk. print:bg-white print:p-0 — on paper there is no desk.
The h1, the count and what stock it is going onto. print:hidden, and it is the only heading on the page.
Stock, quantity, start position, Print and Download PDF, with the dialog settings stated beside them. Sticky on screen, print:hidden, and the only part of the page carrying state.

The sheet at its real size — w-[210mm] with the stock's own px-[7.25mm] py-[15.15mm] — inside an overflow-x-auto print:overflow-visible box. The box is the whole 390px answer: physical size does not reflow, so it scrolls instead.
grid-cols-3 gap-x-[2.5mm] gap-y-0 inside the stock margins, which resolves each column to exactly 63.5 mm. The gutter is the die-cut, not a design gap.
One die-cut position: a fixed h-[38.1mm] box with overflow-hidden and break-inside-avoid, bordered on screen and print:border-0 on paper, where the border is the physical cut.
A reserved box at the symbol's exact printed size with a ruled edge that prints. The substitution point, and the only thing on the label that is not real.
The identifier under the symbol, at label body size, never truncated. What gets keyed in when the scan fails.
A part-used sheet's already-peeled cells: empty, aria-hidden, holding their place in the grid, bg-zinc-50 on screen and blank on paper.

Four plus signs near the corners of every position, drawn in type rather than in rules because a mark that is 16% grey cannot be registered against anything. The offset that produced the sheet is printed with it, absolutely positioned into the stock's bottom margin so it displaces nothing.
Across and down in millimetres, stepped in halves, applied as a margin on the grid so the printed sheet and the preview move together.
Scale 100%, Fit to page off, margins None. Not settable from the page, so it is stated beside the button that opens the dialog.

behaviour: Nothing on a label moves. It has no hover, no disclosure and no tooltip; it is going onto a drum. Everything that moves is in the chrome above the stock.

Print calls window.print() on the sheet already on screen. It does not re-render into a hidden frame — the sheet the operator checked against the stock in their hand is the sheet that has to reach the printer.
Changing the start position redraws the grid with that many empty cells at the front and pushes the same labels down. The count strip and the sheet cannot disagree, because both read the same number.

Changing the quantity changes the number of sheets, and the count says so before the job goes: a hundred labels at a start of nine is five sheets, not four, and the difference is found either here or in the drawer.

The offset applies to the grid on screen and on paper at the same moment. Half a millimetre a press, capped at three, which is as far as the 7.25 mm side margin will absorb before the outer column of labels lands inside the unprintable edge of the page.

The alignment print is one sheet of registration marks and it is meant to be thrown away. The operator holds it against the die-cut stock, reads which way and how far it is out, enters that, and prints one more.

At 390px the stock does not reflow. The sheet keeps its 210 mm and scrolls sideways inside its own box, which is the same exception document-page takes for a line table and taken for the same reason: a preview that rearranged itself to fit a phone is a preview of something that will never come out of the printer. The phone variant is the arrangement that does work in a hand — one label, one printer, one button, and no sheet at all.

A record with no code prints its label with the human-readable line and the symbol area left empty and marked. A symbol generated from an empty string is a valid symbol that scans as nothing, and that failure surfaces at a gate rather than at a desk.
accessibility: One <main> and one <h1>, and the h1 is in the print head above the stock rather than on a label. Regions below it are h2, and on the stock itself there are no headings at all — a label is a record, not a document with an outline.

The sheet is an <ol role="list"> and each position an <li>, so the count and the position are announced. The role is written out because WebKit drops the list role from a list whose list-style is none, and preflight sets that on every ol before anybody writes a class.

Skipped positions are aria-hidden and empty. They exist to hold their place in the grid, and a screen reader that announced eight blank list items before the first real label would be reading the stock rather than the job.
The symbol area is aria-hidden. What it will hold is a picture of the value already written underneath it in text, and the reserved box says nothing to anybody until it is substituted.
The identifier under the symbol is text at full size in the reading order. It is the fallback for a scanner and for a reader alike, and it is the one thing on the label that is never truncated.

The count strip is role="status" so a change of quantity or start position is announced. It is the only live region on the page and it carries one sentence — how many labels, how many sheets, where they start.

The offset fields are real number inputs with the unit in the label rather than in a suffix, so the field is announced as "Across, millimetres" and not as a number with a symbol beside it. Both wear the wrapper focus outline every field in this system wears.
Print is a <button> and Download PDF is an <a> to a server route, named for what they do — Print 21 bin labels, Download as PDF. Print changes nothing and goes nowhere, so it is not a link.
Nothing on the page is autofocused. A stray Enter left over from the previous screen must not be able to start a print job.
