components.name: Portal page
components.description: The screens a supplier signs in to: the orders you have placed with them, the acknowledgement, an invoice against a receipt, what has been paid, and their own details. One vendor is the whole application, and the layout is built to make that visible.
components.when_to_use: A party outside the company — a supplier, a transporter, a contractor — signed in to a URL you gave them, working on the records you share with them and on nothing else. The decision this entry turns on is that it deliberately does not use app-shell, and it is the only signed-in layout in the system that does not, so say what that costs: no command palette, no keyboard shortcuts, no collapsing rail, no nav landmark with thirty destinations under it, no live counts down the side. Every one of those is right for a buyer who is in the console six hours a day and was trained on it for a morning, and every one of them is furniture for a supplier who has four destinations, signs in four times a month, will never be trained, and has three other customers' portals open in other tabs. What replaces the shell is a slim header carrying both company names and four links, and that header is the entire navigation — do not wrap this in app-shell, and do not grow a sidebar onto it later, because the day a portal needs a sidebar it has become a second console and the fix is to take screens away rather than to add chrome. Signing in is auth-page and nothing here reinvents it: the portal reuses that screen with its own next, and a portal that draws a second sign-in form is two credential paths to keep patched and two places to get the timing leak wrong. Against index-page and record-page — those are the internal screens for these same purchase orders, and the portal cannot just show them. They carry the cost centre, the buyer's notes, the approval route, the rate history, the other vendors' quotations against the same enquiry, and a filter band built for a register of 1,438 rows; a supplier has four rows, may see none of that, and does not know the words. Reach for index-page and record-page inside the console and for this outside it, and never for one URL that serves both with the sensitive regions behind a template condition: the queryset behind that page was never scoped, and one missed condition publishes the lot.
rules: This is the one signed-in layout that renders outside app-shell, and the header in the shell variant is the whole of the chrome it replaces. Two things the shell owns still have to exist here and are drawn on the page: the skip link, first in the DOM, and a real <main> landmark for it to reach. The rest of what app-shell carries — the palette, the shortcuts, the rail, the counts — is dropped on purpose, and the test for adding any of it back is whether a supplier who has used the portal twice would find it without being told.

Scope is the security model, and the screen says so rather than looking like a register that happens to be short today. One sentence under the h1 names both parties and states the boundary — this portal holds the orders between Konspec and Gujarat Polymers, and nothing else. It is a sentence and not a filter chip: a chip implies something that can be removed, and this cannot be. The same sentence is what stops a supplier who sees four rows from concluding that the fifth order was lost.

The scoping itself lives in the view and never in the template. Every queryset in the portal starts filtered to the signed-in contact's vendor before anything else touches it, and a template is not allowed to widen it. A template condition is a display rule that a designer will move; a queryset filter is the boundary, and the difference only shows up the first time somebody adds a column.

Two names, one job each. Konspec on the left is the system of record — it says whose numbering, whose terms and whose figures these are. The vendor on the right is the account — it is the check a person makes when they have three customers' portals open and want to know they are typing into the right one. Neither is a logo slot. avatar's rule holds: nothing in this system uploads a picture, an organisation takes rounded-lg where a person takes rounded-full, and a logo arrives at whatever size the vendor emailed it and takes the header height with it.

Their reference sits beside ours on every row and in every heading. PO-2026-0418 means nothing inside Gujarat Polymers; GP/SO/2026/1184 is what their sales office and their accounts clerk search on, and an invoice query that quotes only our number costs a phone call at both ends. It is a column on the list and a line under the heading on every record, and it is theirs to set — the portal shows it back, it does not own it.

No internal vocabulary anywhere on these screens. GRN is a delivery receipt, an indent is nothing they need to hear about, a cost centre is never mentioned, and Approved is meaningless because it does not say approved by whom or what it means for them. The words that survive are the ones a supplier already uses: order, delivery, receipt, invoice, payment. Where a Konspec number has to appear because it will be quoted back — the receipt number, the invoice reference — it is labelled with what it is rather than with what we call it.

The status pill is badge's shape unchanged and the dot keeps its locked colour; what changes is the word, and the word says what the record is doing to them rather than what it is doing to us. Waiting on the supplier is the amber dot, an order running normally is the zinc dot, a delivery past its promised date is the red dot, and a finished one is emerald. The mapping is fixed in the anatomy so two portal screens cannot describe the same state differently.

Each screen does one thing, and the acknowledgement is the proof. It is not the order page with a button on it — it is a page whose whole content is one question, the facts needed to answer it, and the answer. The single most valuable thing a supplier portal does is turn a promised date into a date both sides agreed on, and it does not survive being the fourth control on a record page.

The restricted screen is one screen for two different server answers, and that is the point of it. A record that belongs to another vendor and a record that was never raised return the same page and the same status code, so the URL space cannot be walked to find out which of our suppliers exists or how many orders we place. It says as much in words — this portal answers the same way either way — because a user who is not told that will keep trying.

It keeps the portal header, which is where it parts company with error-page. error-page drops the chrome because there is no working page left to hang it on; here the portal is working perfectly and the header is the supplier's only navigation, so dropping it strands somebody who mistyped a URL with nothing but the browser back button. Everything else about that screen is error-page's: graphite icon well, the status label above the heading, the h1 as a sentence, one primary route back and one human to ask.

A change to the supplier's own details is submitted, not applied. The current value stays on screen as the value in force, and the requested change sits under it in a recessed band saying what was asked for, when, and what has to happen before it takes effect. Applying it optimistically and reverting on rejection is the version that ships fraud: a bank account change is the single most attacked field in any procurement system, so the screen states the verification — a call to the number already on the account — and states that nobody from Konspec will ever ask for that confirmation by email.

An invoice that does not match the receipt is accepted and held, not rejected. Blocking the submit sends the supplier to the telephone and leaves us with no record of what they think they are owed; taking it and holding it puts the disagreement in the system where a buyer can settle it. So the mismatch is stated before the submit, in figures and in days, with the note field beside it already labelled for the explanation.

Sign out is a form POST carrying a CSRF token, never a link. Django's LogoutView has refused GET since 4.1, and a GET sign-out is fired by link prefetchers and by the mail scanners that follow every URL in a notification — the supplier is then signed out by an email nobody has opened.

The phone arrangement is not an afterthought here, and it is a different arrangement rather than a reflow. Suppliers open this on a phone far more often than our own staff open the console on one: the four destinations become a four-across row of labelled tiles under the header instead of a link bar, the list becomes cards ordered by what needs them rather than by date, and the one action on the card that is waiting is a full-width 40px target.

Each variant root here is a bounded preview — h-[640px] with a rounded-xl border — so a whole screen renders in a box on this page. As a real page, drop the wrapper height and border, put bg-zinc-100 on <body>, and let the header stick to the viewport rather than to the wrapper. Ids are prefixed per variant because every variant of this entry renders on one documentation page, and two screens sharing pp-main means the skip link lands on whichever one the parser saw first.

anatomy.description: A single white band: Konspec's mark and name on the left, the vendor's mark, name and signed-in contact on the right, and Sign out as a form POST. Not a topbar — no search, no notifications, no palette trigger.

Four links and no more, in navigation-menu's link-bar shape, with aria-current="page" on the one you are on. Four is the budget: a fifth destination is a screen that should have been merged into one of the four. It appears on the four destinations and not on the two task screens reached from them — a nav bar over a half-answered form is four ways to lose what was typed, and those screens carry a back link instead.
On the acknowledgement and the invoice, above the h1: one route, to the list the task was reached from. It replaces the destination bar rather than joining it.

One sentence under the h1 naming both parties and stating that this is the whole of what the account reaches. Prose, not a chip and not a filter pill, because it describes a boundary rather than a choice.
Our number and the material, their reference, the value, the promised date, and the ask. The ask is the column that makes the screen worth opening.

The status pill plus the one thing we are waiting for, and the link that does it. badge's pill unchanged: bg-zinc-200, ring-zinc-300, zinc-700 text, and only the dot carries the colour — amber waiting on the supplier, zinc running normally, red past the promised date, emerald finished.
A fieldset whose legend is the question in full, two radios, and the follow-up fields under the option that opens them. One question per screen.
On the invoice screen: the receipt value, the invoice value and the difference between them, restated in words as what will happen. Never a blocking validation error.
A bg-zinc-50 band under the value in force, carrying what was asked for, when it was sent, and what has to happen before it applies. The value above it does not move until then.
The named buyer at Konspec with an email address and a direct number. It is the escape hatch for everything the four screens do not do, and it is a person rather than a mailbox.

behaviour: The header is the only navigation on every screen, including the restricted one. Nothing here opens off-canvas, so there is no focus trap to manage and no state to persist.

The order list is not searched, filtered or sorted. Four rows do not need a filter band, and a band that never changes anything teaches a supplier that this portal is the same kind of thing as the console.

The acknowledgement offers two answers. Accepting the promised date submits on its own; proposing a different one reveals a date, a reason and a note, and those controls are disabled while they are hidden so a proposal abandoned halfway is not posted with the acceptance.

The invoice screen compares the amount typed against the value of the receipt it is being raised against, on every keystroke, and states the difference in rupees and the consequence in working days. It never disables the submit.

A change to bank details, tax registration or a contact is submitted for checking. The current value stays in force and on screen; the pending band under it says what was asked and what happens next, and it clears when Konspec accepts or rejects it, never when the page reloads.

The restricted screen renders for a record belonging to another vendor and for a record that does not exist, with the same words and the same status code, so the two cannot be told apart from outside.

Below md the order table is replaced by cards carrying the same fields in the same order, and at 390px the destination bar becomes four labelled tiles. Nothing on any of these screens scrolls sideways.

Every figure is tabular-nums and every rupee amount is grouped the Indian way, because the supplier is reconciling these against their own ledger and a mis-grouped lakh is the sort of thing that gets read as a rate dispute.
accessibility: The skip link is first in the DOM and <main> carries tabindex="-1", because app-shell normally provides both and this layout does not use it. Without the tabindex the fragment scrolls the page and leaves the keyboard at the top of the document.

One <main> and one <h1> per screen, and the h1 names the screen rather than the company — the company is in the header, on every screen, and repeating it as the heading wastes the one landmark a screen-reader user navigates by.

The destination bar is a <nav> with an accessible name and the current destination carries aria-current="page". The tint is what a sighted user sees; the attribute is what everyone else gets, and writing only the tint gives half the users nothing.

The scope sentence is ordinary prose in the document rather than a live region or an alert. It is true on every load and never changes, and a role="status" on a permanent sentence is announced on arrival at every screen.

The acknowledgement is a fieldset whose legend is the whole question, so the question is read once on entry rather than once per arrow key, and the follow-up fields are described by their own message paragraphs with stable ids.

The conditional fields are bound :disabled to the inverse of the condition that shows them. display:none does not remove a control from the POST or from constraint validation, so a hidden required field makes the form unsubmittable with nothing on screen explaining why.
The match line on the invoice screen is pointed at by aria-describedby from the amount field, so the constraint is read when focus lands rather than only being visible beside it.
The restricted screen carries no role="alert". It arrives as a full document load, the <title> states it first, and a live region present at first paint announces nothing anyway.

Both renderings of the order list — the table above md and the cards below it — are in the DOM at once, so neither carries a form control with a name. A display:none input still posts, and two renderings of one row post that row twice.

Every action is a real <a> or <button> with a name that says what it does in the supplier's words — Acknowledge this order, Send your invoice — and wears focus-visible:outline-3 focus-visible:outline-offset-2. No rings anywhere.

components.name: Tabs
components.description: Switches between views of the same record without leaving the page. The panel below changes; the row above is a widget, not a menu, and the keyboard has to know the difference.
components.when_to_use: Two to seven sibling views of one thing — an order and its lines, receipts and history. If the views are unrelated, use the sidebar instead. If each view is its own URL, this is navigation and belongs in the django variant.
rules: role="tab" only when the panel is in this document. If each tab is a URL, it is a nav of links with aria-current="page", and nothing else. Putting role="tab" on a link promises a screen reader that arrows will switch panels and Tab will jump into one, and then neither happens.

A tab carries aria-selected, not aria-current. They look interchangeable and are not: aria-current marks where you are in a set of destinations, aria-selected marks which of several panels is showing.

Exactly one tab in the tab order — the selected one gets tabindex 0, the rest get -1. Without this roving tabindex, Tab walks every tab in the row and the panel is seven presses away, which is the opposite of what the pattern exists to do.
Bind the arrow keys. A tablist without them is a row of buttons that only works with a mouse, whatever the roles say.

Activate automatically only when the panels are already in the page. A tab that fetches uses manual activation, or arrowing from the first tab to the seventh fires seven requests and the user reads whichever one lands last.

Manual activation is not only for tabs that fetch. Any tab whose selection has a consequence somebody has to answer — an unsaved form, a confirmation, a job that starts — moves focus on the arrows and commits on Enter or Space. With automatic activation, walking the row raises a dialog the user never asked for, once per tab crossed.

A button that shares the row with the tabs sits outside role="tablist". Everything inside the list is counted as a member of it, so a print button becomes "tab 4 of 4" to a screen reader, and the roving tabindex takes it out of the tab order on top of that.
Generate the ids with $id(). Static ids look fine until a second copy of the same tab set lands on one page, and then two tabs point aria-controls at one panel and nothing reports an error.

htmx attributes cannot be generated by Alpine. htmx processes an element when it first sees it, and a tab rendered by x-for is not in the document then, so its hx-get is inert and the click does nothing at all. A tab that fetches is written out in the markup — which is also why those variants read the row out of the DOM rather than off an array.
Never wrap the row onto a second line. It scrolls sideways, with the next tab peeking, because a second line of tabs reads as a different control.

Below sm, where the labels genuinely do not fit, a native select is the honest control and a scroller is not. A strip is right for six short nouns; for nine phrases it shows two and gives no sign that there are seven more.
Do not colour the inactive tabs. They are text-zinc-600 and nothing else; the active one is the only one carrying weight.
Counts go in a pill on the tab, not in the label, and the pill is tabular-nums so the row does not jitter when a number changes.

A panel that is its own scroller loses its scroll offset the moment x-show hides it: display:none destroys the scroll position rather than remembering it. Read scrollTop before the switch and write it back after, one offset per tab.
x-cloak on every panel that is not the one showing at first paint, or all of them are visible for the moment before Alpine boots.

anatomy.description: The row itself, holding the arrow-key bindings and a label that says what the set is for.
A button when the panel is in this document, a link when the tab is a URL. The two are not interchangeable.
A 2px zinc-900 underline plus the weight change, and nothing else. Inactive tabs are text-zinc-600.
A tabular-nums pill for a number, a 6px dot for a state. Colour on the dot only, per the status rule, and a word beside it in sr-only text.
The region below, tied to its tab by id in both directions, and focusable so it can be reached when it holds no controls.
A button sharing the row with the tabs — print, export, add — and sitting outside the tablist, because the tablist counts its children as tabs.
The question raised when the panel being left holds unsaved input. Its existence is what makes that tab set activate manually.
The scrolling strip a long row becomes on a narrow screen, with the active tab scrolled into view rather than left off the edge — or, past a certain label length, a select instead of a strip.

behaviour: Only the active tab carries weight and colour. Tinting the inactive ones destroys the one distinction the control exists to make.
Two to seven tabs. Past that the row stops being scannable, and views that numerous are usually unrelated, which makes them sidebar entries.

Left and right arrows move between tabs, Home and End jump to the ends, and Tab leaves the row entirely and lands in the panel. That last one is the whole point of the pattern: seven tabs cost one Tab press, not seven.

Activation is automatic when the panels are local, so an arrow both moves and switches. When a tab fetches its panel or has a question to ask first, the arrow moves focus only and Enter or Space commits, which a native button already does.
The row scrolls rather than wraps, and moving by keyboard brings the tab into view. A focused tab off the edge of the strip is a focus ring nobody can see.
Switching does not reload, so the page keeps the scroll position it had. A panel that scrolls inside itself does not keep its own, and has to be handed its offset back after the switch.
Where the tab is part of the record's address it goes in the query string with replaceState, not pushState, so Back leaves the record instead of undoing a tab.
accessibility: role="tablist" on the row, role="tab" on each control, role="tabpanel" on each region, and an aria-label on the tablist naming the set.
Each tab carries aria-selected and aria-controls; each panel carries aria-labelledby pointing back. Both directions, or the panel is announced without its name.
Roving tabindex: the selected tab is 0, every other tab is -1, so Tab enters the row once and leaves into the panel.
Arrow keys move, Home and End jump, and every one of them calls preventDefault so the page does not scroll underneath.
The panel takes tabindex="0" so it is reachable when it contains nothing focusable, which is most panels made of text.

A count or a state mark belongs inside the tab button, where it joins the accessible name — "Receipts 3, 2 lines short". A coloured dot with no words beside it says nothing to a screen reader, and nothing to a person who cannot separate red from grey.
The reason a tab is unavailable is text under the row, tied to the tab with aria-describedby. A title attribute is not an explanation: there is nothing to hover on a phone, and nothing announces it.
aria-labelledby resolves through an element that is display:none, so a panel can keep pointing at the tab that names it even at a width where the tab row is not drawn at all.

Ids come from $id(), so two tab sets on one page cannot cross-wire their aria-controls. Where the ids have to be static — anywhere htmx reads them — they carry a prefix of their own, because two copies of one variant on a page is how a label ends up bound to the wrong control.

components.name: Breadcrumbs
components.description: The path from the section root down to the record on screen. The last crumb says where you are and is not a link.
components.when_to_use: Any page two or more levels deep. One level deep does not need a trail — it needs a back link, which is the back variant here. A page that is a step in a sequence or a panel over another page is not a location at all, and the sequence variant is what that looks like.
rules: The separator is a slash, always. There is no chevron variant and no icon variant; a trail that reads "Home / Procurement / PO-24-1187" in one file and uses chevrons in another is two components pretending to be one.
The last crumb is plain text with aria-current="page". Making it a link to itself is a dead control, and users click it and get nothing.
Never truncate the last crumb. It is the one that says where you are. Truncate the middle, or collapse it into an overflow menu.
The trail is the information hierarchy, not the browsing history. It does not change based on how the user arrived, so two people on the same record see the same trail.

Where a record has more than one plausible parent — a GRN reachable from the order, from the vendor and from the receipt register — the trail takes the one parent that is the same for everybody and the other routes are written beside it as relationships. A crumb chosen from the referrer is history again, and it is the worst kind: it looks like structure, so it is believed.

A crumb the user may not open is named and not linked. Dropping the level makes the trail claim a depth the record does not have; leaving the link in ships a path whose third step is a 403. The same shape covers a parent that was deleted — the stored label, no href, and one line saying why. Where the label itself is what the permission protects, the crumb reads "Restricted" instead of the name, because naming it leaks exactly the thing that was locked.

Only the levels the route already proves get a placeholder while the record is fetched. A GRN URL proves there is a register above it and a section above that, so those two can wait as bars. Nothing proves how many levels sit above a search result, and guessing draws a trail that is a different length when it lands.

A step in a sequence is not a level, and neither is a dialog. Steps are not addressable, they hold unsaved input, and a crumb promises a page that can be bookmarked and reloaded. The trail on a wizard names the page the wizard is; the step count sits with the title.
Crumbs are not underlined, unlike every other link in the system. Five underlined links in a row is a fence, not a path; the muted colour and the hover carry it instead.

anatomy.description: A <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"> holding an ordered list, because the order is the information and a screen reader needs to be able to skip it.
A link to an ancestor page, text-zinc-600, darkening to zinc-900 on hover.
A zinc-500 slash. Decorative and aria-hidden, so it is never read aloud. zinc-400 is the on-dark step of the text scale and is a shade too light for a mark on white.
Plain text in zinc-900 font-medium, never a link, carrying aria-current="page".
The collapsed middle of a long trail: an ellipsis button and, behind it, a nested ordered list of the levels it hides.
An h-2.5 bg-zinc-200 bar in a one-line box, standing where a label will land that the fetch has not returned yet. Not a link, and aria-hidden, so nothing tabs into a grey rectangle.
A level that exists in the hierarchy but not for this user: the label in zinc-500 behind a lock icon, no href, and the reason written on the page under the trail.
The other records this one belongs to, under the trail and labelled — ordinary underlined links, so nothing there is mistaken for a level.
Anything that belongs to the record rather than the page — a status pill, a copy-id button. They sit outside the <ol> entirely, beside the nav, never inside the last <li>.

behaviour: The last crumb is the current page and is not a link. A link to the page you are on is a dead control.
The last crumb is never truncated or collapsed — it is the one that says where you are.
A long trail collapses its middle into an overflow menu rather than wrapping onto two lines.
Below sm the trail collapses to the parent and the current page. Four crumbs at 390px either wrap or push the page sideways, and both are worse than showing two.
The trail reflects the hierarchy, not the history, so it does not change based on how the user arrived.
Crumb labels match the titles of the pages they point at, so following one is not a surprise.

While the parents are in flight, everything the page already knows is drawn for real — the root, and the record number that came out of the URL. Only the labels that are actually waiting are bars, and the trail reflows when they land while the title under it does not move.
A crumb with no href is inert to the pointer and to the keyboard. It does not hover, it does not focus, and it is not a tab stop, because there is nowhere for it to go.
When the page content is swapped without a page load, the trail is swapped with it. A trail left behind by an htmx swap is wrong and silent about it, which is worse than a trail that is missing.
accessibility: A <nav> with aria-label="Breadcrumb", so assistive technology can identify it and skip past it.
An ordered list inside, because the sequence carries the meaning.
Separators are aria-hidden, or a screen reader reads "slash" between every crumb.
The current page carries aria-current="page" — that, not the styling, is what announces it.
The overflow button has an aria-label naming how many levels it hides, because an ellipsis says nothing on its own.

The overflow panel is a list of links and carries no role="menu". role="menu" promises the menu keyboard model — arrows between items, Home and End, one tab stop for the set — and a panel of plain anchors delivers none of it. Links in a list are already navigable; take the role and the browser stops treating them as links.

Crumb links declare the same focus outline as every other control in the system: focus-visible:outline-3 focus-visible:outline-offset-2 focus-visible:outline-zinc-700/15. The trail is often the first thing under the skip link, so it is the first place a keyboard lands on a record page, and leaving it to the user agent means the indicator changes between browsers on the one control that is guaranteed to be reached by keyboard.

While the trail is loading, aria-busy sits on the <nav> and the placeholder crumbs are aria-hidden, with one sr-only role="status" naming the record outside them. Read out, a bar is an empty list item, and three of them is a trail that appears to have lost its labels.
A crumb that is not a link says so in text — an sr-only clause after the label — rather than in the lock icon, which is aria-hidden, or in the grey, which is not announced at all.

components.name: Menubar
components.description: A row of menus across the top of a document — File, Edit, View — sharing one tab stop and one keyboard model. A desktop-application affordance, and most internal screens should not have one.
components.when_to_use: A document-shaped screen with a genuine File / Edit / View set of commands that will not fit in a toolbar: a purchase-order editor, a BOM editor, a rate-contract sheet, a report designer — something somebody sits inside for an hour and edits. Almost nothing else. A register, a dashboard or a list has no document and no File menu; what those need is a topbar carrying the page actions and a dropdown of row actions per record, and painting a menubar over them dresses a CRUD screen up as an application it is not. The test is blunt: if you cannot fill three menus with commands that already exist, you do not have a menubar, you have four buttons pretending.
rules: Reach for this last, not first. A menubar is the right control when the screen is a document and the command set is large enough that a toolbar would need a second row — a purchase-order editor with fifteen line-level commands, a BOM editor, a report designer. It is the wrong control on a register, a dashboard, a settings page or anything whose verbs are Filter, Export and New: there a topbar plus a per-row dropdown says the same thing with a third of the machinery and none of the keyboard model. Fitted to a list screen it costs a tab stop, a hover model and eight roles to hide four buttons that were fine where they were.

dropdown owns the single menu behind a trigger; this owns the persistent bar of them, and the line between them is not the panel. The panels are near enough the same markup. What differs is who owns the keyboard: a dropdown is one trigger, one tab stop and one Escape, so a register can hold twelve of them and none of them knows the others exist. A menubar is one widget wearing several panels — Left and Right belong to the bar rather than to any menu, hovering a sibling switches which panel is up without a click, and Escape hands focus back to the title you came in through rather than to the page. Build a bar out of dropdowns and you get a row of independent controls standing in a line: five tab stops, no arrow keys between them, a click for every menu, and no styling makes it read as one thing. Go the other way and a menubar of one is a lie told to a screen reader — a single trigger with a panel is a dropdown, which is why the collapsed variant here sheds the menubar roles rather than keeping a bar with one item in it.

The whole bar is one tab stop, not one per menu. Every trigger takes tabindex="-1" except the one the roving focus is currently on, which takes 0. Skip this and a five-menu bar costs five Tab presses to walk past on the way to the document underneath it, on top of the thirty controls already in the form — which is the precise opposite of why the pattern exists. Tab enters the bar once, Left and Right walk the triggers, Down opens, and the next Tab leaves.

Open on hover, but only once a menu is already open. Cold hover-opening a menubar means a pointer travelling diagonally from the sidebar to the first field of the form drops a panel over the document on the way past, and the user has to click somewhere harmless to get rid of it. Once something is open the bar is in menu mode and hovering a sibling switches to it without a click, because that is how the user got a menu open in the first place and clicking each one is tedious. The state that gates it is the open menu itself, so there is no timer and nothing to tune.

When the open menu changes, move focus before the old panel is hidden. Hiding an element that contains document.activeElement drops focus onto <body>, and the next Tab restarts at the top of the document — usually the skip link, occasionally the browser chrome. Every path that changes which menu is open (Left, Right, typeahead, hover-switch) focuses the new trigger synchronously in the handler and only then writes the new open id, which Alpine flushes afterwards. Focus is on a visible element the whole time.

role="menubar" is not navigation. A row of links to other pages is a <nav> of anchors, whatever it looks like — the menu roles promise a command model where arrow keys walk items, Escape closes and Enter fires an action against the thing on screen, and a link that navigates away honours none of that. Put menuitem on a set of links and a screen reader announces a menu of commands and then the first one leaves the page. That control is navigation-menu; this one is for commands.

Disabled items stay in the walk. They take aria-disabled="true" and keep tabindex="-1", never the disabled attribute — a disabled button is not focusable and drops out of the query the arrow keys read the item order from, so the third press of Down lands on Duplicate line in one document and Delete line in another depending on whether there was anything to undo. A menubar is learned by position; commands that come and go destroy that. The item is also where the reason belongs: put "Nothing to undo" in the hint column where the shortcut would go, and the greyed row explains itself instead of being a dead end.

A shortcut hint is aria-keyshortcuts, and the glyphs beside it are decoration. The visible column reads ⌘S or Ctrl S because that is what the user has to press; the attribute takes the formal syntax — aria-keyshortcuts="Control+S" — because that is what assistive technology parses and surfaces in its own shortcut list. Leave the glyphs in the accessible name and the item announces as "Save, command S" with the ⌘ read as whatever the synthesiser makes of an unmapped codepoint, so aria-hidden the span and let the attribute carry it. And the attribute is a claim: if nothing on the page listens for Control+S, do not write it.

Escape closes the panel, returns focus to the trigger, and stops there. The handler is guarded on the open state and calls stopPropagation only when it actually closed something, so a second Escape does nothing here and passes through to whatever is outside — the dialog or the sheet the editor is sitting in. Without the guard the bar silently eats every Escape on the screen, and the only way out of the dialog is the mouse.

Panels are x-cloak and z-40, and no ancestor may be overflow-hidden. Wrapping the editor card in overflow-hidden to keep its corners tidy clips every panel to the height of the bar, and the menu opens as a one-pixel sliver that looks like it failed to load. The panels also cannot be overflow-hidden themselves once anything flies out of them, so the rounded corner is protected by the panel's own py-1 instead: an item that never touches the corner never pokes a square tint through it.

Toggling closes, choosing closes, ticking does not. An action item and a radio item both finish a decision the moment they are pressed, so both close the menu and hand focus back to the trigger. A checkbox item does not: nobody opens View to show exactly one column, and a menu that shuts after each tick has to be reopened four times to do one job. Focus stays on the item and aria-checked changes underneath it, which is announced because the item is the focused element.

Below md it collapses to a single Menu button, and it stops being a menubar when it does. A wrapped bar is not a menubar — the second row reads as a separate control and Left and Right no longer match what the eye sees. The collapsed form drops role="menubar" entirely and becomes one button with one role="menu" panel, sections divided by role="group" labels, because a bar with one item in it is a lie told to a screen reader. Both forms are rendered from the same list in the template; maintained as two hand-written copies they drift within a sprint. The panels below md are a separate problem with a separate answer: give each menu wrapper relative max-md:static so that on a phone the panel anchors to the bar instead of to a trigger halfway along it. Anchor it to the trigger and the fourth menu opens 100px off the right of a 390px screen; anchor the last one right-0 to fix that and the first one hangs off the left.

One reason for one row, one reason for a whole menu, and they are different treatments. A single unavailable command among four says why in its own hint column, because the rows around it are fine and the question is about that one. A menu where every command is unavailable for the same reason — the order is approved, the GRN is posted — puts the reason on the role="group" instead: announced once as focus enters it, drawn once above the rows, and the rows left carrying nothing but their labels. Repeating a date on eight rows is the version that looks thorough, and it fills the hint column with the same sentence until nothing in the panel is scannable. A menu with nothing live in it also needs one live item — Raise amendment, Request reopen — or the user has learned only that they cannot proceed.

An item that acts on a selection puts the count in its label and never on the trigger. The panel opens over the grid, so at the moment the label is read the ticked rows are underneath it, and "Delete 3 lines" is the only place the number can still be seen. Bind it: written once it says three the next time the menu is opened with five rows ticked, and the label is the accessible name, so the announcement is wrong as well as the text. On the trigger it is worse than wrong — a title that grows from Lines to Lines (3) shifts every menu to the right of it while the pointer is resting on one, and the bar whose positions the user learned is a different bar after every tick.

A destructive command closes the menu before it asks, and the order is load-bearing. close() first, so focus is on the trigger and the bar's tab stop is on the menu the command came out of; then the dialog, so x-trap captures a node that will still be focusable when it restores. Open the dialog first and the trap memorises a menu item x-show is about to hide, and Cancel drops the user on <body>. This is also the variant that pays for the Escape guard: because the bar only swallows Escape when it actually has a menu open, the dialog it just opened can still be dismissed from the keyboard.

Permission decides whether an item exists; the record's state decides whether it is disabled. A command this user will never be allowed to run is not rendered — a permanently greyed Void order is a tease, and it also tells them which powers somebody at the next desk has. A command they may run but not yet is rendered, disabled and carrying the reason, because that one comes back. The consequence is that a menu can empty out, so the permission check goes around the whole menu wrapper and not just its items: a title that opens an empty panel is a stop on the arrow walk that does nothing. For the same reason the roving tab stop is rendered rather than hard-coded — at: 'file' on a bar whose File menu was dropped leaves no trigger holding tabindex="0", and Tab walks straight past the bar.

A sticky bar pins to the page, never to a scrolling box. An absolutely positioned panel is clipped by the nearest scrolling ancestor, so putting the scroll on the card to keep the bar in view clips every menu to the height of the bar — the same failure as overflow-hidden, reached by a more reasonable-looking route. Let the page scroll and the panels hang free. If the region genuinely has to scroll on its own, the bar goes above it rather than sticky inside it. Sticky also brings a z order that has to be decided rather than discovered: the bar above the rows, the table head below the bar, the panels above both, and nothing else in the document above the bar — and because a sticky element with a z-index opens a stacking context, the panels are only ever as high against the page as the bar is.

Do not let the menubar be the only route to a command. Save lives in File as an accelerator for the people who learn it, and the Save button at the foot of the form is the one everybody else presses. A command reachable only from a menu on a screen that also has a toolbar has been hidden, not organised, and the first support call is somebody insisting the feature was removed.

anatomy.description: The role="menubar" strip itself, holding the roving-focus state, the typeahead buffer and which menu is open. It is the strip and nothing else — anything in the same row that is not a menu, a status or a Save button, sits outside it.

A button with role="menuitem" and aria-haspopup="menu". One of them carries tabindex="0" and the rest -1. While its menu is open it takes the bg-zinc-200 tint, because focus has moved into the panel and the trigger has no focus ring left to say which menu you are in. The open tint carries hover:bg-zinc-300 with it: hover: beats a plain fill whichever order they are written in, so without it the ordinary hover:bg-zinc-100 washes the tint back down — and in menu mode the pointer is on the open trigger by definition, which makes the one menu that is open the one that looks least engaged.

Absolutely positioned under its own trigger, z-40, x-cloak, role="menu" and named with the trigger's own word. Always left-0: the containing block is what changes on a phone, because the menu wrapper is relative max-md:static and the panel then anchors to the bar rather than to a trigger halfway along it.
A full-width button, role="menuitem", tabindex="-1", icon left of the label so the labels form one reading column. Real focus moves item to item; nothing here uses aria-activedescendant.

A right-aligned 12px zinc-500 column, aria-hidden, with the real claim carried by aria-keyshortcuts on the item. Also where the reason goes on a disabled item, which is not aria-hidden because it is the explanation.

role="menuitemcheckbox" and role="menuitemradio" with aria-checked bound, a fixed size-4 marker slot on the left so the labels stay aligned whether ticked or not, and radios wrapped in a role="group" that names the choice.

A second panel flying out of an item that carries aria-haspopup and aria-expanded of its own. One level deep, never two, and below md it drops beneath its trigger instead of flying off the side of the screen.

The one line a whole menu shares when every command in it is unavailable for the same reason: carried by the role="group" aria-label and drawn once above the rows as an aria-hidden line. It replaces the per-row hint rather than joining it, and the group under it holds the one item that is still live.

An item label carrying the count it will act on, bound to the selection and not written. It reads "Duplicate lines" with nothing ticked, when the item is also aria-disabled with the reason in the hint column.

An alert dialog inside the component root and outside the role="menubar", raised only after the menu has closed and focus has landed back on its trigger. Naming the record and the consequence in figures, with the verb on the button.
The single Menu button the whole bar becomes below md. Not a menubar of one — a plain menu whose sections are role="group" carrying the names the triggers used to have.

behaviour: Tab enters the bar once and the next Tab leaves it. Left and Right walk the triggers and wrap, Home and End jump to the ends, Down opens the menu onto its first item and Up opens it onto its last.
Once a menu is open, hovering a sibling trigger switches to it with no click. From cold, hovering a trigger does nothing at all — the bar only enters menu mode when somebody asks it to.

Left and Right from inside an open panel walk the bar rather than the items: the current menu closes, the next one opens, and focus lands on its trigger. It is the same gesture whether a panel is open or not, which is what makes it learnable, and Down enters the panel that is now open.
Escape closes the panel and leaves focus on the trigger. Escape again does nothing and is not swallowed, so it reaches the dialog or sheet the editor may be sitting inside.

Typing a letter on the bar moves to the trigger whose label starts with it, and keeps moving as more letters arrive inside half a second. The typeahead belongs to the bar only — inside an open panel the same keys do nothing, because the item list is short and reading it is faster than guessing at it.
Choosing an action closes the menu and returns focus to the trigger. Ticking a checkbox item leaves the menu open and focus on the item, because View is opened to change three columns and not one.

Disabled items keep their place and their keyboard position, and say why in the column where the shortcut would be. Nothing is removed from a menu because the document is in the wrong state; the map stays the same shape.
Tab from inside a panel closes the menu and continues from the trigger, so the focus order after the bar is the document, not the third item of the File menu.

A destructive item does not act on the press. The menu closes, focus lands back on its trigger, and an alert dialog names the record and the consequence. Escape then reaches the dialog rather than the bar, because the bar only takes Escape while it has a menu open.

An item that acts on a selection says how much it will act on, keeps its place when nothing is selected, and explains itself there in the column where the shortcut would go. The bar itself never carries the count.
A sticky bar pins to the top of the page and not to the top of a scrolling box, because a scrolling ancestor clips every panel to the height of the bar.
Below md the bar collapses to one Menu button. It does not wrap, it does not scroll sideways, and it stops carrying menubar roles when it stops being a bar.
accessibility: The strip is role="menubar", each trigger is a button with role="menuitem" and aria-haspopup="menu", and aria-expanded is bound to whether that menu is the open one. The panel is role="menu" and each row role="menuitem", menuitemcheckbox or menuitemradio.

Exactly one trigger is in the tab order at a time: tabindex="0" on the one roving focus is on, -1 on the rest. This is the same roving tabindex a tablist uses and for the same reason — the set is one widget, so it is one stop.

Focus is real focus, moved trigger to trigger and item to item. This is where a menu and a combobox part company: a combobox keeps focus in its text box and points at a row with aria-activedescendant, but a menuitem is the thing being operated, so it has to be the thing focused. It also means no path may ever hide a panel while focus is still inside it.

Each panel is named with aria-label carrying the trigger's own word rather than aria-labelledby pointing at the trigger, because ids on a component that can appear twice on one page cross-wire, and the label is one word either way.

Shortcuts are declared with aria-keyshortcuts in its formal syntax — Control+S, Shift+Control+Z — and the visible glyph column is aria-hidden so it does not join the accessible name. An item announces as "Save" with the shortcut exposed as a property, not as "Save command S".

Disabled items use aria-disabled="true" and stay focusable. The disabled attribute would take them out of the tab-free arrow walk as well as out of the pointer, which changes the position of every item below them.

Checkbox and radio items carry aria-checked bound to the state, never written once in markup, and a set of radio items is wrapped in role="group" with an aria-label naming the choice. A visible group heading inside a menu is aria-hidden, because a bare paragraph is not a permitted child of role="menu" and the group is already named.

When every item in a menu is unavailable for one reason, the reason belongs on the role="group" holding them and not on each row. A group is named as focus enters it, so it is announced once on the way in; the same sentence on eight rows is announced eight times, and the label a user is listening for arrives at the end of each one.

An item label that depends on the selection is bound, never written once, because it is the accessible name. A stale label announces a command against a number of rows that is not the number of rows it will touch, and the item that announces "Delete 3 lines" and deletes 5 is the worst version of this component there is.

Anything in the same strip that is not a menu — a save indicator, a Submit button — sits outside the role="menubar" element. A non-menuitem child of a menubar is either dropped from the announced item count or reported as one of the menus, and both are worse than a plain button beside the bar.

components.name: Navigation menu
components.description: A horizontal bar of links to places, some of which open a panel of more links. Every item is an anchor, so the browser's own navigation gestures keep working, and aria-current says which one you are on.
components.when_to_use: The top-level route map of an application that has more sections than a sidebar can hold at once — Procurement, Inventory, Reports — where a section is worth showing as a panel of its pages rather than a single link. If the items are commands that act on the document in front of you, that is a menubar. If there is one trigger and one list of actions behind it, that is a dropdown. The test is whether an item has a URL: a set of URLs is navigation and belongs here, and anything without one does not.
rules: Every item that goes somewhere is an <a href>. This is the whole component and it is the thing that gets built wrong: a navigation menu assembled out of role="menu" and <button>s looks identical on screen and throws away middle-click, Ctrl-click, Open in new tab, Copy link address, the status bar preview, and the browser's own history — every affordance a link gets for free and none of which you can put back. It also tells a screen reader that arrow keys drive the thing and that Tab will step over it in one press, and then neither is true. If it has a URL it is an anchor, and no amount of ARIA makes a button into one.

The panel is a plain container holding a <ul> of links. It is not role="menu" and its links are not role="menuitem". Those roles are a promise that the contents are commands, that the arrows move between them and that the whole panel is one tab stop; a panel of links is none of those, and applying them makes NVDA and VoiceOver stop announcing "link" for things that are links, which is the one word the user needed.

The trigger is a <button>, because it does not navigate — it reveals. aria-expanded belongs on a control that opens something and is a lie on a link, where a reader told "collapsed" presses Enter and leaves the page. The section that the trigger appears to name still needs a route, so the first link inside the panel is the section overview — All of Procurement — and the trigger loses nothing by not being a link itself.

Two delays, and they are different lengths for different reasons. Opening waits about 140ms so a pointer travelling across the bar toward something else does not flash three panels on the way. Closing waits about 280ms so the pointer can leave the trigger, cross the gap and land in the panel without the panel disappearing underneath it — it is off both elements for a frame or two in between. Drop the open delay and the bar strobes; drop the close delay and the panel can be seen but never reached.

Once a panel is open, crossing to a sibling trigger swaps instantly and skips the open delay. The delay exists to filter out a pointer that is passing through, and a pointer already inside an open menu is not passing through — it is reading the bar. Keep the delay in that state and moving between two sections feels like the bar is arguing with you.

The gap between the bar and the panel is padding on the positioned wrapper, never a margin on the panel. A margin is dead space belonging to nothing, so the pointer leaves the component halfway across it and the close timer starts. And the panel drops flush under the bar, full width, so the shortest route from a trigger to it is straight down — indent the panel or offset it sideways and the route becomes a diagonal, the diagonal passes over the next trigger, and that trigger takes the pointer. The cheap fix is the geometry; the expensive one is a safe-triangle hit test, and this system does not want the second. Keep the panel a DOM descendant of the nav while you are at it — mouseleave accounts for an element and its descendants in the tree rather than its box, so a panel inside the nav never fires the nav's mouseleave no matter where it is painted, and a panel portalled to the body to escape a clipping ancestor fires it the instant the pointer arrives.

Tab reaches every trigger. This is the line between this and a menubar: a menubar is one widget and takes one tab stop with a roving tabindex inside it, and a navigation bar is a list of destinations that a keyboard user has to be able to walk. Give this a roving tabindex and Tab jumps the entire route map in one press, which is the opposite of what a route map is for.

Focus leaving the whole component closes the panel, and the only way to detect that is @focusout on the root with a containment check on relatedTarget, because blur does not bubble and focusout does. relatedTarget is the element about to receive focus, so !$el.contains($event.relatedTarget) is the question "did focus land outside me". It is null when focus leaves the document entirely — the address bar, another window — and contains(null) is false, so that case closes too, which is correct. Bind blur instead and nothing fires; skip the check and the panel closes while the user is tabbing through its own links.

Guard the hover handlers with matchMedia('(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)'). A tap on a touch screen fires a synthetic mouseenter and then a click, so an unguarded bar opens the panel on the mouseenter and closes it again on the click, and the section is unreachable by tapping it. The click path has to be the whole story on touch.

aria-current="page" marks the exact page and nothing else; the trigger of the section you are inside takes aria-current="true", which means the current item of a set. They are not interchangeable and a trigger with page on it claims to be a page it has no URL for. aria-selected has no business here at all — that word belongs to a tab, which switches a panel in this document rather than moving you somewhere.

Nav items are not underlined, which is the documented exception to the interactive-text rule and the same exception breadcrumbs take. A row of underlined links reads as a fence rather than a bar; the tint on the current item and the hover carry it instead. Inside a panel the links stay unadorned for the same reason — twelve underlined lines in three columns is a grid of rules.

A destination the user cannot reach is not one grey row with one meaning — there are two reasons for it and they want two treatments. A page closed by the state of the record or the period — a rate contract during the price revision, a GRN while the store is frozen for counting — is one the user opens most days, so it stays an anchor with its href, takes aria-disabled, and points at the reason with aria-describedby. Dropping the href instead makes it unfocusable and the reason unreachable by keyboard. A page refused by permission is not a link at all, because there is no URL this user may follow: a lock, the name and who owns it, out of the tab order and still in the reading order. And the default for a permission refusal is to leave the row out altogether — keep it only where its absence reads as the menu being broken.

When the panel's links are scoped to a plant, a company or a financial year, say so once at the head of the panel and put the scope in the path rather than only in the session. Scope held in the session is shared by every tab: switching plant in the second one silently changes the first, which goes on showing a bar that is now lying about where it points. A path segment makes each tab answer for itself, and it is what makes Copy link address produce a URL that still means the same thing tomorrow. Counts in the panel are scoped by the same rule, and a count that moves when the plant changes reads as data going missing unless the scope is written where the user has already looked.

When the page on screen is not one of the menu's own items — a record, a filtered register, a step of a wizard — nothing in the menu takes aria-current="page". The section trigger and the deepest panel link that contains the page both take aria-current="true", which is legal together because aria-current is scoped to a set and the bar and the panel are two sets. Naming the record is the breadcrumb's job, and a menu that grows an entry for whatever is open changes shape as the user browses and stops being a map.

Which side a narrow panel opens on is decided in the markup, not measured at open. right-0 on the wrapper of the last trigger is the whole fix; measuring means laying the panel out before it is visible and reading its width back, and the first open near the viewport edge is the one that jumps. A panel too wide for either alignment is anchored to the nav at w-full instead of being nudged sideways, because the nudge turns the pointer's route into a diagonal that crosses the neighbouring trigger.

At 390px this is not a hover bar and must not try to be one. There is no hover to open with, four section names do not fit on one line, and a floating panel over a phone screen needs a dismiss affordance a bar does not have. Ship the disclosure list instead, sm:hidden against hidden sm:block, and accept that they are two pieces of markup rather than one that flexes.

anatomy.description: The <nav aria-label> holding the open state, the two timers, and the mouseleave, focusout, escape and click-outside handlers. It is the common parent of every trigger and every panel, which is the only place that can tell "left the trigger" from "left the component".
An <a href> straight to a page, with aria-current="page" when it is that page. No panel, no chevron, no state of its own.
A <button> carrying aria-expanded and aria-controls. It looks exactly like a link item apart from the chevron, and the chevron is the only signal that anything is behind it.
pt-2 on the positioned wrapper. The strip the pointer crosses on its way down, and it belongs to the component so crossing it is not leaving.
A white rounded-xl bordered surface below the bar, z-40, holding a <ul> of links. Not a role="menu", not focus-trapped, and not scrollable — if it needs to scroll it needs to be a page.
A real <h3> above each column, 11px uppercase zinc-600. It is a heading and not a styled div, because jumping by heading is how a screen reader reads a panel of thirty links.
A 12px zinc-600 line under the link label, inside the anchor so the whole block is the target. Six words at most: it joins the accessible name and is read out every time.

A zinc-100 block at the head of a panel naming the plant, company or year every link below it points at, with a link to where that is changed. It states the scope; it never switches it, because switching reloads every count and every open record and that belongs to the topbar.

A row that cannot be opened. Closed by application state it stays an anchor with aria-disabled and a reason bound by aria-describedby; refused by permission it is not an anchor at all, and most of the time it is not in the list.

An optional zinc-100 block at the head of the panel holding one promoted destination — a recently opened record. It is first in the DOM only when it is genuinely the most likely next click, because DOM order is keyboard order.

behaviour: Hover opens after about 140ms and closes about 280ms after the pointer has left the trigger and the panel together. Coming back inside during the close delay cancels it, so a pointer that overshoots the panel edge and returns finds it still there.
With a panel already open, moving to another trigger swaps immediately. Only the first panel of a pass costs the open delay.

Clicking a trigger opens the panel and moves focus onto its first link. That is what makes Enter and Space work with nothing bound to them, because a native button turns both into a click, and it costs a mouse user nothing since focus-visible does not paint for a pointer.

Down on a trigger opens the panel and lands on the first link. Inside the panel there are no arrow keys at all — Tab walks the links, because they are links. Arrow navigation inside would be the one thing that makes it feel like a menu, and it is deliberately absent.
Escape closes the open panel and returns focus to the trigger it belongs to, and it stops propagating so it does not also close the dialog the bar happens to be inside.
Focus leaving the component closes the panel; clicking outside closes it without moving focus, because the user has already put focus somewhere by clicking.
One panel at a time falls out of holding a single id on the root rather than a boolean per item. There is nothing to keep in sync and no way to reach a state with two panels open.

A panel that is fetched is fetched on open, not on mouseenter, and once — the hover delay exists precisely so that dragging a pointer across the bar does not fire three requests. A failed fetch leaves the flag unset so the next open retries.

A link closed by application state keeps its href and refuses the click, and the view refuses it as well. @click.prevent stops a click and nothing else — Ctrl-click, Copy link address and the address bar never see the attribute, so the lock is the server and the attribute is advice to the person reading.
At 390px the bar is replaced, not reflowed: a stack of disclosure sections, several of which can be open at once, because collapsing one section as another opens moves every link under the thumb.
accessibility: Destinations are <a href> and nothing else. Middle-click, Ctrl-click, Open in new tab and the browser's status-bar preview all come from the element being an anchor, and none of them can be reimplemented on a button.
The panel is a plain container of links, not role="menu". Those roles change what a screen reader announces and what it promises about the keyboard, and both promises are false here.

The trigger is a button with aria-expanded bound to the open state and aria-controls pointing at the panel; the panel points back with aria-labelledby, so it is announced with the name of the section it belongs to rather than as an unnamed group.
Every trigger is in the tab order. A roving tabindex is correct for a menubar and wrong here: it would collapse the whole route map into one tab stop.
aria-current="page" on the exact page and aria-current="true" on the trigger of the section you are inside. The tint is the visual echo of the attribute, never the state itself.
Escape closes and hands focus back to the trigger, so the keyboard does not end up on a hidden element or dumped on the body.
Column headings are real <h3> elements so a panel of thirty links can be read by heading instead of link by link.

aria-labelledby needs a role to land on. The panel wrapper is a <div>, and a div with no role is generic, which browsers refuse to give an accessible name to — so the wrapper carries role="group" and the trigger's name reaches it. Without the role the attribute parses, validates and does nothing.

Nothing carries aria-current="page" when the page on screen is not in the menu. The trigger of the section takes aria-current="true" and so does the panel link the page sits under, one per set, and the record itself is named by the breadcrumb rather than added to the menu.

A row refused by permission is not a link and is not focusable, because there is nothing there to do. A row closed by application state is a link with aria-disabled, and it stays focusable precisely so the sentence saying why is one tab stop away rather than nowhere.
Focus is an outline with an offset, never a ring, and nothing here writes outline-none. Inside a panel the links are far enough from the edge for a positive offset to sit clear of the border.
